es.title: Español
es.guide: Espagnol d'Espagne (castillan), standard et naturel, tel qu'on le parle à Madrid. On enseigne vosotros (Espagne) et on signale, quand c'est utile, l'usage d'Amérique latine (ustedes, vocabulaire) en simple remarque. Les explications sont en français, par contraste avec le français : ce qui est pareil, où un francophone se trompe (ser/estar, por/para, subjonctif après cuando, faux amis, accent écrit). Orthographe espagnole complète : accents écrits, ñ, ¿ ? et ¡ ! ouvrants. Aucune notion de grammaire avant la leçon où elle est étudiée (vérifier les g et b des leçons précédentes). Sujets du quotidien, pas de politique clivante, pas de paroles de chansons, pas de marques.

he.builtin: Cours d'hébreu : le programme (champ plan, JSON) commence par l'alef-bet (niveau A0) ; une leçon correspond au document lessons/<id>.
he.desc: From the alef-bet to B1: first you learn to read, then to speak, 20 minutes a day.
he.name: hébreu
he.title: Ivrit
he.guide:
Hébreu moderne israélien, prononciation israélienne standard. Niqqud (voyelles) : TOUJOURS complet dans le vocabulaire, à tous les niveaux. Aux niveaux A0 et A1, tout l'hébreu (exemples, exercices, dialogues) a le niqqud complet ; à partir de A2, les phrases peuvent être sans niqqud, sauf les mots nouveaux. Translittération : dans chaque traduction française (vocab, dlg, paires « p »), ajoute la prononciation entre crochets à la fin : « bonjour [shalom] ». Système simple : sh, kh (ח et כ sans point), ts (צ), ch n'est jamais employé, ' entre deux voyelles pour א/ע (me'od), e, a, i, o, u pour « ou ». Exercices « f » : réponse en hébreu avec niqqud, puis la translittération en variante : "שָׁלוֹם|shalom". Un exercice « f » de lecture peut aussi demander la translittération seule (« Comment se lit שָׁלוֹם ? ___ » → "shalom"). Exercices « o » : la phrase en hébreu, mots séparés par des espaces, sans variante. Exercices « m » : en A0, beaucoup de questions de lecture (quelle lettre fait tel son, comment se lit tel mot, quel mot veut dire…). Genre : l'hébreu distingue tu masculin et tu féminin, et le présent s'accorde en genre et en nombre ; donne toujours les deux formes (m. / f.) dans le vocabulaire et les explications. Pas de verbe être au présent (אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט). Au niveau A0 (alef-bet), n'emploie que les lettres déjà vues dans les leçons précédentes et celles du jour, comme l'indiquent les consignes de la leçon ; un mot très courant qui contient d'autres lettres est signalé « mot à reconnaître ». Dans les explications HTML, mets chaque mot ou phrase en hébreu dans … (il s'affiche alors de droite à gauche) ; dans
, la phrase hébraïque est dans . Les tableaux de lettres ont une colonne lettre, une colonne nom, une colonne son. Prénoms et lieux israéliens (Noa, Avi, Maya, Tel Aviv, Haïfa, Jérusalem). Sujets du quotidien ; aucun sujet politique ou religieux clivant.

it.builtin: Dix leçons embarquées dans la page, d'identifiants 0 à 9, réutilisées dans le programme via le champ use. Le programme (champ plan, JSON) liste niveaux, unités et leçons ; une leçon sans use correspond au document lessons/<id>.
it.desc: A step-by-step program, from the basics to C1, at 20 to 30 minutes a day.

{"lessons": ["

Irregular verbs in the present

These are the most frequent verbs in the language. Once they roll off your tongue, the rest of the journey will be much easier.

iotului/leinoivoiloro
esseresonoseièsiamosietesono
averehohaihaabbiamoavetehanno
andarevadovaivaandiamoandatevanno
venirevengovienivieneveniamovenitevengono
farefacciofaifafacciamofatefanno
uscireescoesciesceusciamousciteescono
diredicodicidicediciamoditedicono
saperesosaisasappiamosapetesanno
poterepossopuoipuòpossiamopotetepossono
volerevogliovuoivuolevogliamovoletevogliono
doveredevodevidevedobbiamodovetedevono

Handy landmark: noi and voi are almost always regular (andiamo, andate). The irregularity mostly affects io, tu, lui and loro.

To address someone formally, Italian uses the 3rd person singular (Lei): “Scusi, può aiutarmi?”

", "

Articulated prepositions

English keeps “to the” as two words. Italian fuses them into one: a + il = al. Five prepositions merge like this with all the definite articles.

illol'laiglile
aalalloall'allaaiaglialle
dideldellodell'delladeideglidelle
dadaldallodall'dalladaidaglidalle
innelnellonell'nellaneineglinelle
susulsullosull'sullasuisuglisulle
Il treno delle otto parte dal binario tre.The eight o'clock train leaves from track three.
Il biglietto è nella borsa, sul tavolo.The ticket is in the bag, on the table.
", "

Going somewhere: a, in or da?

PrepositionBeforeExample
aa cityVado a Roma
ina country, a regionVado in Italia, in Toscana
daa person (“to someone's place”)Vado da Marco, dal medico
ina means of transportationin treno, in macchina

Da also expresses where you're coming from: “Vengo da Parigi” (I'm coming from Paris). For origin, it's di: “Sono di Parigi” (I'm from Paris, I'm Parisian).

One exception to remember: a piedi (on foot).

Forming the passato prossimo

This is the everyday Italian past tense, used for both “I spoke” and “I have spoken”. Like the English present perfect, it has two parts: avere or essere in the present, followed by the past participle.

InfinitiveParticipleExample
parlareparlatoho parlato
venderevendutoho venduto
dormiredormitoho dormito

With essere, the participle agrees with the subject: Marco è andato, Maria è andata, i ragazzi sono andati, le ragazze sono andate.

", "

Essere or avere?

English always uses “have”, but Italian uses essere with verbs of movement, change of state, and all reflexive verbs.

andare, venire, partire, arrivare, tornare, uscire, entrare, salire, scendere, restare, rimanere, nascere, morire, diventare+ all reflexive verbs: mi sono alzato, ci siamo visti

Essere where you might not expect it

Italian (essere)English
sono statoI was, I have been
mi è piaciutoI liked it
è costatoit cost
è successoit happened
è duratoit lasted
sono riuscitoI managed, I succeeded

On the other hand, camminare and viaggiare take avere: ho camminato, ho viaggiato.

", "

Irregular participles

Most -ere verbs are irregular. Here are the ones that come up all the time.

farefattodiredetto
leggerelettoscriverescritto
vederevistoprenderepreso
metteremessoaprireaperto

nascerenatosuccederesuccesso

Non goes before the auxiliary, and words like “yet” or “never” sit between the auxiliary and the participle, as in “I have never been”: “Non ho ancora finito” (I haven't finished yet), “Non sono mai stato a Napoli” (I've never been to Naples).

{"lessons": ["

Forming the imperfetto

This is the most regular tense in Italian. Drop the -re and add -vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano.

parlareprenderedormire
ioparlavoprendevodormivo
tuparlaviprendevidormivi
lui/leiparlavaprendevadormiva
noiparlavamoprendevamodormivamo
voiparlavateprendevatedormivate
loroparlavanoprendevanodormivano

Only four irregulars: essere (ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano), fare (facevo), dire (dicevo), bere (bevevo).

Pronunciation: the stress falls on the a in “parlavano”, not on the ending.

", "

Which one to choose?

English often uses the simple past for both (“I went”), so this takes a little practice. A good guide: if English could say “was …ing” or “used to”, or if you're setting the scene, it's the imperfetto; if it's one completed event (“I did”), it's the passato prossimo.

ImperfettoPassato prossimo
background, descriptionspecific event
past habit (“used to”)finished action, with a time
action in progress (“was …ing”)the action that interrupts it
Mentre aspettavo il treno, è arrivato Paolo.While I was waiting for the train, Paolo arrived.
Da bambino andavo al mare ogni estate.As a child, I used to go to the beach every summer.

Two nuances to know

Ho conosciuto = I met (for the first time). Ho saputo = I found out (a piece of news).

To stress that an action was in progress: stare in the imperfetto + gerund, just like English “was + -ing”. “Stavo mangiando” = I was eating.

{"lessons": ["

Direct object pronouns

mitilolacivilile
meyouhim, ither, itusyou (pl.)them (m.)them (f.)

Unlike English, they go before the conjugated verb, or attach to the end of an infinitive.

Il pane? Lo compro io.The bread? I'll buy it.
Voglio vederlo. = Lo voglio vedere.I want to see him (it). Both word orders are correct.

In the passato prossimo, the participle agrees with lo, la, li, le: “Giulia? L'ho vista ieri.” “I biglietti? Li ho comprati.”

", "

Indirect pronouns and piacere

mitiglilecivigli
to meto youto himto herto usto you (pl.)to them

Just like English “to him” / “to her”, Italian makes the distinction: gli telefono (I call him), le telefono (I call her). Note that telefonare takes an indirect object (telefonare a), while English “call” takes a direct one.

Formal address: La as a direct object, Le as an indirect one. “Signora, La ringrazio.” “Signore, Le telefono domani.”

Piacere

It works like “to be pleasing to”: the verb agrees with the thing that is liked, and the person who likes it is an indirect pronoun.

Mi piace il gelato. Mi piacciono gli spaghetti.I like ice cream. I like spaghetti. (literally: ice cream is pleasing to me, spaghetti are pleasing to me)
", "

Ci and ne

English has no exact equivalent. Ci replaces a place (“there”); ne replaces a quantity (“of it, of them”), which English often leaves unsaid. In Italian, you can't leave them out.

Vai a Roma? — Sì, ci vado domani.Are you going to Rome? Yes, I'm going (there) tomorrow.
Quanti caffè bevi? — Ne bevo tre.How many coffees do you drink? I drink three (of them).

With ne in the passato prossimo, the participle agrees with the quantity: “Quante mele hai comprato? — Ne ho comprate quattro.”

“There is one (of them)” is ce n'è uno / ce n'è una.

{"lessons": ["

The simple future

Where English adds “will”, Italian uses a single word built on the infinitive minus its final -e. Careful: -are verbs change their a to e.

parlareprenderepartire
ioparleròprenderòpartirò
tuparleraiprenderaipartirai
lui/leiparleràprenderàpartirà

loroparlerannoprenderannopartiranno

Irregular stems

esseresaròavereavrò
andareandròfarefarò
poterepotròdoveredovrò
vederevedròsaperesaprò
venireverròvolerevorrò
rimanererimarròbereberrò

Unlike English, Italian uses the future after quando: “Quando arriverò, ti chiamerò.” (When I arrive, I'll call you; literally “when I will arrive”.) The future is also used to make a guess: “Sarà in ufficio” (he must be at the office).

", "

The conditional

Same stem as the future, with the endings -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero. It's the Italian “would”.

volerepoteredovere
iovorreipotreidovrei
tuvorrestipotrestidovresti
lui/leivorrebbepotrebbedovrebbe
noivorremmopotremmodovremmo
voivorrestepotrestedovreste
lorovorrebberopotrebberodovrebbero
Vorrei un caffè. Potrebbe portarmi il conto?Asking politely.
Dovresti riposarti. Al tuo posto, partirei subito.Giving advice.
Mi piacerebbe vivere a Roma.Expressing a wish.

Just one m separates the future from the conditional: andremo (we will go), andremmo (we would go). You can hear the double consonant.

{"lessons": ["

False friends for English speakers

Italian and English share thousands of words from Latin, so it's easy to let your guard down. These words don't mean what you think.

ItalianMeansNot

la camerathe bedroom, the roomthe camera (la macchina fotografica)
la firmathe signaturethe firm (l'azienda)
la cantinathe cellarthe canteen (la mensa)
morbidosoftmorbid (morboso)
la libreriathe bookstorethe library (la biblioteca)
annoiatoboredannoyed (infastidito)
il magazzinothe warehouse, the storeroomthe magazine (la rivista)

The C on an Italian faucet stands for caldo: that's the hot water!

", "

Talk like an Italian

You'll hear these expressions ten times a day. They'll take you straight from the textbook to real conversation.

In bocca al lupo! — Crepi!Good luck! (literally “into the wolf's mouth”, a bit like “break a leg”). The answer is “may it die!”, never “grazie”.

Meno male!Thank goodness! Phew!

Mi raccomando!Please, make sure you do! Don't forget!
Che ne dici?What do you say? How about it?
Ce l'ho fatta!I did it! I made it!
Non ne posso più.I can't take it anymore.
Fare due passi.To go for a little walk, a stroll.
Dai! / Boh.Come on! / No idea.

The exercises that follow mix these new expressions with everything you've seen since Torino.

{"lessons": ["

Forming the imperative

You'll need it to ask for directions, and above all to understand the answer. English has a single form (“Turn left!”), but Italian has one for a friend (tu), one for formal address (Lei), and one for a group (voi).

parlareprenderedormirefinire
tuparlaprendidormifinisci
Leiparliprendadormafinisca
noiparliamoprendiamodormiamofiniamo
voiparlateprendetedormitefinite

The trap: the vowels swap. For -are verbs, tu = -a and Lei = -i. For the others, it's the reverse: tu = -i, Lei = -a.

Common irregulars

tuLei
andareva' (vai)vada
farefa' (fai)faccia
dareda' (dai)dia
diredi'dica
staresta' (stai)stia

", "

Negation and pronouns

In the negative, the tu form uses the infinitive. The other persons don't change.

Non parlare! Non parlate! Non parli!Don't talk! (to a friend, to a group, then formal)

Where does the pronoun go?

With tu, noi and voi, it attaches to the end of the verb. With Lei, it stays in front.

Prendilo! Scrivetemi! Andiamoci!Take it! Write to me! Let's go (there)!
Lo prenda! Mi dica!Take it! Tell me! (Lei)

With the short forms (va', fa', da', di', sta'), the pronoun's consonant doubles: dimmi (tell me), fallo (do it), dammi (give me), vacci (go there).

Reflexive verbs follow the same rule: siediti (sit down, to a friend), sedetevi (sit down, to a group), si sieda (Lei).

{"lessons": ["

More than, less than, as… as

English only has “than”. Italian chooses between di and che.

ComparingWordExample
two people or thingsdiRoma è più grande di Milano
with a pronoundiLuca è più alto di me
two qualitiescheÈ più simpatico che bello
two quantitiescheMangio più pasta che carne
two verbscheÈ più facile dirlo che farlo
with a prepositioncheMeglio in treno che in macchina

Rule of thumb: di when two different things share a quality, che when a single thing is compared on two aspects.

For equality (“as… as”): come or quanto. “Marta è alta come me.”

", "

Superlatives and irregular forms

È la città più bella d'Italia.It's the most beautiful city in Italy.
La pizza è buonissima. Il museo è interessantissimo.Very, extremely: add -issimo to the adjective, which agrees.

Migliore or meglio?

English says “better” for both, but Italian makes a distinction: the adjective (goes with a noun) comes from buono, the adverb (goes with a verb) comes from bene.

AdjectiveAdverb
+buono → migliorebene → meglio
−cattivo → peggioremale → peggio
Questo vino è migliore. Oggi sto meglio.This wine is better. I feel better today.

Also good to know: ottimo (excellent), pessimo (terrible), maggiore and minore for age: “mio fratello maggiore” (my older brother).

8.topic: Combined and relative pronouns: glielo, che, cui

{"lessons": ["

Two pronouns in a row

When an indirect pronoun meets lo, la, li, le or ne, it changes its vowel: mi → me, ti → te, ci → ce, vi → ve.

Me lo dai? — Sì, te lo do.Will you give it to me? Yes, I'll give it to you.

In the third person, gli and le merge with the direct pronoun into a single word, which works for him, her, them and the formal “you”.

lolalilene
mime lome lame lime leme ne
tite lote late lite lete ne
gli / leglieloglielaglieliglielegliene
cice loce lace lice lece ne
vive love lave live leve ne

The order is the reverse of English: “I tell it to him” becomes “glielo dico”, indirect first, and both pronouns go before the verb.

When attached, they form a single word: dammelo (give it to me), voglio dirglielo (I want to tell him). In the past: te l'ho detto, gliel'ho data.

", "

Che, cui, chi

Che means “who”, “which” and “that”. It never changes, and unlike English, you can never leave it out: “the book I'm reading” is “il libro che leggo”.

Il treno che parte. Il libro che leggo.The train that is leaving. The book (that) I'm reading.

After a preposition, che becomes cui. English often puts the preposition at the end (“the city I live in”); Italian always puts it before cui.

La città in cui vivo. L'amico con cui viaggio.The city I live in. The friend I travel with.
La ragazza di cui ti ho parlato. Il motivo per cui sono qui.The girl I told you about. The reason why I'm here.

Between the article and the noun, cui means “whose”: “il vicino il cui cane abbaia” (the neighbor whose dog barks).

Chi means “whoever, the one who”: “Chi dorme non piglia pesci” (literally: whoever sleeps catches no fish; the early bird catches the worm). And “what” in the sense of “the thing that” is quello che.

{"lessons": ["

Forming the present subjunctive

It's the hallmark of the B1 level. The three singular persons are identical, which is why people often add the pronoun: “che io parli”, “che tu parli”.

parlareprenderedormirefinire
io, tu, luiparliprendadormafinisca
noiparliamoprendiamodormiamofiniamo
voiparliateprendiatedormiatefiniate
loroparlinoprendanodormanofiniscano

You already know these forms: they're the formal (Lei) imperatives you saw in Salerno (parli, prenda, vada, faccia).

Irregulars

esseresiaavereabbia
andarevadafarefaccia
venirevengapoterepossa
volerevogliasaperesappia
diredicastarestia
darediadoveredebba
", "

When to use it

English has almost lost its subjunctive (it survives in “I insist that he be on time”), so this is new territory. Italian uses it after wanting, emotions and necessity, and it goes even further: it also requires it after an opinion.

TriggerExample
opinionPenso che sia tardi
doubtNon credo che venga
hopeSpero che tu stia bene
wantingVoglio che tu venga
emotionHo paura che piova
necessityBisogna che partiate
benché, prima che…Benché sia stanco, esco

So “I think he is late” is “Penso che sia in ritardo”. Same with spero che, where English says “I hope he'll come” or “I hope he comes”. Note too that English “I want you to come” becomes “I want that you come”: voglio che tu venga.

When to do without it

Certainty: indicative. “So che è vero”, “Secondo me è vero”.

Same subject in both clauses: di + infinitive. “Penso di partire” (I'm thinking of leaving), “Spero di rivederti” (I hope to see you again).

es-u01-l1.title: Ser and tener
es-u01-l1.topic: ser and tener in the present; definite and indefinite articles; gender and plural of nouns
es-u01-l1.why: Your very first Spanish lesson: we set up ser and tener, the articles and the plural, before any other verb. You'll use these two verbs from your first conversation to give your nationality, age and job, and they prepare the regular verbs of the next lesson.
es-u01-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Ser and tener: the two pillars

Welcome to your first Spanish lesson! We start with the two most useful verbs: ser (to be) and tener (to have). Just like \"to be\" and \"to have\" in English, they're irregular: learn them by heart, out loud.

ser (to be)tener (to have)
yo (I)soytengo
tú (you, one friend)erestienes
él, ella, usted (he, she, you formal)estiene
nosotros, nosotras (we)somostenemos
vosotros, vosotras (you all, friends)soistenéis
ellos, ellas, ustedes (they, you all formal)sontienen

The subject is usually dropped: in English you always need \"I\" or \"you\", but in Spanish the verb ending already tells you who's speaking. You say Soy francés (I'm French); Yo soy francés is only for emphasis or contrast (Yo soy francés y tú eres español).

Soy francesa y tengo treinta años.I'm French (a woman speaking) and I'm thirty.

\"You\": tú, vosotros or usted?

English has a single \"you\". Spanish has four, depending on how many people you address and how formal you are. Besides the familiar form for one friend (in the table above), there are:

  • vosotros / vosotras = \"you\" for several people you're on first-name terms with (friends, colleagues): ¿Sois de Lyon?
  • usted = polite \"you\" for one person (think \"sir\" or \"ma'am\"). It takes the same verb form as él: ¿Usted es de Madrid? In the plural: ustedes, conjugated like ellos.

In Latin America, people don't use vosotros: they always say ustedes. In Spain, both are used.

Three structures to remember

  • Age uses tener, not \"to be\": Spanish literally says \"I have thirty years\": Tengo treinta años.
  • A job is given without an article, unlike English \"I'm a teacher\": Soy profesor (I'm a teacher), never \"soy un profesor\".
  • A yes/no question needs no \"do\" and no word swapping: intonation alone does it, and it's written between ¿ and ?: ¿Eres de París?

For ages, here are a few numbers until the lesson on numbers: uno (1), dos (2), tres (3), diez (10), veinte (20), treinta (30), cuarenta (40).

To say hi: ¡Hola! (hi, hello). To say \"nice to meet you\": encantado if you're a man, encantada if you're a woman.

", "

Articles and the gender of nouns

This is new for an English speaker: every Spanish noun is either masculine or feminine, even objects, and the article changes with the gender and the number. Where English has just \"the\" and \"a\", Spanish has eight forms.

definite (the)indefinite (a, some)
masculine singularel libroun libro
feminine singularla llaveuna llave
masculine plurallos librosunos libros
feminine plurallas llavesunas llaves

Two things to notice:

  • The gender also applies to people, of course: \"the friend\" is el amigo for a man, la amiga for a woman.
  • \"The\" has two plural forms: los (masculine) and las (feminine). Same for unos / unas (some, a few).

Recognizing the gender

  • Nouns ending in -o are almost always masculine: el libro, el amigo, el hermano.
  • Nouns ending in -a are almost always feminine: la amiga, la hermana, la casa.
  • Nouns ending in -dad and -ción are feminine: la ciudad, la estación.
  • For other endings, learn the noun with its article: el móvil, el ordenador, la llave, el coche.

A few exceptions to know right away: el día (the day), el mapa (the map), el idioma (the language) are masculine despite their -a.

Genders you can't guess

With endings like -e or a consonant, nothing tells you the gender: learn these with their article from day one.

SpanishEnglish
el cochethe car
el colorthe color
la lechethe milk
la salthe salt

Jobs and people often have two forms: el profesor / la profesora, el camarero / la camarera, el enfermero / la enfermera. Nouns ending in -ante don't change, only the article does: el estudiante / la estudiante.

Pablo tiene un ordenador y una llave.Pablo has a computer and a key.

Unlike English, nationalities are written with a lowercase letter, even for people: los franceses (the French). And watch the accent: francés has one, but francesa, franceses and francesas don't. Same for inglés → inglesa, alemán → alemana.

", "

The plural of nouns

Good news: the Spanish plural works a lot like the English one, with -s or -es.

The noun ends in…Examples
vowel → + -sel libro → los libros
la llave → las llaves
el coche → los coches
consonant → + -esel móvil → los móviles
la ciudad → las ciudades
el profesor → los profesores
-z → -cesel lápiz → los lápices

The written accent can move

When you add -es, the word gains a syllable, and the written accent appears or disappears so the stress stays in the same place:

  • el francés → los franceses, el alemán → los alemanes: the accent disappears.
  • el examen → los exámenes, el joven → los jóvenes: the accent appears.

Masculine plural for a mixed group

A group of men and women is referred to in the masculine plural. This gives Spanish handy words where English needs a different one:

SpanishMeaning
los hermanosthe brothers, or the siblings (brothers and sisters)
los amigosthe friends (men and women)
los padresthe parents (father and mother)

So to ask whether someone has any brothers or sisters, you simply say: ¿Tienes hermanos?

—¿Tienes hermanos? —Sí, tengo dos hermanos: un hermano y una hermana.—Do you have any siblings? —Yes, I have two: a brother and a sister.
Carmen y Javier son españoles. Son camareros.Carmen and Javier are Spanish. They're waiters.

The trap for an English speaker: since \"the\" never changes in English, you'll be tempted to use the same article everywhere. \"The keys\" is las llaves, not \"los llaves\". Always check the noun's gender in the singular: la llave → las llaves.

es-u01-l2.title: -ar verbs
es-u01-l2.topic: present tense of regular -ar verbs; negation with no
es-u01-l2.why: After ser and tener, here's the first big conjugation pattern: regular -ar verbs, by far the most common. With the negation no, you can already talk about your job, your studies and what you don't do.
es-u01-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Hablar, trabajar, estudiar: the present of -ar verbs

The great majority of Spanish verbs end in -ar. They're all conjugated the same way: remove -ar and add an ending that tells you who's doing the action.

hablar (to speak)trabajar (to work)estudiar (to study)
yohablotrabajoestudio
túhablastrabajasestudias
él, ella, ustedhablatrabajaestudia
nosotros, nosotrashablamostrabajamosestudiamos
vosotros, vosotrashabláistrabajáisestudiáis
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablantrabajanestudian

In English the verb barely changes (\"I speak, you speak, we speak, they speak\": only \"he speaks\" gets an -s), so you need the pronoun. In Spanish every ending is different and clearly heard: hablo, hablas, habla, hablan. That's why the subject is usually dropped.

Hablo francés y estudio español.I speak French and I'm studying Spanish.

Traps for an English speaker

  • Each person has its own ending: with yo it's -o, so \"I speak\" is hablo. Don't reuse a single form for everyone, as English does with \"speak\".
  • With vosotros, the written accent is required: habláis, trabajáis.
  • With usted (polite \"you\"), use the él form: ¿Usted habla francés? (Do you speak French?)
  • As in English, languages take no article after hablar and estudiar, but they're lowercase: Hablo inglés, Estudio español.

Tip: the nosotros ending is -amos, the ellos ending is -an. Think \"me and my friends\" → hablamos: an m for \"we\", an n for \"they\".

", "

Today's verbs

All these verbs are regular: they follow the hablar pattern exactly. Knowing the infinitive is enough to conjugate them.

VerbMeaningExample
escucharto listen (to)Escucho la radio.
mirarto look at, to watchMiras el móvil.
comprarto buyCompra un libro.
tomarto have (a drink, food)Tomamos un café.
llegarto arriveLlegáis tarde.
buscarto look forBuscan trabajo.
necesitarto needNecesito un ordenador.
desayunarto have breakfastDesayuno en casa.
cenarto have dinnerCenamos tarde.

Notice two things:

  • desayunar and cenar are verbs: one word for \"to have breakfast\" and \"to have dinner\".
  • necesitar works just like \"to need\", with no extra word: Necesito un café (I need a coffee). It can also be followed by an infinitive: Necesito trabajar.

Me llamo: a set phrase

To give your name, Spanish doesn't say \"my name is\" but \"I call myself\". It's a reflexive verb, which we'll study later. For now, learn these forms as set phrases:

SpanishEnglish
me llamomy name is
te llamasyour name is
se llamahis, her name is; your name is (usted)
—¿Cómo te llamas? —Me llamo Lucía.—What's your name? —My name is Lucía.

To take the bus, in Spain you say coger el autobús. Tomar is mainly for what you drink or eat, like \"to have\" in English: tomar un café, tomar una cerveza.

", "

Negation: no

English needs a helper to say no: \"I don't work\", \"she doesn't speak\". Spanish has no \"do\" at all: just put no right before the verb.

No trabajo los sábados.I don't work on Saturdays.
Marta no habla alemán.Marta doesn't speak German.
No me llamo Ana, me llamo Elena.My name isn't Ana, it's Elena.

When answering a question with \"no\", you'll often hear two no: the first one answers the question, the second one negates the verb.

—¿Hablas inglés? —No, no hablo inglés.—Do you speak English? —No, I don't speak English.

Questions

As with ser and tener, a yes/no question is made with intonation only: no \"do\", the sentence doesn't change, only your voice rises at the end.

SpanishEnglish
Trabajas en Madrid.You work in Madrid.
¿Trabajas en Madrid?Do you work in Madrid?
No trabajas en Madrid.You don't work in Madrid.
¿No trabajas en Madrid?Don't you work in Madrid?

To say \"on Saturdays\" (every Saturday), Spanish uses the article: los sábados. The days of the week will come later; for now, just remember this phrase.

Don't look for a Spanish \"do\" or \"don't\": \"I don't work\" is simply no trabajo, never \"trabajo no\".

es-u01-l3.title: Asking questions
es-u01-l3.topic: question words with a written accent; ¿ ? and ¡ !; intonation
es-u01-l3.why: With ser, tener and -ar verbs, you can already answer; now you learn to ask questions. The lesson tackles the two written traps (the opening ¿ and the accent on question words) and gives you the ready-made questions for meeting someone new.
es-u01-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

¿ ? and ¡ !: announcing what's coming

In Spanish you can tell right away that a sentence is a question or an exclamation: it opens with an upside-down mark, ¿ or ¡, and closes with the usual one, ? or !. It isn't decoration: without the opening mark, the sentence is incorrect.

¿Hablas francés?Do you speak French?
¡Hola! ¡Qué bien!Hi! Great!

The mark opens where the question really starts, not necessarily at the beginning of the sentence:

Soy de Lyon. Y tú, ¿de dónde eres?I'm from Lyon. And you, where are you from?
Eres española, ¿verdad?You're Spanish, aren't you?

No \"do\", no word swapping

In English, a question needs \"do/does\" or a change in word order: \"Do you work here?\", \"Where does Marta work?\". Spanish keeps the normal sentence and lets the intonation rise. With a question word, put it first and the verb follows:

EnglishSpanish
Do you work here?¿Trabajas aquí?
Where do you work?¿Dónde trabajas?
Where does Marta work?¿Dónde trabaja Marta?

On the app's keyboard, you'll find ¿ and ¡ with the accented letters. Get into the habit of writing them right now, even in your text messages.

", "

Question words

They always have a written accent when they ask a question. The same word without an accent exists, but it has another job (like \"that\" or \"where\" in an ordinary sentence).

SpanishEnglishExample
¿qué?what? which?¿Qué estudias?
¿quién? ¿quiénes?who?¿Quién es Pablo?
¿dónde?where?¿Dónde trabajas?
¿de dónde?where from?¿De dónde eres?
¿cuándo?when?¿Cuándo cenas?
¿cómo?how?¿Cómo te llamas?
¿por qué?why?¿Por qué estudias español?
¿cuánto? ¿cuánta? ¿cuántos? ¿cuántas?how much? how many?¿Cuántos años tienes?
¿cuál? ¿cuáles?which one? what?¿Cuál es la capital de Francia?

Por qué and porque

Just like \"why\" and \"because\" in English, the question and the answer have different forms:

  • ¿Por qué? = why? (two words, with an accent);
  • porque = because (one word, no accent).
—¿Por qué estudias español? —Porque trabajo en Madrid.—Why are you studying Spanish? —Because I work in Madrid.

Cuánto agrees

Cuánto agrees with the noun that follows, like an adjective: ¿Cuántos años tienes? (años, masculine plural), ¿Cuántas hermanas tienes? (hermanas, feminine plural). English says \"how many\" for everything; Spanish shows gender and number in the ending.

Qué or cuál?

  • qué + noun: ¿Qué idioma estudias? (Which language are you studying?)
  • \"What is…?\" asking for a piece of information is ¿Cuál es…? and \"what are…?\" is ¿Cuáles son…?, never \"qué es\": ¿Qué es? means \"what is it?\" (asking for a definition). ¿Cuál es el problema? (What's the problem?) This is a classic trap for English speakers.

The trap: forgetting the accent. ¿Donde trabajas? or ¿Como te llamas? are incorrect. In a question, these words always have an accent.

", "

Ready-made questions for getting to know someone

Here are the questions you'll hear the first time you meet someone. Learn them as a block, with a possible answer.

QuestionMeaningPossible answer
¿Qué tal?How's it going?Bien, ¿y tú?
¿Cómo te llamas?What's your name?Me llamo Elena.
¿De dónde eres?Where are you from?Soy de Toulouse.
¿A qué te dedicas?What do you do (for a living)?Soy enfermera. / Trabajo en una oficina.
¿Cuántos años tienes?How old are you?Tengo treinta años.
¿Qué idiomas hablas?What languages do you speak?Hablo francés e inglés.
¿Dónde trabajas?Where do you work?En un hospital.

¿A qué te dedicas?, literally \"What do you devote yourself to?\", is the natural way to ask about someone's job. Keep it as it is: it's a set phrase.

Notice Hablo francés e inglés: before a word starting with the \"ee\" sound, y (and) becomes e.

Speaking formally (usted)

With someone you address as usted, the verb switches to the 3rd person, and te becomes se:

Informal (tú)Formal (usted)
¿De dónde eres?¿De dónde es usted?
¿Cómo te llamas?¿Cómo se llama usted?
¿A qué te dedicas?¿A qué se dedica usted?

To keep the conversation going, bounce the question back with ¿Y tú? (And you?) or ¿Y usted? (And you? — formal).

es-u01-l4.title: -er and -ir verbs
es-u01-l4.topic: present tense of regular -er and -ir verbs
es-u01-l4.why: After -ar verbs, this lesson completes the regular present with -er and -ir verbs, which differ only with nosotros and vosotros. You can now say where you live and talk about your habits and simple hobbies, just before the unit review.
es-u01-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Comer and vivir: the other two groups

You know the -ar verbs. There are two more regular groups: verbs in -er (comer, to eat) and verbs in -ir (vivir, to live). Same principle: remove the infinitive ending and add the ending for the person.

hablar (review)comer (to eat)vivir (to live)
yohablocomovivo
túhablascomesvives
él, ella, ustedhablacomevive
nosotros, nosotrashablamoscomemosvivimos
vosotros, vosotrashabláiscoméisvivís
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablancomenviven

Look carefully at the columns: with yo, it's always -o. After that, where hablar has an a, comer and vivir have an e: hablas → comes, vives; habla → come, vive; hablan → comen, viven.

-er or -ir: only two forms change

comer and vivir are identical, except with nosotros and vosotros, where they keep the vowel of the infinitive:

-er: keep the e-ir: keep the i
nosotroscomemosvivimos
vosotroscoméisvivís
Vivimos en Lyon y comemos en casa.We live in Lyon and we eat at home.

The vosotros accents: -áis, -éis, -ís. The -ís of -ir verbs has no a or e: vivís, never \"viveis\".

", "

Today's verbs

All these verbs are regular. Spot their group from the infinitive, then apply the comer or vivir pattern.

-er verbMeaningExample
comerto eat; to have lunchComo en casa.
beberto drink¿Bebes agua?
leerto readLeemos el periódico.
aprenderto learnAprendo español.
comprenderto understand¿Comprendéis la pregunta?
correrto runCarmen corre en el parque.
venderto sellVenden el coche.
-ir verbMeaningExample
vivirto liveVivo en Lyon.
escribirto writeEscribes un mensaje.
abrirto openAbrimos la ventana.
recibirto receive, to getRecibe un correo.
compartirto shareCompartís piso.
subirto go up, to climbAna sube las escaleras.

Remember

  • leer keeps the e of its stem before the ending, which gives two e in a row for several persons: leo, lees, lee, leemos, leéis, leen.
  • \"I live in Lyon\" is Vivo en Lyon: en works just like \"in\" here.
  • In Spain, comer also means \"to have lunch\", the midday meal (eaten around two o'clock): ¿Comemos juntos? = shall we have lunch together?
  • compartir piso (to share an apartment) = to have roommates. In Spain, an apartment is el piso.

For water, say el agua: the word is feminine, but it takes el for pronunciation reasons. You'll see this again later.

", "

Talking about your habits

The present tense is used for what you usually do, as in English. Three little expressions will help you say how often:

SpanishMeaningExample
todos los díasevery dayLeo el periódico todos los días.
a vecessometimesA veces como en un bar.
muchoa lot¿Lees mucho?

Mucho goes after the verb, like \"a lot\": Ana lee mucho (Ana reads a lot). For the negative, keep no before the verb: No corro mucho.

—¿Lees mucho? —Sí, leo todos los días.—Do you read a lot? —Yes, I read every day.
—¿Dónde vives? —Vivo en Bilbao. Comparto piso con dos amigos.—Where do you live? —I live in Bilbao. I share an apartment with two friends.
A veces escribimos mensajes en español.Sometimes we write messages in Spanish.

All three groups together

You now have the whole regular present. Here's a summary to keep handy:

-ar-er-ir
yo-o-o-o

ellos, ellas, ustedes-an-en-en

The most common trap: writing \"vivemos\" or \"vivéis\" for vivir. For -ir verbs, think i: vivir → vivimos, vivís.

{"lessons": ["

The present: everything you already know

Well done, you've finished your first unit! This lesson brings no new rules: it puts everything together so you can introduce yourself in detail and ask someone about themselves.

The two pillars

sertener
yosoytengo
túerestienes
él, ella, ustedestiene
nosotros, nosotrassomostenemos
vosotros, vosotrassoistenéis
ellos, ellas, ustedessontienen

The three regular groups

yohablocomovivo
túhablascomesvives
él, ella, ustedhablacomevive
nosotros, nosotrashablamoscomemosvivimos
vosotros, vosotrashabláiscoméisvivís
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablancomenviven

Three reflexes to keep:

  • the subject is dropped most of the time, unlike in English: Vivo en Lyon;
  • the negative is one word, before the verb, with no \"do\": No trabajo los sábados;
  • a yes/no question keeps the normal word order and is written between ¿ and ?: ¿Hablas inglés?

For a habit, use the plural article: los sábados (on Saturdays, every Saturday), los fines de semana (on weekends, every weekend).

", "

Introducing yourself in detail

Here's a complete introduction, sentence by sentence. Read it out loud, then replace the details with your own.

¡Hola! Me llamo Ana y soy francesa, de Toulouse.Hello! My name is Ana and I'm French, from Toulouse.
Tengo treinta años.I'm thirty.
Vivo en Madrid y soy ingeniera. Trabajo en una oficina.I live in Madrid and I'm an engineer. I work in an office.
Hablo francés, inglés y un poco de español.I speak French, English and a little Spanish.
Los fines de semana leo, cocino y bailo. A veces corro en el parque.On weekends, I read, cook and dance. Sometimes I run in the park.

Questions for getting to know someone

To ask about…You say
their name¿Cómo te llamas?
where they're from¿De dónde eres?
their age¿Cuántos años tienes?
their city¿Dónde vives?
their job¿A qué te dedicas? ¿Dónde trabajas?
their languages¿Qué idiomas hablas?
their reason¿Por qué aprendes español?
their hobbies¿Lees? ¿Cocinas? ¿Practicas deporte?

For hobbies, you don't know the verbs for likes and dislikes yet: just ask yes/no questions with regular verbs. Practicar deporte = to play sports, to exercise.

To react naturally: ¡Qué bien! (great!), ¡Qué interesante! (how interesting!), ¿Y tú? (and you?). And at the end: Encantado if you're a man, Encantada if you're a woman.

These are the mistakes English speakers make most often at the start. Read them again before the exercises.

WrongRightWhy
Soy treinta años.Tengo treinta años.Age uses tener, not \"to be\".

Soy Francés.Soy francés.Nationalities are lowercase.
Yo soy Ana. Yo vivo en Lyon.Soy Ana. Vivo en Lyon.The subject is usually dropped.
vivemos, viveisvivimos, vivís-ir verbs keep the i.
¿Donde trabajas?¿Dónde trabajas?Question words have an accent.
—¿Por qué? —Por qué…—¿Por qué? —Porque…The answer is written as one word.
Hablo no inglés.No hablo inglés.No goes before the verb.

Agreement to watch

  • Nationalities agree, like adjectives: un amigo francés, una amiga francesa, unos amigos franceses.
  • Cuánto agrees with the noun: ¿Cuántos idiomas hablas?, ¿Cuántas hermanas tienes?
  • A mixed group takes the masculine plural: Ana y Javier son españoles.
—¿Cuántos idiomas hablas? —Hablo tres idiomas: francés, inglés y español.—How many languages do you speak? —I speak three languages: French, English and Spanish.

The best practice: introduce yourself out loud every day in one minute, then ask yourself the questions from the previous table as if you were meeting someone.

{"lessons": ["

Me levanto: reflexive verbs

To describe your daily routine, Spanish uses lots of reflexive verbs. Where English says \"I get up\", Spanish says \"I raise myself\": me levanto. A small pronoun goes before the verb, then the verb is conjugated as you already know (levantar is a regular -ar verb).

levantarse (to get up)ducharse (to shower)
yome levantome ducho
túte levantaste duchas
él, ella, ustedse levantase ducha
nosotros, nosotrasnos levantamosnos duchamos
vosotros, vosotrasos levantáisos ducháis
ellos, ellas, ustedesse levantanse duchan

English has no pronoun at all in \"I get up\" or \"I shower\", so the trap is forgetting it. Remember:

  • \"we get up\" is nos levantamos: the pronoun is required, the subject isn't;
  • \"you all get up\" (vosotros) is os levantáis: the pronoun is os;
  • se is used for he, she, usted and for they, ustedes: se levanta, se levantan;
  • in the infinitive, the pronoun is attached to the end: levantar → levantarse (to get up).

You already know one: me llamo, te llamas, se llama. It's the verb llamarse, conjugated exactly like levantarse.

Three verbs to learn as they are

These verbs change their vowel in the present; you'll see why later. For now, just remember the yo form:

InfinitiveMeaningI…
despertarseto wake upme despierto
vestirseto get dressedme visto
acostarseto go to bedme acuesto
Me despierto a las siete, me ducho y me visto.I wake up at seven, I shower and I get dressed.

The negation no goes before the pronoun: No me levanto temprano (I don't get up early). And where English says \"my teeth\", Spanish uses the article: me lavo los dientes (I brush my teeth).

", "

¿Qué hora es? Telling the time

First, the numbers you need for the time:

NumberSpanishNumberSpanish
1uno7siete
2dos8ocho
3tres9nueve
4cuatro10diez
5cinco11once
6seis12doce

For minutes, add veinte (20) and veinticinco (25).

Es la una, son las dos

You don't say a word for \"o'clock\": just the feminine article and the number (the hidden word is la hora, \"the hour\").

TimeSpanish
1:00Es la una.
2:00Son las dos.
3:05Son las tres y cinco.
4:15Son las cuatro y cuarto.
5:30Son las cinco y media.
6:40Son las siete menos veinte.
7:45Son las ocho menos cuarto.
9:00 sharpSon las nueve en punto.
  • Es la una in the singular; for all other hours, son las… in the plural.
  • After half past, start from the next hour and take away the minutes with menos, like \"a quarter to eight\" or \"twenty to seven\".
  • For \"at eight\", say a las ocho (and a la una). The question is ¿A qué hora…? (At what time…?)

The time of day

  • With a time (like a.m. / p.m.): de la mañana (in the morning), de la tarde (in the afternoon), de la noche (at night, in the evening): a las diez de la noche.
  • Without a time: por la mañana (in the morning), por la tarde (in the afternoon), por la noche (in the evening, at night): Me ducho por la mañana.
  • 12 noon = las doce or el mediodía; midnight = las doce de la noche or la medianoche.

Greetings depend on the time: Buenos días (good morning), Buenas tardes (good afternoon, until nightfall), Buenas noches (good evening, and also good night).

", "

Meals and the Spanish schedule

You already know the meal verbs: desayunar, comer, cenar. What surprises visitors is the time: in Spain, people eat late!

The mealThe verbThe usual time
el desayunodesayunar7–9 a.m.
la comidacomer2–3:30 p.m.
la meriendamerendararound 6 p.m.
la cenacenar9–10:30 p.m.

Careful: comer means \"to eat\" in general, but also \"to have lunch\", the midday meal. And la comida means that midday meal (or food in general).

—¿A qué hora comes? —Como a las dos y media.—What time do you have lunch? —I have lunch at half past two.
En España, la gente cena a las diez de la noche.In Spain, people have dinner at ten at night.

Notice la gente (people): it's a feminine singular noun, so the verb is singular, unlike English \"people are\": la gente cena, la gente come.

Describing your morning

Me despierto a las siete menos cuarto. Me levanto a las siete, me ducho y me visto. Desayuno a las siete y media.I wake up at a quarter to seven. I get up at seven, I shower and I get dressed. I have breakfast at half past seven.
Por la noche ceno a las diez y me acuesto a las doce.In the evening I have dinner at ten and I go to bed at midnight.

La merienda is the afternoon snack, for children and adults alike. Merendar also changes its vowel (meriendo): mostly just remember the noun la merienda.

es-u02-l2.title: Ser or estar?
es-u02-l2.topic: ser and estar: identity, origin, character / state, location, result
es-u02-l2.why: After ser, tener and reflexive verbs, here's estar, the second "to be" that English doesn't have. The lesson gives simple guidelines (what you are / where and how you are) and the adjective pairs that change meaning, so you avoid the most common mistakes from the very start.

{"lessons": ["

Estar: the second \"to be\"

English has only one verb \"to be\". Spanish has two: ser, which you know, and estar. It's the big challenge of Spanish for an English speaker… but with a few simple guidelines, you'll choose correctly almost every time.

serestar
yosoyestoy
túeresestás
él, ella, ustedesestá
nosotros, nosotrassomosestamos
vosotros, vosotrassoisestáis
ellos, ellas, ustedessonestán

Look at the accents in estar: every form has one, except estoy and estamos. The stress falls on the last syllable: es-tás, es-tá, es-tán.

Watch the accent on está: está (he is, she is) and esta (this) are two different words. ¿Dónde está? = Where is it? Always write the accent.

The simplest question: ¿Cómo estás?

You'll hear it everywhere. It asks how you are right now: that's a state, so it takes estar.

—¿Cómo estás? —Estoy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?—How are you? —I'm fine, thanks. And you?
—¿Cómo está usted? —Muy bien, gracias.—How are you? (formal) —Very well, thank you.

Take Muy bien (very well) as a set phrase: the word muy (very) will be covered in an upcoming lesson.

Don't mix up ¿Cómo estás? (how are you?) and ¿Cómo eres? (what are you like? what's your personality?): ¿Cómo es Ana? — Es simpática.

Bien (well, fine) and mal (bad, unwell) always go with estar: Estoy bien, Estoy mal. Never \"soy bien\".

", "

Ser or estar: the guidelines

Ser says what you are: what defines a person or a thing. Estar says where you are and how you are right now.

SER: what you areExamples
identitySoy Pablo. Es la hermana de Lucía.
nationality, originSomos franceses. Es de Bilbao.
professionElena es enfermera.
personalityJavier es simpático y tranquilo.
materialLa mesa es de madera.
timeSon las tres. Es la una.
ESTAR: where and how you areExamples
locationEstoy en casa. ¿Dónde está el museo? Madrid está en España.
temporary stateEstoy cansado. Lucía está enferma.
moodEstamos contentos. Diego está enfadado.
how you're doing¿Cómo estás? Estoy bien.

The test for choosing

  • Am I saying who or what (name, job, origin, personality)? → ser.
  • Am I saying where? → estar. Even for a city or a country, which never move: Sevilla está en Andalucía.
  • Am I saying how I feel right now? → estar: Hoy estoy cansada.
Soy francés, pero estoy en Madrid.I'm French, but I'm in Madrid.
Carmen es simpática, pero hoy está enfadada.Carmen is nice, but today she's angry.

Unlike English, adjectives agree with the person, like nationalities: Pablo está cansado, Lucía está cansada, estamos cansados. So a woman says Estoy cansada, a man Estoy cansado.

", "

Same adjective, different meaning

Some adjectives change meaning depending on the verb. With ser, it's the nature of the person or thing; with estar, it's a state of the moment.

Adjectivewith SERwith ESTAR
aburridoEs aburrido: he's boring.Está aburrido: he's bored.
listoEs listo: he's smart, clever.Está listo: he's ready.
maloEs malo: he's bad, mean.Está malo: he's sick.
ricoEs rico: he's rich.Está rico: it's delicious.
La película es aburrida y estoy aburrido.The movie is boring and I'm bored.
—¿Estás lista? —¡Sí, estoy lista!—Are you ready? —Yes, I'm ready!
¡La tortilla está rica!The omelet is delicious!

With the time and reflexive verbs

The time always takes ser, and now you can describe how you feel during the day:

Son las siete. Me levanto, pero estoy cansado.It's seven o'clock. I get up, but I'm tired.
Me acuesto a las doce porque estoy nervioso.I go to bed at midnight because I'm nervous.

Learn the first two pairs by heart: \"boring / bored\" and \"smart / ready\". English speakers often say soy aburrido for \"I'm bored\"… and end up saying they're a boring person!

es-u02-l3.why: With the time (My day), you already handle numbers up to 12; this lesson takes them up to 1000. It gives you what you need right away in Spain: saying your age, understanding a price, giving a date, and telling el lunes (this Monday) from los lunes (every Monday).

{"lessons": ["

Numbers from 0 to 99

You already know the numbers for telling the time. Here's the rest up to 30. From 16 to 29, the number is written as a single word: dieciséis = \"ten and six\", veintiuno = \"twenty and one\".

NumberSpanishNumberSpanish
0cero16dieciséis
11once17diecisiete
12doce18dieciocho
13trece19diecinueve
14catorce20veinte
15quince21veintiuno
22veintidós26veintiséis
23veintitrés27veintisiete
24veinticuatro28veintiocho
25veinticinco29veintinueve

Watch the accents: dieciséis, veintidós, veintitrés, veintiséis.

From 31 on: tens + y + units

30 treinta · 40 cuarenta · 50 cincuenta · 60 sesenta · 70 setenta · 80 ochenta · 90 noventa

After 30, you write three words, with y (and) in the middle: treinta y uno (31), cuarenta y cinco (45), noventa y nueve (99). Like English \"thirty-one\", it's simply tens then units, with \"and\" instead of the hyphen. No surprises after sixty: Spanish counts in tens, just like English.

Uno becomes un or una

Before a noun, uno becomes un (masculine) or una (feminine), even at the end of a bigger number:

Tengo veintiún años. Javier tiene treinta y un años.I'm twenty-one. Javier is thirty-one.
Somos veintiuna personas en clase.There are twenty-one of us in class.

With no noun after it, keep uno: —¿Cuántos años tiene? —Veintiuno. And in a date: el veintiuno de mayo.

", "

From 100 to 1000, and prices

Cien = exactly 100, or 100 before a noun: cien euros. As soon as another number follows, say ciento: ciento uno (101), ciento veinte (120).

NumberSpanish
200doscientos
300trescientos
400cuatrocientos
500quinientos
600seiscientos
700setecientos
800ochocientos
900novecientos
1000mil
  • Three irregular forms: quinientos (not \"cincocientos\"), setecientos, novecientos.
  • Hundreds agree with a feminine noun: doscientos euros, but doscientas personas.
  • The y only goes between the tens and the units: trescientos cuarenta y cinco (345), never \"trescientos y cuarenta\", even though English says \"three hundred and forty-five\".
  • Mil takes no \"one\" (no \"a thousand\") and doesn't change: mil euros, dos mil.

Prices

To ask a price, you use two set phrases. The verb agrees with whatever costs money:

One thingSeveral things
¿Cuánto cuesta el libro?¿Cuánto cuestan los zapatos?
Cuesta quince euros.Cuestan noventa euros.

As in English, euro takes an -s in the plural: un euro, dos euros. For cents: tres euros con cincuenta (céntimos) or simply tres cincuenta.

To react to a price: ¡Es caro! (it's expensive!) or ¡Es barato! (it's cheap!). The trap: saying \"cuánto cuesta los zapatos\". Look at the noun: plural, so cuestan.

", "

Days, months and dates

SpanishEnglish
lunesMonday
martesTuesday
miércolesWednesday
juevesThursday
viernesFriday
sábadoSaturday
domingoSunday

Unlike English, days are written with a lowercase letter, and they're masculine. From Monday to Friday, the plural doesn't change: el lunes, los lunes; but el sábado → los sábados, el domingo → los domingos.

El lunes or los lunes?

SpanishMeaning
El lunes trabajo en casa.On Monday (this one Monday).
Los lunes trabajo en casa.On Mondays (every Monday).
Los domingos como con la familia.On Sundays (every Sunday).

Where English uses \"on\", Spanish always puts an article before the day (except after es: Hoy es martes). So \"On Monday I work\" is El lunes trabajo, never \"en lunes trabajo\" or \"lunes trabajo\".

Months and the date

enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre: lowercase too, unlike English.

The date is el + number + de + month, like \"the third of May\": el tres de mayo, el veinte de julio. No ordinals (\"third\") except for the 1st, which can be el uno or el primero.

—¿Qué día es hoy? —Hoy es jueves, el siete de mayo de dos mil veintiséis.—What's the date today? —Today is Thursday, May 7th, 2026.
—¿Cuándo es el cumpleaños de Ana? —Es el catorce de julio.—When is Ana's birthday? —It's July 14th.

Age uses tener, and cuántos agrees with años: ¿Cuántos años tienes? —Tengo cuarenta y dos años.

es-u02-l4.title: Describing with adjectives
es-u02-l4.topic: adjective agreement; position; muy and mucho
es-u02-l4.why: After ser and estar, you learn to describe: adjective agreement, position after the noun, the short forms buen, mal, gran, and the difference between muy and mucho. You can now describe your city, your neighborhood and your home before the unit review.
es-u02-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Adjective agreement

In English, an adjective never changes: \"a pretty street, pretty streets\". In Spanish, the adjective agrees in gender and number with the noun, and you can always hear it, because the -a and the -s are pronounced.

Endingmasc. sing.fem. sing.masc. pl.fem. pl.
-o / -abonitobonitabonitosbonitas
-egrandegrandegrandesgrandes
consonantfácilfácilfácilesfáciles
-or / -oratrabajadortrabajadoratrabajadorestrabajadoras
nationalityespañolespañolaespañolesespañolas
  • Adjectives in -o make their feminine in -a: un barrio bonito, una calle bonita.
  • Adjectives in -e don't change in the feminine: un piso grande, una casa grande. Never \"granda\"!
  • Most adjectives ending in a consonant don't change either: un ejercicio fácil, una pregunta fácil. In the plural, they take -es: fáciles, jóvenes.
  • Adjectives in -or and nationalities add -a in the feminine: trabajadora, española.
Las calles son antiguas y los edificios son modernos.The streets are old and the buildings are modern.
Elena y Javier son trabajadores.Elena and Javier are hardworking.

A mixed group takes the masculine plural: Elena y Javier son simpáticos. And the adjective also agrees after ser and estar: La casa es bonita, Las chicas están cansadas.

", "

Where the adjective goes

In Spanish, the adjective almost always goes after the noun, the opposite of English:

un piso luminoso, una ciudad tranquila, un coche nuevoa bright apartment, a quiet city, a new car

Colors and nationalities always go after the noun: un coche rojo (a red car), una amiga francesa. Where English says \"a small apartment\", Spanish usually says un piso pequeño.

Buen, mal, gran: adjectives that get shorter

Three common adjectives often go before the noun. They then lose their ending:

Adjectivebefore a masculine singular nounbefore a feminine singular noun
buenoun buen libro (a good book)una buena idea (a good idea)
maloun mal día (a bad day)una mala noticia (bad news)
grandeun gran amigo (a great friend)una gran ciudad (a great city)
  • bueno and malo lose their -o only before a masculine singular noun: un buen día, but una buena idea, unos buenos amigos.
  • grande becomes gran before any singular noun, masculine or feminine: un gran amigo, una gran ciudad.
  • After the noun, they keep their full form: un día bueno, un piso grande.

A handy distinction: before the noun, gran means \"great, important\": un gran amigo (a great friend). After the noun, grande is about size: un piso grande (a big, spacious apartment).

", "

Muy or mucho?

English says \"very\" before an adjective and \"a lot (of)\", \"much\" or \"many\" before a noun or after a verb. Spanish makes the same distinction, with muy and mucho.

UseFormExamples
muy + adjective or adverbnever changesmuy bonito, muy bonitas, muy bien
mucho + nounagrees with the nounmucho tráfico, mucha gente, muchos bares, muchas tiendas
verb + muchonever changesTrabajo mucho. Leemos mucho.
Madrid es una ciudad muy bonita y tiene muchos museos.Madrid is a very beautiful city and it has a lot of museums.
En el centro vive mucha gente.A lot of people live downtown.
—¿Es caro el piso? —Sí, mucho.—Is the apartment expensive? —Yes, very.

Traps for an English speaker

  • No \"of\" after mucho: \"a lot of bars\" = muchos bares.
  • la gente is singular: mucha gente (a lot of people), and the verb stays singular.
  • Never \"muy\" before a noun, never \"mucho\" before an adjective: muy grande, mucho trabajo.
  • On its own as an answer, where English says \"Yes, very\", Spanish says mucho: —¿Es interesante? —Sí, mucho.

Describing your city and your home

To say that a place has something, you can use tener: El barrio tiene muchas tiendas. And to say where it is, estar: El piso está en el centro.

El piso es pequeño, pero muy luminoso. Está en una calle tranquila.The apartment is small, but very bright. It's on a quiet street.

Reminder: ser to describe (la calle es ruidosa), estar to locate or express a state (la calle está en el centro, estoy contento).

es-u02-l5.title: Review: describing your week
es-u02-l5.why: Review of the "My everyday life" unit, with nothing new: you bring together reflexive verbs, the time, days, ser and estar and adjectives to describe your typical week. The shared apartment in Valencia makes you use all of it, before tackling the irregular verbs of the next unit.
es-u02-l5.json:
{"lessons": ["

Describing your week: the tools

Last lesson of the unit: nothing new, but everything you need to describe your typical week. Let's start with reflexive verbs and time expressions.

levantarse
yome levanto
túte levantas
él, ella, ustedse levanta
nosotros, nosotrasnos levantamos
vosotros, vosotrasos levantáis
ellos, ellas, ustedesse levantan

And the three forms given with yo: me despierto (I wake up), me visto (I get dressed), me acuesto (I go to bed).

Time expressions

SpanishEnglish
a las ocho, a la unaat eight, at one
de nueve a seisfrom nine to six
por la mañana, por la tarde, por la nochein the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening
el luneson Monday (one time)
los luneson Mondays (every Monday)
de lunes a viernesfrom Monday to Friday
el fin de semanathe weekend
todos los días, a vecesevery day, sometimes
temprano, tardeearly, late
De lunes a viernes me levanto a las siete y trabajo de nueve a seis.From Monday to Friday, I get up at seven and I work from nine to six.
Los sábados me despierto tarde y desayuno a las once.On Saturdays, I wake up late and have breakfast at eleven.

To say \"OK\", Spaniards say vale all the time. At the end of a sentence, ¿vale? means \"OK?\", \"all right?\".

", "

Ser, estar and adjectives: the summary

What you're sayingExampleVerb
identity, nationality, jobSoy Marta. Es valenciano. Son enfermeras.SER
personality, descriptionSergio es trabajador. La cocina es pequeña.SER
time, dateSon las nueve. Hoy es el tres de mayo.SER
locationEl piso está en el centro.ESTAR
state, moodEstoy cansada. Estamos muy ocupados.ESTAR

Agreement to watch

  • The adjective agrees with the noun or the person: Las habitaciones son luminosas, Lucía está ocupada.
  • Adjectives in -e or a consonant don't change in the feminine: una casa grande, una pregunta fácil.
  • buen, mal, gran before the noun: un buen compañero, un mal día, una gran ciudad.
  • muy + adjective, never changes; mucho + noun, agrees: muy limpio, mucha gente, muchos platos.

Numbers for the week

For times, dates and prices, remember: es la una / son las dos; el veintiuno de marzo but veintiún años; ¿Cuánto cuesta? for one thing, ¿Cuánto cuestan? for several.

Hoy es lunes, el veintiuno de marzo. Son las ocho y estoy muy cansado.Today is Monday, March 21st. It's eight o'clock and I'm very tired.

The quick test: if you're answering \"where?\" or \"how do you feel?\", it's estar. Otherwise, it's almost always ser.

", "

A week in a shared apartment

Here's Marta's story; she shares an apartment in Valencia. Read it out loud and spot the reflexive verbs, the times, ser and estar.

Me llamo Marta y vivo en Valencia. Comparto piso con Sergio, un compañero muy trabajador.My name is Marta and I live in Valencia. I share an apartment with Sergio, a very hardworking roommate.
El piso está en el centro. Es antiguo, pero es muy luminoso y la cocina es grande.The apartment is downtown. It's old, but it's very bright and the kitchen is big.
De lunes a viernes me levanto a las siete y media. Trabajo por la mañana, en una oficina.From Monday to Friday, I get up at half past seven. I work in the morning, in an office.
Como a las dos y media. Por la tarde estoy libre: a veces corro en el parque.I have lunch at half past two. In the afternoon I'm free: sometimes I run in the park.
Los martes y los jueves Sergio cocina. Cenamos juntos a las nueve y media.On Tuesdays and Thursdays, Sergio cooks. We have dinner together at half past nine.
Los sábados limpiamos el piso. Los domingos son tranquilos: me levanto tarde y leo mucho.On Saturdays, we clean the apartment. Sundays are quiet: I get up late and read a lot.

Your turn: replace each detail with your own. Where do you live? What's your home like? What time do you get up? When are you free?

To talk about your home without a possessive, Spanish uses the article where English says \"my\": El piso es pequeño (my apartment is small), La cocina es luminosa. Possessives will come in an upcoming unit.

es-u03-l1.title: Ir, venir, salir
es-u03-l1.topic: present tense of ir, venir, salir; a, en, de with places; al and del
es-u03-l1.why: First lesson on irregular verbs in the present: ir, venir and salir let you say where you're going, where you're coming from and when you leave. It also sets up a and de with places, the contractions al and del, and means of transport, which will come back throughout the next unit, in the city.
es-u03-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Voy, vengo, salgo

So far, you've mostly used regular verbs, plus ser, tener and estar. This unit tackles the irregular verbs you need all the time. We start with three verbs of movement: ir (to go), venir (to come) and salir (to go out, to leave).

ir (to go)venir (to come)salir (to go out, to leave)
yovoyvengosalgo
túvasvienessales
él, ella, ustedvavienesale
nosotros, nosotrasvamosvenimossalimos
vosotros, vosotrasvaisveníssalís
ellos, ellas, ustedesvanvienensalen

What to notice

  • Ir looks nothing like its infinitive, a bit like \"to be\" in English: all its forms start with v- and take the endings of an -ar verb (voy, vas, va).
  • Vengo and salgo take a g in the first person, like tengo, which you already know. You'll see this -go family again in the next lesson.
  • Venir works like tener: vienes, viene, vienen with ie, but venimos, venís without ie.
  • Vais has no accent (it's one syllable), whereas venís and salís do.

Vamos means \"we go\", but also \"let's go!\": ¡Vamos! You'll hear it everywhere in Spain.

¿Vienes a la fiesta de Lucía? Sí, voy con Pablo.Are you coming to Lucía's party? Yes, I'm going with Pablo.
", "

Ir a, venir de, salir de: al and del

With a verb of movement, the destination is marked with a (to), and the starting point with de (from). The traps: English says \"go home\" or \"leave the station\" with no preposition, but Spanish always needs one: a destination always takes a.

EnglishSpanish
I'm going to Madrid.Voy a Madrid.
I'm going to Spain.Voy a España.
I'm going to Portugal.Voy a Portugal.
I'm going to the beach.Voy a la playa.
I'm coming from Lyon.Vengo de Lyon.
I'm leaving the station.Salgo de la estación.

Two required contractions

Before the masculine article el, the prepositions a and de merge with it:

  • a + el = al: Voy al cine. (never \"a el cine\")
  • de + el = del: Vengo del trabajo. (never \"de el trabajo\")

These are the only two contractions: a la, a los, a las, de la, de los, de las stay separate. And the pronoun él (with an accent) never contracts: Es el coche de él.

Home, from home

Without an article, casa means \"home\": Voy a casa (I'm going home), Salgo de casa a las ocho (I leave home at eight). Note the prepositions that English leaves out.

To ask about the destination, say ¿Adónde vas? (or ¿A dónde vas?), \"where are you going (to)?\"; for where a trip starts, ¿De dónde vienes? Both have the accent of question words.

Salimos del cine a las diez y vamos a casa.We leave the movie theater at ten and go home.
", "

En tren, en coche, a pie

For means of transport, Spanish uses en where English says \"by\": en bici (by bike), just like en coche (by car). Only one exception to remember: a pie (on foot).

SpanishEnglish
en trenby train
en cocheby car
en autobúsby bus
en metroby subway (metro)
en aviónby plane
en biciby bike
a pieon foot

The everyday word for car in Spain is el coche. In Latin America, you'll mostly hear el carro or el auto.

The meanings of salir

  • to go out of, to leave a place: Salgo del metro en Sol.
  • to go out, to have fun: Los viernes salimos con amigos.
  • to leave, to depart (a train, a bus): El tren sale a las siete y media.

Ir or venir?

Venir means movement toward where the speaker is. When you're moving toward the other person, Spanish usually says ir, where English says \"come\": someone calls you for dinner, and you answer ¡Voy! (I'm coming!).

¿Vienes a cenar? ¡Sí, ya voy!Are you coming to dinner? Yes, I'm coming!

Hago, digo, pongo, doy

These four verbs have one thing in common: it's mostly the first person that's irregular. Once you've got hago, pongo and doy down, the rest is conjugated like a regular verb.

hacer (to do, to make)decir (to say)poner (to put)dar (to give)
yohagodigopongodoy
túhacesdicesponesdas
él, ella, ustedhacediceponeda
nosotros, nosotrashacemosdecimosponemosdamos
vosotros, vosotrashacéisdecísponéisdais

What to notice

  • Hacer and poner: only the yo form changes (hago, pongo). Everything else is regular -er.
  • Decir is doubly irregular: digo with a g, and the e becomes i everywhere except with nosotros and vosotros (dices, dice, dicen but decimos, decís).
  • Dar gives doy, like soy, estoy and voy. Dais has no accent: it's one syllable, like vais.

The -go family

Make a list: tengo, vengo, salgo, hago, pongo, digo. Six very common verbs whose yo form ends in -go. If you're unsure about the first person of a common verb, think of this family.

The classic trap: \"hazo\" or \"haco\" for \"I do\". The only form is hago.

¿Qué haces los domingos? Hago deporte y doy un paseo.What do you do on Sundays? I play sports and go for a walk.
", "

The weather: hace calor

English says \"it's hot\"; Spanish says \"it makes heat\", with hace. And there's no subject, no \"it\": \"it's hot\" is simply hace calor.

SpanishEnglish

Hace sol.It's sunny.
Hace viento.It's windy.
Hace buen tiempo. / Hace mal tiempo.The weather is nice. / The weather is bad.
Llueve. / Nieva.It's raining. / It's snowing.
Está nublado.It's cloudy.

Mucho, not muy

Calor, frío, sol and viento are nouns (el calor, el frío: \"heat\", \"cold\"). Remember the rule: muy goes before an adjective, mucho before a noun. So \"it's very hot\" is Hace mucho calor (\"it makes a lot of heat\"), never \"hace muy calor\".

Hace calor or tengo calor?

Hace calor is about the weather. For a person, Spanish uses tener, as for age: Tengo calor (I'm hot), ¿Tienes frío? (are you cold?). Literally: \"I have heat\", \"do you have cold?\".

Llueve and nieva come from llover and nevar: learn them as set forms, since you always talk about the weather in the 3rd person.

En Sevilla, en agosto, hace mucho calor.In Seville, in August, it's very hot.

dar un paseoto go for a walkwith dar (\"give\"), not hacer
dar las graciasto say thank you, to thankwith dar

Decir

Decir is used like \"to say\" or \"to tell\": Digo la verdad (I tell the truth), Elena dice que no (Elena says no). When you haven't understood, ask ¿Qué dices? (what are you saying?).

One Spanish verb for two English ones: hacer means both \"do\" and \"make\". \"Make the bed\" and \"do sports\" both use it, as in hacer deporte.

Yo hago la comida y tú pones la mesa, ¿vale?I'll make lunch and you set the table, OK?

es-u03-l3.title: Wanting, being able to, having to
es-u03-l3.topic: querer, poder, tener que, deber + infinitive; asking politely
es-u03-l3.why: After verbs of movement and hacer, decir, poner, dar, here are querer, poder, tener que and deber, which let you say what you want to, can and have to do. The lesson sets up the ie and ue forms, the que in tener que, the negation trap, and the phrases for politely asking a favor.
es-u03-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Quiero, puedo, tengo que

With these verbs, you can say what you want to do, can do and have to do. They're followed directly by an infinitive, with no \"to\": Quiero salir (I want to go out), No puedo venir (I can't come).

querer (to want)poder (can, to be able to)tener que (to have to)deber (should, must)
yoquieropuedotengo quedebo
túquierespuedestienes quedebes
él, ella, ustedquierepuedetiene quedebe
nosotros, nosotrasqueremospodemostenemos quedebemos
vosotros, vosotrasqueréispodéistenéis quedebéis
ellos, ellas, ustedesquierenpuedentienen quedeben

The \"boot\"

Look at the forms in bold: the e of querer becomes ie, the o of poder becomes ue… except with nosotros and vosotros. If you circle the forms that change in the table, you draw a boot. English has nothing like this, so this shape is the easiest way to remember it.

The traps

  • I can = puedo, never \"podo\". We can = podemos, never \"puedemos\".
  • We want = queremos, without ie.
  • Deber is a regular -er verb: debo, debes, debe…

Querer also means \"to love\" someone: Te quiero (I love you). With an object or a dish, it means \"to want\": Quiero un café.

¿Quieres venir al cine? Hoy no puedo.Do you want to come to the movies? I can't today.
", "

Tener que or deber?

Good news: these two work a lot like English \"have to\" and \"should / must\".

UseExample
tener que + infinitivea concrete obligation, like \"have to\"; the most common form in speechTengo que trabajar el sábado.
deber + infinitiveadvice, moral duty, like \"should\" or \"must\"; a bit more formalDebes descansar.

Never forget the que, just as you never forget the \"to\" in \"have to\": Tengo que salir, never \"tengo salir\". And only tener is conjugated: Tenemos que esperar.

The negation

Here again, Spanish works like English. No tengo que trabajar means \"I don't have to work\" (it isn't necessary), not \"I mustn't work\". For advice or a prohibition, use no deber: No debes salir hoy (you shouldn't go out today).

SpanishMeaning
No tengo que ir.I don't have to go.
No debes ir.You shouldn't go (it's not a good idea).

To talk about an obligation, tener que is always the right choice in everyday speech. Save deber for advice.

Mañana tenemos que salir muy temprano.Tomorrow we have to leave very early.
", "

Asking politely

These verbs are mainly used to ask for things: permission, a favor, an invitation. Here are the phrases to know.

You want to…You say
ask for permission¿Puedo abrir la ventana? (can I open the window?)
ask a friend for a favor¿Puedes cerrar la puerta? / ¿Me puedes ayudar?
invite someone¿Quieres cenar con nosotros?
politely say what you'd likeQuería una información. / Quería reservar una mesa.
speak to a stranger (formal)¿Puede repetir, por favor?

¿Me puedes…?

¿Me puedes ayudar? means \"can you help me?\". Learn it as a set phrase: the little word me (me) goes before puedes, not at the end as in English. Same with ¿Me puedes esperar? (can you wait for me?).

Quería: the magic phrase

In a store or at a ticket window, Quiero… (\"I want…\") sounds a bit blunt. Spaniards say Quería… (literally \"I wanted\"), which sounds like \"I'd like\". It's a past form you'll study later; for now, take it as a ready-made polite phrase.

¿Puede repetir? is for someone you address formally: Spanish uses usted with the 3rd person singular for this. You'll see it in detail in the next unit.

Buenos días, quería un billete para Zaragoza.Good morning, I'd like a ticket to Zaragoza.

es-u03-l4.title: Saber and conocer
es-u03-l4.topic: saber and conocer; the a before a person as direct object
es-u03-l4.why: After querer, poder and tener que, the lesson separates saber and conocer, the two Spanish verbs for "to know", with a few traps. It also introduces the personal a before a person as direct object, a rule with no English equivalent that you'll use all the time.
es-u03-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Sé and conozco

English has one verb, \"to know\". Spanish has two: one for facts and skills, the other for people and places you're familiar with. Good news on the conjugation side: only the first person is irregular.

saber (to know a fact)conocer (to know a person, a place)
yoséconozco
túsabesconoces
él, ella, ustedsabeconoce
nosotros, nosotrassabemosconocemos
vosotros, vosotrassabéisconocéis
ellos, ellas, ustedessabenconocen

Two forms to watch

  • Sé (I know) has a written accent. Without it, se is the pronoun in se llama or se levanta. The accent makes the difference in writing.
  • Conozco takes a z before the c: conozco. Most verbs ending in -ocer and -ecer do the same, like parecer (to seem).

Everything else is regular -er: sabes, sabe, sabemos; conoces, conoce, conocemos.

No sé (I don't know) is one of the most useful phrases in Spanish. Add a smile and a shrug, and everyone understands.

¿Sabes dónde está Pablo? No sé, no conozco a Pablo.Do you know where Pablo is? I don't know, I don't know Pablo.
", "

Saber or conocer?

VerbUseExample
sabera piece of information, a factSé dónde vive Marta. (I know where Marta lives)
saberknowing the answer to a question¿Sabes a qué hora sale el tren?
saber + infinitiveknowing how to do somethingSé nadar. / ¿Sabes cocinar?
conocera personConozco a Javier.
conocera place, a city, a restaurantConozco Granada. / ¿Conoces este bar?

Traps for an English speaker

  • \"To know the answer, the address, the price\": that's information, so saber: Sé la respuesta.
  • \"To know\" a language: you can say saber inglés but, more often, hablar inglés (to speak English).
  • English \"can\" covers two Spanish verbs. Saber + infinitive is a learned skill (\"know how to\"); poder is what's possible right now. Sé nadar, pero hoy no puedo: hace mucho frío. (I can swim, but I can't today: it's very cold.)

The simplest test: if you can put \"that\", \"where\", \"when\", \"how\" or an infinitive after it, it's saber. Before a person or a place (\"to be familiar with\", \"to have met\"), it's conocer.

No sé bailar flamenco, pero conozco un bar muy bueno en Sevilla.I can't dance flamenco, but I know a very good bar in Seville.
", "

The \"personal a\"

Here's a rule that doesn't exist in English: when the direct object of a verb is a specific person, you put a before it.

A person: aA place or a thing: nothing
Conozco a Marta.Conozco Madrid.
¿Conoces a la profesora?¿Conoces el museo del Prado?
Espero a Diego.Espero el autobús.
Busco a Lucía.Busco las llaves.

And as always, a + el = al: Conozco al profesor de guitarra.

When not to use it

  • Before a thing or a place: Conozco Bilbao, no a.
  • With tener: Tengo dos hermanos, no a.
  • Before an unspecified person: Busco un profesor de español (any teacher at all).

A few Spanish cities

Toledo, Segovia, Granada, Córdoba, Cádiz, Bilbao, San Sebastián, Santiago de Compostela, Salamanca. Watch the accents: Córdoba, Cádiz, San Sebastián, Málaga, León.
