es-u03-l5.title: Stem-changing verbs
es-u03-l5.topic: e → ie, o → ue, e → i, u → ue in the present tense
es-u03-l5.why: After querer and poder, this lesson extends the “boot” pattern to all the common stem-changing verbs: e → ie, o → ue, e → i and jugar. It's the last big group of present-tense irregulars before the unit review, practiced through likes, sports and eating out.
es-u03-l5.json:
{"lessons": ["

The boot: e → ie, o → ue

You already know quiero and puedo. Lots of very common verbs work the same way: the stressed vowel of the stem changes (it becomes a “diphthong”), but not with nosotros and vosotros, where the stress falls on the ending. Draw a line around the forms that change in the table and you get the shape of a boot, which is why these are often called “boot verbs.”

pensar (e → ie)preferir (e → ie)dormir (o → ue)volver (o → ue)
yopiensoprefieroduermovuelvo
túpiensasprefieresduermesvuelves
él, ella, ustedpiensaprefiereduermevuelve
nosotros, nosotraspensamospreferimosdormimosvolvemos
vosotros, vosotraspensáispreferísdormísvolvéis
ellos, ellas, ustedespiensanprefierenduermenvuelven

The endings, on the other hand, are perfectly regular: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an for -ar verbs, and so on. Only the stem moves.

Verbs to know

  • e → ie: pensar, empezar, preferir, cerrar, querer
  • o → ue: dormir, volver, poder, encontrar, costar

English has nothing like this in the present tense: “I think, we think” never changes. The closest thing is the vowel shift in pairs like “sing / sang” or “foot / feet.” In Spanish, just remember the boot: the vowel changes everywhere except we and you all.

Nosotros volvemos a las seis, pero Marta vuelve a las ocho.We get back at six, but Marta gets back at eight.
", "

e → i and u → ue

A few -ir verbs change their e to i (not ie). They follow the same boot: nosotros and vosotros keep the e.

pedir (e → i)seguir (e → i)jugar (u → ue)
yopidosigojuego
túpidessiguesjuegas
él, ella, ustedpidesiguejuega
nosotros, nosotraspedimosseguimosjugamos
vosotros, vosotraspedísseguísjugáis
ellos, ellas, ustedespidensiguenjuegan

What to notice

  • e → i: pedir (to ask for, to order), repetir (to repeat), servir (to serve), seguir (to follow, to keep on).
  • Seguir drops its u in the first person: sigo. Before o, the hard “g” sound (as in “go”) is written with a plain g (as in tengo). Everywhere else you keep gu: sigues, sigue, siguen.
  • Jugar is the only u → ue verb: juego, juegas… Where English just says “play soccer,” Spanish needs a before the sport: jugar al fútbol, jugar al tenis (a + el = al).

Pedir or preguntar?

English uses “ask” for both, and only the little word “for” tells them apart. Spanish has two separate verbs:

VerbMeaningExample
pedirto ask for something, to orderPido un café. / Pido ayuda.
preguntarto ask a questionPregunto la hora. / Pregunto dónde está el baño.

In a restaurant, “I'll have a salad” is usually pido una ensalada (I'm ordering a salad). If there's a “for” after “ask” in your English, or you could add one, it's the first verb.

", "

Every day: likes, sports, eating out

These verbs come up all day long. Here are some sentences to learn as they are:

SpanishEnglish
Empiezo a trabajar a las nueve.I start work at nine.
Vuelvo a casa a las siete.I get home at seven.
Duermo ocho horas.I sleep eight hours.
Prefiero el té.I prefer tea.
¿Qué piensas?What do you think?
La tienda cierra a las nueve.The store closes at nine.
No encuentro las llaves.I can't find the keys.
¿Cuánto cuesta? ¿Cuánto cuestan?How much is it? How much are they?
El camarero sirve el vino.The waiter serves the wine.
Juego al pádel los martes.I play padel on Tuesdays.

You'll recognize ¿Cuánto cuesta?, which you learned as a set phrase: it's simply costar (o → ue) in the third person.

Empezar takes a before an infinitive: empiezo a trabajar, “I start to work.” English can say “start working” or “start to work”; Spanish only allows the second pattern, with the little word in between.

How do you know if a verb changes its stem? Dictionaries often show it in parentheses: pensar (ie), dormir (ue), pedir (i). Learn each new verb with its marker.

¿Qué prefieres, carne o pescado? Prefiero pescado.Which do you prefer, meat or fish? I prefer fish.

es-u03-l6.title: Review: planning a night out
es-u03-l6.why: This review brings together all the present-tense irregulars from the unit (ir, venir, salir, hacer, querer, poder, tener que, saber, conocer, the stem changers) and sorts them into families. You'll put them to work suggesting, accepting or turning down plans in Seville, weather included, before heading into town in the next unit.
es-u03-l6.json:
{"lessons": ["

Recap: present-tense irregulars

In five lessons, you've seen all the common present-tense irregulars. To remember them, sort them into families: it's much easier than learning them one by one.

FamilyWhat changesVerbs
-goonly yotengo, vengo, salgo, hago, pongo, digo
-zcoonly yoconozco
yo in -oyonly yosoy, estoy, voy, doy
one of a kindonly yosé
e → iethe bootquiero, pienso, empiezo, prefiero, cierro
o → uethe bootpuedo, duermo, vuelvo, encuentro, cuesta
e → ithe bootpido, repito, sirvo, sigo
u → uethe bootjuego

Double trouble

Three verbs have both irregularities: a g in the first person and a vowel change in the other “boot” forms (ie for tener and venir, i for decir).

tenervenirdecir
yotengovengodigo
tútienesvienesdices
él, ella, ustedtienevienedice
nosotros, nosotrastenemosvenimosdecimos
vosotros, vosotrastenéisvenísdecís
ellos, ellas, ustedestienenvienendicen

And ir is in a class of its own: voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van. It's the most irregular verb, and also the most useful one for suggesting a night out.

", "

Suggesting, accepting, turning down

A handful of phrases is all you need to make plans. They use every verb from the unit.

To…You sayEnglish
suggest¿Quieres venir al cine?Do you want to come to the movies?
suggest¿Vamos a la playa el sábado?Shall we go to the beach on Saturday?
suggest¿Por qué no vamos al parque?Why don't we go to the park?
accept¡Vale! / ¡Genial! / Sí, claro.OK! / Great! / Yes, of course.
turn downLo siento, no puedo: tengo que trabajar.Sorry, I can't: I have to work.
suggest something elsePrefiero ir a la piscina.I'd rather go to the pool.
set the time¿A qué hora quedamos?What time shall we meet?
set the place¿Dónde quedamos? Quedamos en la plaza.Where shall we meet? Let's meet in the square.

Quedar

Quedar (a regular -ar verb) means “to meet up, to arrange to meet.” Spaniards use it all the time when making plans: Quedamos a las ocho en la puerta del cine. It's close to the English “meet up,” but it also covers the arranging part: one word for “let's meet” and “we're meeting.”

Lo siento (I'm sorry) is a set phrase: learn it as it is. Notice that Spanish uses the present tense for plans where English often says “shall we…?” or “let's…”: a plain present-tense question is all you need.

¿Vamos al concierto el viernes? Lo siento, el viernes no puedo.Shall we go to the concert on Friday? Sorry, I can't on Friday.
", "

The weather and plan B

Plans often depend on the weather. Remember: hace + noun, with mucho before the noun. Where English says “it's hot” with an adjective, Spanish literally says “it makes a lot of heat.”

SpanishEnglish
Hace sol y hace mucho calor.It's sunny and it's very hot.
Hace buen tiempo.The weather's nice.
Hace frío y hace viento.It's cold and windy.
Llueve.It's raining.

Si llueve…

For a plan B, Spanish uses si + present tense, exactly like English: Si llueve, vamos al cine (if it rains, we'll go to the movies). Si without an accent means “if”; sí with an accent means “yes.”

Seville in practice

  • In summer, afternoons are scorching: people in Seville go out late, often after ten at night.
  • A favorite place to meet is a square or the riverside, along el río Guadalquivir.
  • The Triana neighborhood, across the river, is famous for flamenco and tapas bars.
Si hace mucho calor, quedamos a las diez de la noche en Triana.If it's very hot, let's meet at ten at night in Triana.

es-u04-l1.title: Little words: a, de, en, con, para, desde, hasta
es-u04-l1.topic: simple prepositions and how they're used
es-u04-l1.why: The first lesson of the “around town” unit sorts out the simple prepositions (a, de, en, con, para, desde, hasta, entre), starting from the mix-ups English speakers typically make. It builds on al and del and the verbs of movement from the previous unit, and gets you ready for hay / está and asking for directions.
es-u04-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

A, de, en: the three pillars

Prepositions are short but sneaky: they never map neatly onto English. Start with the three most common ones.

PrepositionUseExample
adirection, destination (to)Voy a Madrid. / Voy al médico.
aclock time (at)La clase empieza a las diez.
apersonal a (no English equivalent)Espero a Lucía.
deorigin (from)Soy de Lyon. / Vengo del trabajo.
depossession (’s, of)el coche de Pablo
dematerial, contentsuna mesa de madera, un vaso de agua
enplace, no movement (in, at)Vivo en Sevilla. / Estoy en casa.
enin, onLas llaves están en la mesa.
enmeans of transportation (by)Voy en tren. (but a pie, on foot)
enmonth, season, year (in)en mayo, en verano

Trap #1: at, in, on

Good news first: for cities, English already does what Spanish does. “To” for movement, “in” for being there:

EnglishSpanish
I'm going to Madrid.Voy a Madrid. (movement)
I'm in Madrid.Estoy en Madrid. (no movement)
I live in Madrid.Vivo en Madrid.

The real trap is that English has three words for location, “at,” “in” and “on,” and Spanish uses just one for all of them: at home, in the kitchen, on the table, at the station all take the same little word. Don't go looking for a separate “on” or “at.”

The question to ask yourself: is there movement toward the place? Yes: a. No: en.

Vivo en Valencia, pero mañana voy a Madrid en tren.I live in Valencia, but tomorrow I'm going to Madrid by train.
", "

Con, para, desde, hasta, entre

PrepositionUseExample
conwithCeno con Marta. / un café con leche
parapurpose: (in order) to + verbEstudio español para trabajar en Madrid.
pararecipient: forEste regalo es para Lucía.
desde… hastafrom… to, from… until (time, place)desde las nueve hasta las dos / desde Madrid hasta Toledo
de… afrom… to (shorter)Trabajo de nueve a cinco.
entrebetween, amongEl banco está entre la farmacia y el bar.

Conmigo, contigo

After a preposition, “me” is mí (with an accent) and “you” is ti (no accent): para mí, para ti. But with con, they fuse into a single word:

With…Spanish
meconmigo
you (tú)contigo
him, her, you (usted)con él, con ella, con usted
uscon nosotros, con nosotras
you (plural)con vosotros, con vosotras
themcon ellos, con ellas

Exception: after entre, you keep yo and tú: entre tú y yo (between you and me).

In this lesson, English “for” is para. Spanish has a second word, por, which you'll study later; for now, para is all you need for purpose and recipient.

¿Vienes conmigo? Sí, voy contigo.Are you coming with me? Yes, I'm going with you.
", "

Traps for English speakers

Here are the mistakes English speakers make most often. Read each line, comparing the two columns.

EnglishSpanishWhy
on the trainen el tren“on” and “in” = en
at Marta's (I'm having dinner)en casa de Martano “’s”: say “in the house of”
to Marta's (I'm going)a casa de Martamovement: a
my mother's housela casa de mi madreno “’s”: possession with de, the owner comes last
the eight o'clock trainel tren de las ochothe time keeps its article and comes after
in Mayen mayosame as English
on Monday (this Monday)el lunesno preposition before a day: no “on”
a wooden tableuna mesa de maderamaterial goes after, with de

Mi (my) comes up in the next unit; for now, just remember the pattern la casa de…

Don't forget al and del

They come back with all these prepositions: Voy al centro, Vuelvo del trabajo, el coche del profesor, desde el parque hasta el río (no contraction with desde or with en: only with a and de).

Esta noche ceno en casa de Carmen y después voy al cine con ella.Tonight I'm having dinner at Carmen's, and afterwards I'm going to the movies with her.

es-u04-l2.title: Hay or está? Finding your way around
es-u04-l2.topic: hay / está(n); prepositions and adverbs of place
es-u04-l2.why: After the simple prepositions, this lesson teaches you to get your bearings: hay to say what there is, está / están to locate a specific thing, and the expressions of place (cerca de, al lado de, enfrente de…). It's the essential foundation for describing your neighborhood or home, and for asking directions later in the unit.
es-u04-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Hay or está?

For “there is” and “there are,” Spanish has a single word that never changes: hay. To say where a specific thing is, it uses estar: está (singular), están (plural). It all depends on what comes next.

What comes nextExample
hayun, una, unos, unasHay un banco cerca. (there's a bank nearby)
haya number, mucho, poco…Hay dos farmacias en la calle. / Hay mucha gente.
haya noun with no article¿Hay pan? / No hay metro.
está / estánel, la, los, las, a proper nameEl banco está a la derecha. / Las llaves están en la mesa.

Two mistakes to avoid

  • “Hay el banco”: impossible. With the definite article, it's está: El banco está aquí.
  • Hay never goes plural: English switches from “there is” to “there are,” but Spanish says Hay dos bancos with the very same word.

The logic is the same as in English: “Is there a bank near here?” / “Where's the bank?” Questions follow the same split:

You're looking for…You ask
any bank at all¿Hay un banco cerca?
a specific bank¿Dónde está el banco de la plaza?
the restroom¿Dónde está el baño?
Hay un supermercado en la plaza. Está al lado de la farmacia.There's a supermarket on the square. It's next to the pharmacy.
", "

Saying where: cerca de, al lado de…

SpanishEnglish
cerca de / lejos denear, close to / far from
al lado denext to
enfrente deopposite, across from
delante de / detrás dein front of / behind
encima de / debajo deon top of, above / under, underneath
a la derecha (de) / a la izquierda (de)on the right (of) / on the left (of)
en el centro (de)in the center (of)
en la esquinaon the corner
todo rectostraight ahead
aquí / ahí / allíhere / there (near you) / over there

Watch out for de + el

Almost all of these expressions end in de. Before a masculine noun, don't forget the contraction: al lado del banco, cerca del metro, enfrente del parque. Before a feminine noun, nothing changes: al lado de la farmacia.

En: in or on

En means both “in” and “on”: Las llaves están en la mesa (on the table), La leche está en la nevera (in the fridge). Encima de is mainly for emphasis: on top, above.

With nothing after it, drop the de: El metro está cerca (the subway is nearby), but El metro está cerca de la plaza. English does the same with “near” and “close to.” In Latin America, “straight ahead” is often derecho; in Spain, it's todo recto.

La parada está enfrente del parque, a la izquierda.The stop is across from the park, on the left.
", "

The neighborhood and the home

To describe a place, you naturally alternate between hay (what there is) and está (where it is). Read this description of an apartment:

En el piso hay un salón, una cocina, dos dormitorios y un baño. El salón está a la derecha; la cocina está al lado del salón.In the apartment, there's a living room, a kitchen, two bedrooms and a bathroom. The living room is on the right; the kitchen is next to the living room.
En el salón hay un sofá y una estantería. El sofá está delante de la ventana.In the living room, there's a sofa and a bookcase. The sofa is in front of the window.

And the neighborhood

To…You say
ask if there's a shop¿Hay una panadería cerca?
ask where it is¿Dónde está la panadería?
ask how far it is¿Está lejos? / ¿Está cerca?
answer with a distanceEstá a cinco minutos a pie.
say there isn't oneNo hay panadería en esta calle.

Notice está a cinco minutos: distance is marked with a, where English says “five minutes away.”

With no hay, the article is often dropped: No hay farmacia, No hay metro. It's just like English “there's no pharmacy.”

es-u04-l3.title: Grocery shopping: quantities
es-u04-l3.topic: quantities, weights, containers; asking and paying
es-u04-l3.why: After hay and está, this lesson takes you to the market: quantities, weights and containers, how Spanish handles “some,” and the phrases for ordering and paying (me pone, ¿algo más?, ¿cuánto es?). It recycles numbers, prices and present-tense irregulars, and sets you up for the restaurant lesson.
es-u04-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Un kilo de, una botella de…

For quantities, Spanish works like English: quantity + de (“of”) + product, with no article. Un kilo de tomates, just like “a kilo of tomatoes.”

SpanishEnglish
un kilo de naranjasa kilo of oranges
medio kilo de fresashalf a kilo of strawberries
un kilo y medio de patatasa kilo and a half of potatoes
un cuarto de kilo de quesoa quarter kilo of cheese
cien gramos de jamóna hundred grams of ham
una docena de huevosa dozen eggs
una botella de aceitea bottle of oil
una lata de atúna can of tuna
un paquete de arroza package of rice
un litro de lechea liter of milk

Medio: no article

“Half a kilo” is medio kilo, with no un in front (never “a half kilo” word for word). And medio agrees in gender: media docena (half a dozen), media botella. After a number, it goes at the end, just like English “and a half”: un kilo y medio, una hora y media. Notice too that English says “a dozen eggs” with no “of,” while Spanish always needs its “of” there too.

Cien gramos: before a noun, 100 is always cien, never “ciento.” You saw this with numbers.

Medio kilo de tomates y una docena de huevos, por favor.Half a kilo of tomatoes and a dozen eggs, please.
", "

No word for “some” here

When English says “some” or “any” for an unspecified amount, Spanish usually says nothing at all: just the bare noun. Don't try to translate “some bread” or “any water.”

EnglishSpanish
I want some bread.Quiero pan.
Do you have any water?¿Tienes agua?
I'm buying some apples.Compro manzanas.
There's no milk.No hay leche.

Un poco de, algo de, nada de

SpanishEnglishExample
un poco dea little, a bit ofUn poco de queso, por favor.
algo desome, something to¿Quieres algo de beber? (would you like something to drink?)
mucho, muchaa lot of, much, manyHay mucha fruta. (no de!)
nada deno… at allNo hay nada de pan. (there's no bread at all)

Careful: “a lot of” is mucho with no de, and as you already know, mucho agrees with its noun: muchas naranjas.

No… nada: Spanish uses a double negative, which standard English avoids. No quiero nada = I don't want anything (literally “I don't want nothing”), and in Spanish that's perfectly correct. On its own, Nada más means “nothing else.”

¿Tienes leche? No, no hay nada de leche.Do you have any milk? No, there's no milk at all.
", "

At the market: ordering and paying

At the market or the corner store, the exchange almost always follows the same pattern. Here are the lines, for the customer and the vendor:

WhoSpanishEnglish
customer¿Quién es el último?Who's last? (to find your place in line)
vendor¿Qué quería?What can I get you?
customerMe pone un kilo de tomates, por favor.Could I have a kilo of tomatoes, please?
customer¿Cuánto cuestan las fresas?How much are the strawberries?
vendorAquí tiene. ¿Algo más?Here you go. Anything else?
customerSí, también quería una docena de huevos.Yes, I'd also like a dozen eggs.
customerNo, nada más, gracias. ¿Cuánto es?No, nothing else, thanks. How much is that?
vendorSon ocho euros con cincuenta.That's eight euros fifty.
vendor¿Con tarjeta o en efectivo?Card or cash?

Me pone…: the shop phrase

Me pone comes from poner (to put), in the polite usted form. Literally, “you put me…” It's the most natural way to order in a shop in Spain, and it doesn't sound rude at all, even without a “could you”: learn it as it is. Quería… (I'd like…) works very well too.

At a Spanish market, there isn't always a visible line: when you arrive, you ask ¿Quién es el último? (or ¿Quién es la última?), and you go after that person.

For prices: ocho euros con cincuenta, or simply ocho cincuenta (€8.50).

es-u04-l4.title: At the restaurant
es-u04-l4.topic: ordering and paying at a restaurant; tapas and the menú del día
es-u04-l4.why: After the market, it's restaurant time: the menú del día, tapas and raciones, and the phrases for ordering and paying, with usted introduced as the polite third-person form. The lesson recycles quantities and stem-changing verbs, and gives you the cultural landmarks (mealtimes, aperitivo, tipping) to eat like a Spaniard.

{"lessons": ["

The menú del día

At lunchtime on weekdays, almost every restaurant in Spain offers a menú del día: a full fixed-price meal (often between 12 and 16 euros). It includes:

SpanishEnglishExamples
el primero (de primero)the first course, the startergazpacho, ensalada mixta, sopa
el segundo (de segundo)the main coursemerluza, pollo asado, filete con patatas
el postre (de postre)dessertflan, fruta, arroz con leche
la bebidathe drinkagua, vino, una caña
el panbreadalways included

Ordering

To say what you'd like, use de primero, de segundo, de postre, and para mí (for me):

Para mí, de primero, el gazpacho, y de segundo, la merluza.For me, the gazpacho to start, and the hake for the main course.
¿Y para beber? Una botella de agua sin gas, por favor.And to drink? A bottle of still water, please.

Careful: don't translate the “for” in “for the main course” or “for dessert”: it's always de primero and so on, never “para primero.” And para mí takes an accent (the pronoun “me”), unlike mi (my).

The English word “menu” (the list of dishes) is la carta. El menú is the fixed-price set meal. To ask for the list: ¿Me trae la carta, por favor?

", "

Talking to the waiter: usted

English has one “you” for everyone. Spanish has a polite “you,” usted, which takes the third person singular, as if you were talking about “him” or “her” (a bit like an old-fashioned “Would sir like…?”). For several people, it's ustedes with the third person plural.

tú (friend, young waiter)usted (polite)
traer (to bring)¿Me traes agua?¿Me trae agua?
recomendar (ie)¿Qué me recomiendas?¿Qué me recomienda?
poder¿Puedes traer la cuenta?¿Puede traer la cuenta?
tener¿Tienes mesa?¿Tiene mesa?

¿Me trae…? (could you bring me…?) comes from traer, which is irregular in the first person (traigo) but regular in the third: trae. Learn it as a set phrase, like me pone at the market.

To…You say
ask for a table¿Tienen mesa para dos? (you're addressing the whole restaurant: ustedes)
ask for a recommendation¿Qué me recomienda?
ask for something¿Me trae un poco de pan, por favor?
ask for the checkLa cuenta, por favor. / ¿Nos trae la cuenta?

In Spain, people are on informal terms a lot, even in bars: a young waiter will often say ¿Qué quieres? to you. In a more traditional restaurant or with an older person, usted is still the right choice. In Latin America, ustedes replaces vosotros in every situation.

Buenas noches. ¿Tienen mesa para cuatro?Good evening. Do you have a table for four?
", "

Tapas, raciones and mealtimes

SpanishWhat it is
una tapaa small plate to go with a drink; in some cities (Granada, León), it comes free with your drink
una media racióna half portion, for tasting
una racióna full portion to share in the middle of the table
una cañaa small glass of draft beer
el aperitivoa drink and a tapa before the meal, around 1 p.m.

Quantities come back here: una ración de calamares, una botella de vino, un vaso de agua, un poco de pan.

Mealtimes

  • La comida (lunch): roughly 2 p.m. to 4 p.m.
  • La cena (dinner): from 9 p.m., often later on weekends.
  • At 7 p.m., lots of kitchens are closed: that's tapas time.

The check and tipping

You have to ask for la cuenta: the waiter won't bring it until you do. La propina (the tip) isn't expected the way it is in the US; people leave a little change if they're happy. Among friends, you'll often hear pagamos a medias (let's split it) or invito yo (it's on me).

Una ración de calamares y dos cañas, por favor.A portion of calamari and two draft beers, please.

es-u04-l5.title: Asking for directions
es-u04-l5.topic: giving directions in the present tense; seguir, girar, cruzar; usted
es-u04-l5.why: This lesson teaches you to ask for and understand directions: phrases for approaching someone, the route verbs (seguir, girar, cruzar, tomar) in the present tense, and ordinal numbers. It sets up the usted forms in the third person and recycles hay / está and prepositions of place, before the unit review; the imperative comes at A2.

{"lessons": ["

Asking the way politely

In the street, you approach a stranger with an “excuse me,” then ask a short question. Spaniards rarely use a full sentence: ¿Para ir a…? (literally “to go to…?”) is enough, where English would say “How do I get to…?”

To…You sayEnglish
approach someone (polite)Perdone…Excuse me…
approach someone (informal)Perdona…Excuse me…
ask the way¿Para ir a la catedral?How do I get to the cathedral?
ask where it is¿Dónde está la estación?Where's the train station?
look for a shop¿Hay una farmacia por aquí?Is there a pharmacy around here?
ask the distance¿Está lejos? ¿Está cerca?Is it far? Is it close?

Perdone and perdona are imperative forms, which you'll study later: learn them as set phrases. Por aquí (around here) is a set phrase too.

Tú or usted?

English has a single “you,” but Spanish makes you choose. With an older stranger, a police officer, or in an upscale shop: usted. With someone your age, out on the street in Spain: tú is perfectly fine. With usted, the verb is in the third person singular:

Verbtúusted
seguir (to keep going)siguessigue
girar (to turn)girasgira
cruzar (to cross)cruzascruza
tomar (to take)tomastoma
llegar (to arrive, to get to)llegasllega
ir (to go)vasva
Perdone, ¿para ir al museo? ¿Está lejos?Excuse me, how do I get to the museum? Is it far?
", "

Giving directions in the present tense

English usually gives directions in the imperative (“turn right”). Spanish can do that too, but it very often uses the present tense, as if narrating the route: sigues todo recto, giras a la derecha… It's like the English “you go straight, then you turn right…” It's perfectly natural, and it's what you'll use for now.

Spanish (tú)Spanish (usted)English
Sigues todo recto.Sigue todo recto.You keep going straight.
Giras a la derecha.Gira a la derecha.You turn right.
Giras a la izquierda.Gira a la izquierda.You turn left.
Cruzas la plaza.Cruza la plaza.You cross the square.
Tomas la primera calle.Toma la primera calle.You take the first street.
Llegas a una plaza.Llega a una plaza.You come to a square.

Ordinal numbers

To count streets: la primera (1st), la segunda (2nd), la tercera (3rd), la cuarta (4th) calle. Unlike English “first,” they agree with the noun: el primer semáforo, la primera calle (primero and tercero drop their -o before a masculine noun, like buen).

Landmarks

el semáforo (the traffic light), la rotonda (the traffic circle), el cruce (the intersection), la esquina (the corner), al final de la calle (at the end of the street).

Seguir changes its e to i: sigo, sigues, sigue. Cruzar is regular: cruzo, cruzas, cruza. In Spain, people also say coger for taking a street or a bus: coges la segunda calle. In Latin America, avoid coger, which is vulgar there: say tomar.

Sigues todo recto hasta el semáforo y giras a la izquierda.You keep going straight as far as the traffic light and turn left.
", "

Understanding the answer

The hardest part is understanding the answer, which is often fast. Listen for the key words: the verb (sigue, gira, cruza, toma), the direction (derecha, izquierda, todo recto) and the landmark (la plaza, el semáforo, la iglesia).

Usted sigue esta calle todo recto hasta la plaza. Cruza la plaza y toma la segunda calle a la derecha. El museo está al final de la calle, enfrente de la iglesia.You go straight along this street as far as the square. You cross the square and take the second street on the right. The museum is at the end of the street, across from the church.
You hearIt means
Está a cinco minutos a pie.It's a five-minute walk.
Está muy cerca.It's really close.
Está un poco lejos: mejor en autobús.It's a bit far: better to take the bus.
No tiene pérdida.You can't miss it.
Hasta el final de la calle.All the way to the end of the street.

If you didn't catch everything, just ask: ¿Puede repetir, por favor? or Más despacio, por favor (more slowly, please). And to double-check: ¿La segunda a la derecha?

Use what you already know: hay for any place (Hay un banco en la esquina), está for a specific place (El banco está en la esquina), and hasta for how far to go.

es-u04-l6.title: Basics review: verbs and prepositions
es-u04-l6.why: This review wraps up units u03 and u04: a full day in Salamanca where you ask for directions, shop for groceries and have lunch, mixing present-tense irregulars, prepositions, hay / está and quantities. Nothing new: it's the moment to check that your present-tense basics hold up in real situations before you start talking about the people close to you in the next unit.

A day in town

This review takes you through a full day in a Spanish city: finding your way, shopping, having lunch. Nothing new: you've already seen everything you need. Here are the key sentences, situation by situation.

looking for a shop¿Hay un mercado por aquí?Sí, está detrás de la plaza.

at the restaurantPara mí, de primero, la sopa.¿Y de segundo?
asking for a recommendation¿Qué me recomienda?El menú del día está muy bien.
finishing the mealLa cuenta, por favor.¿Con tarjeta o en efectivo?
opening hours¿A qué hora cierra el museo?Cierra a las ocho.

Salamanca in a nutshell

A university city in Castile, Salamanca is famous for its Plaza Mayor, its two cathedrals and the carved facade of its university. The city is small: you can do almost everything a pie.

En Salamanca, todo está cerca: puedes ir a pie a todas partes.In Salamanca, everything is close: you can walk everywhere.
", "

Prepositions, hay and está: the summary

PrepositionUseExample
adirection, clock time, personal a, distanceVoy a la plaza a las diez. Está a cinco minutos.
enplace with no movement (in, at, on), transportationEstoy en Salamanca. Voy en tren.
deorigin, possession, material, quantitySoy de Lyon. Un kilo de naranjas.
conwith (conmigo, contigo)¿Vienes conmigo?
parapurpose, recipientUn regalo para Ana. Para mí, el pollo.
desde… hastastarting point and limitSigue todo recto hasta el puente.
entrebetween two thingsEstá entre el banco y el bar.

Hay or está?

Hay + an indefinite noun (un, una, a number, no article): Hay un mercado cerca. Está / están + a definite noun (el, la, a proper name): El mercado está detrás de la plaza.

Contractions

Just two: al (a + el) and del (de + el). Voy al mercado, al lado del puente, Conozco al profesor.

The English speaker's reflex to fix: don't hunt for separate words for “at,” “in” and “on.” “I'm in Salamanca” is Estoy en Salamanca; “I'm going to Salamanca” is Voy a Salamanca.

Hay una librería muy bonita enfrente de la catedral.There's a really nice bookstore across from the cathedral.

The irregulars that keep coming up in town

In town, a dozen irregular verbs do almost all the work. Go over them again in context:

VerbFormExample

cerrarcierraEl museo cierra a las ocho.

recomendarrecomienda¿Qué me recomienda?

Usted, again and again

In town, you often talk to strangers: usted = third person singular. ¿Sabe…?, ¿Puede…?, ¿Tiene…?, Sigue…, Gira…. With friends, back to tú: ¿Sabes…?, ¿Puedes…?

Watch out for this false friend: la librería is a bookstore, not a library (that's la biblioteca).

es-u05-l1.title: Mi, tu, su: possessives
es-u05-l1.why: After the units on the present tense and getting around town, this lesson opens the unit on the people around us: possessives and family vocabulary. It sorts out the traps for English speakers (mis with a plural noun, su for his, her, their and the polite your, nuestra for a feminine noun) and gets you ready to describe people and talk about likes in the next lessons.

{"lessons": ["

Mi, tu, su: whose is it?

Good news first: mi, tu and su don't change for gender, just like English “my,” “your,” “his.” You say mi padre and mi madre. The difference is that the Spanish possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner, so it takes an -s when the thing is plural: mis libros, my books. English “my” never changes; Spanish “my” does.

OwnerOne thingSeveral thingsEnglish
yomimismy
tútutusyour
él, ella, ustedsusushis, her, its, your (polite)
nosotros, nosotrasnuestro, nuestranuestros, nuestrasour
vosotros, vosotrasvuestro, vuestravuestros, vuestrasyour (plural)
ellos, ellas, ustedessusustheir, your (plural, polite)

Nuestro and vuestro: four forms

Only nuestro and vuestro also agree in gender, like an -o / -a adjective: nuestro piso, nuestra casa, nuestros hijos, nuestras amigas. The gender is the gender of the thing, never of the owner: two men say nuestra casa, because casa is feminine.

Vivimos en Toledo con nuestras hijas.We live in Toledo with our daughters.

Never an article in front

Just like in English, there's no article before the possessive: mi casa, never “la mi casa.” If you're also learning Italian, careful: la mia casa doesn't translate word for word.

Don't mix up tu (your) and tú (you, the subject): Tú vives con tu hermano. The possessive never has an accent.

", "

Su: one word, several owners

Su and sus do the work of “his,” “her,” “its,” “their” and the polite “your,” all on their own. That's handy, but sometimes ambiguous: su coche can be Pablo's car, Lucía's, my neighbors'… or yours.

SpanishEnglish
Pablo vive con su madre.Pablo lives with his mother.
Lucía habla con sus primos.Lucía is talking with her cousins.
Mis vecinos venden su piso.My neighbors are selling their apartment.
Señora López, ¿cómo se llama su hijo?Mrs. López, what's your son's name?

Context almost always makes it clear. If there's any doubt, you clarify with de + the person, after the noun: el coche de él (his car), la casa de ella (her house), la maleta de usted (your suitcase).

¿Es el móvil de Diego o el móvil de Marta? — Es el móvil de ella.Is it Diego's phone or Marta's phone? — It's hers.

Mío, tuyo: “mine,” “yours”

In answer to ¿De quién es? (Whose is it?), you'll hear long forms. For now, just learn to recognize them: Es mío (it's mine), Es tuyo (it's yours), Es suyo (it's his, it's hers). Unlike English “mine,” they agree with the object: la maleta → es mía, las llaves → son tuyas.

¿De quién es la chaqueta? — Es mía.Whose jacket is this? — It's mine.

For now, just say Es mi chaqueta: it's correct and natural. Mío and tuyo will come back later.

", "

La familia

Almost all family words come in -o / -a pairs. The masculine plural also covers a mixed group: mis hermanos means “my brothers,” but also “my brothers and sisters,” my siblings.

SpanishEnglishPluralEnglish
el padre / la madrefather / motherlos padresparents
el hermano / la hermanabrother / sisterlos hermanossiblings, brothers and sisters
el hijo / la hijason / daughterlos hijoschildren (sons and daughters)
el abuelo / la abuelagrandfather / grandmotherlos abuelosgrandparents
el nieto / la nietagrandson / granddaughterlos nietosgrandchildren
el tío / la tíauncle / auntlos tíosaunts and uncles
el primo / la primacousin (male / female)los primoscousins
el sobrino / la sobrinanephew / niecelos sobrinosnieces and nephews
el suegro / la suegrafather-in-law / mother-in-lawlos suegrosin-laws (parents-in-law)

For couples: el marido (husband), la mujer (wife, and also “woman”) and la pareja, very common, which means “partner” whatever the gender, and also “couple.”

Tengo dos hermanos: un hermano mayor y una hermana pequeña.I have two siblings: an older brother and a younger sister.
Mis padres viven en Zaragoza y mis abuelos viven con ellos.My parents live in Zaragoza and my grandparents live with them.

False friend: your parents are los padres (father and mother). The word los parientes exists, but it means relatives, the extended family, not “parents.” And a family's “children” are los hijos: ¿Tienes hijos? (Do you have kids?)

es-u05-l2.title: Describing someone
es-u05-l2.topic: describing looks and personality; ser, tener, llevar
es-u05-l2.why: After possessives and the family, this lesson gives you the tools to describe a person: ser for looks and personality, tener for hair and eyes, llevar for clothes. It recycles adjective agreement and the ser / estar contrast, and sets up the lesson on likes.
es-u05-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

¿Cómo es? Looks and personality with ser

To describe what someone is like, Spanish uses ser: it's their identity, what doesn't change from one day to the next. The question is ¿Cómo es? (What's he like? What does she look like?). Don't confuse it with ¿Cómo está?, which asks how someone is doing. English uses “to be” for both; Spanish makes you choose.

¿Cómo es tu hermano? — Es alto, moreno y muy simpático.What's your brother like? — He's tall, dark-haired and really nice.

Looks

SpanishEnglish
alto / altatall
bajo / bajashort (height)
delgado / delgadaslim, thin
moreno / morenadark-haired, dark-skinned
rubio / rubiablond / blonde
pelirrojo / pelirrojared-haired, redhead
guapo / guapagood-looking, handsome, pretty
joven (jóvenes)young
mayor (mayores)older, elderly (polite)

Personality

SpanishEnglish
simpático / simpáticanice, friendly (not “sympathetic”!)
antipático / antipáticaunfriendly, unpleasant
tímido / tímidashy
divertido / divertidafunny, fun
serio / seriaserious
trabajador / trabajadorahardworking
hablador / habladoratalkative, chatty
amablekind, nice
alegrecheerful, upbeat

As you've seen, Spanish adjectives agree in gender and number, while English ones never change: mis primas son simpáticas. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant don't change in the feminine (amable, joven), except those in -or: trabajador → trabajadora.

For an older person, the polite way to put it is Es mayor. To soften a flaw, add un poco: Es un poco tímido. Muy makes it stronger: Es muy divertida. Joven takes an accent in the plural: jóvenes.

", "

Tener and llevar: hair, eyes, clothes

Tener: what you naturally have

As in English, you “have” long hair or blue eyes, but Spanish adds the definite article: Tiene el pelo largo. Tiene los ojos azules. Note that el pelo is singular, just like English “hair.”

SpanishEnglish
tener el pelo largo / cortoto have long / short hair
tener el pelo rizado / lisoto have curly / straight hair
tener el pelo blancoto have white hair
tener los ojos azules / verdes / marronesto have blue / green / brown eyes
tener barba / bigoteto have a beard / a mustache

For a beard or a mustache, Spanish uses no article, where English says “a”: Mi padre tiene barba (my dad has a beard).

Llevar: what you're wearing

Llevar is a regular -ar verb that means “to wear”: clothes, glasses, a bag. It's the verb you use to describe what someone has on today.

Hoy Marta lleva una camiseta blanca y unos vaqueros.Today Marta is wearing a white T-shirt and jeans.
Mi abuela lleva gafas.My grandmother wears glasses.

Colors are adjectives, so they agree, and they come after the noun. Azul, verde and marrón only change in the plural (azules, verdes, marrones); rojo, blanco, negro, amarillo have four forms: una chaqueta negra, unos zapatos negros.

Las gafas is always plural, like English “glasses”: Lleva gafas. And marrón loses its accent in the plural: los ojos marrones.

", "

Parecerse a: who do you look like?

“To look like, to resemble” is parecerse a, a reflexive verb. Its first person is irregular, like conozco: me parezco. Learn it as it is; the other forms are regular. And don't forget the little preposition after it, which English “look like” doesn't need.

Personparecerse
yome parezco
túte pareces
él, ella, ustedse parece
nosotros, nosotrasnos parecemos
vosotros, vosotrasos parecéis
ellos, ellas, ustedesse parecen
Me parezco a mi madre: tengo sus ojos y su pelo.I look like my mother: I have her eyes and her hair.
Mi hermana y yo no nos parecemos nada.My sister and I don't look alike at all.

A full description

A good description strings the three verbs together: ser for the person, tener for features, llevar for clothes.

Mi primo Álvaro es alto y delgado. Tiene el pelo corto y barba. Siempre lleva gafas. Es muy trabajador, pero un poco serio.My cousin Álvaro is tall and slim. He has short hair and a beard. He always wears glasses. He's very hardworking, but a bit serious.

A common trap for English speakers: “he's dark-haired” is not said with tener on its own. You say Es moreno (he's dark-haired) or Tiene el pelo moreno (he has dark hair), but never “tiene moreno.” And moreno can also mean “tanned”: in summer, estoy muy moreno, with estar since it's temporary.

es-u05-l3.topic: gustar, encantar, interesar; the pronouns me, te, le, nos, os, les; también / tampoco
es-u05-l3.why: After the family and describing people, this lesson teaches you to say what you like with gustar, encantar and interesar, where the thing you like controls the verb. It introduces the pronouns me, te, le, nos, os, les and the reactions a mí también / tampoco, which you'll need in every conversation.
es-u05-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Me gusta: the thing you like is in charge

Gustar doesn't work like “to like.” It works like “to be pleasing (to)”: Me gusta el café is literally “coffee is pleasing to me.” The subject of the verb is the thing you like; the person who likes it is a pronoun placed in front: me, te, le, nos, os, les.

The result: the verb doesn't agree with you, but with whatever is pleasing. One thing or one activity → gusta; several things → gustan.

EmphasisPronounOne thingSeveral things
(a mí)meme gusta el caféme gustan los libros
(a ti)tete gusta el caféte gustan los libros
(a él, a ella, a usted)lele gusta el caféle gustan los libros
(a nosotros, a nosotras)nosnos gusta el cafénos gustan los libros
(a vosotros, a vosotras)osos gusta el caféos gustan los libros
(a ellos, a ellas, a ustedes)lesles gusta el caféles gustan los libros

With a verb: always gusta

Before an infinitive, even if there are several, the verb stays singular: Me gusta bailar. Me gusta leer y escuchar música. Where English says “I like dancing” or “I like to dance,” Spanish uses the infinitive.

The article: unlike English

To talk about something in general, Spanish keeps the article, where English drops it: Me gusta el chocolate (I like chocolate), No me gustan las verduras (I don't like vegetables). The negative no goes right at the front: No me gusta.

Me gusta mucho la música, pero no me gustan los conciertos.I really like music, but I don't like concerts.

The trap: saying “yo gusto el café.” Yo gusto would mean “I am pleasing”! Always start with the pronoun: me gusta. And “I like it a lot” is never “me gusta muy”: it's me gusta mucho.

", "

A mí, a Lucía: emphasizing and clarifying

You can add a mí, a ti, a él… before the pronoun. It's like stressing the “I” in English: “I like it.” You're emphasizing or contrasting. But the little pronoun is still required: A mí me gusta, never “a mí gusta.”

A mí me gusta el mar, pero a mi hermano le gusta la montaña.I like the sea, but my brother likes the mountains.

Le and les are ambiguous (him, her, you). To be clear, name the person with a: A Pablo le gusta el fútbol. A mis padres les gusta viajar. Again, le or les stays in the sentence, even if it feels repetitive.

Verbs that work the same way

VerbMeaningExamples
encantarto love (things, activities)Me encanta la playa. Nos encantan las tapas.
interesarto interest¿Te interesa la historia? Me interesan los idiomas.
dolerto hurtMe duele la cabeza. Me duelen los pies.

Encantar is already very strong: “I love it” is simply me encanta. Doler changes its vowel like poder: remember me duele (one thing) and me duelen (several). With body parts, Spanish uses the article, not the possessive: Me duele la cabeza (my head hurts, I have a headache), not “mi cabeza.”

For anything interesting, fascinating or gripping, think interesar: Me interesa mucho el arte.

", "

A mí también, a mí tampoco

To react to someone's likes, Spanish has four short answers, matching English “me too,” “me neither,” “I do” and “I don't.”

Someone saysYou answerEnglish
Me gusta el cine.A mí también.Me too.
Me gusta el cine.A mí no.I don't. / Not me.
No me gusta el fútbol.A mí tampoco.Me neither.
No me gusta el fútbol.A mí sí.I do.

With gustar, the answer starts with a mí (not yo), since the person is the one “to whom it's pleasing.” With a normal verb, you keep yo: Vivo en Madrid. — Yo también.

— A mis hijos no les gustan las verduras. — A mi hija tampoco.— My kids don't like vegetables. — Neither does my daughter.

Asking

The question keeps the same word order, and only the intonation changes (no “do” needed): ¿Te gusta bailar? ¿A tu pareja le gusta cocinar? ¿Qué te gusta hacer los fines de semana?

Remember the logic: agreeing with a positive sentence → también; agreeing with a negative sentence → tampoco. Disagreeing → the opposite of the sentence: no after a positive, sí after a negative. Sí takes an accent when it means “yes” (or “I do”).

es-u05-l4.title: Lo, la, los, las
es-u05-l4.topic: direct object pronouns in the present tense
es-u05-l4.why: After gustar and its pronouns, this lesson introduces the direct object pronouns lo, la, los, las and me, te, nos, os, placed before the conjugated verb. They save you from repeating yourself in every everyday situation (shopping, lost items, invitations) and set up the unit review.
es-u05-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

Lo, la, los, las: no more repeating

Like “it,” “him,” “her” and “them” in English, lo, la, los, las replace a direct object so you don't have to repeat it. They take the gender and number of the noun they replace. The big difference from English: there's no neutral “it.” Masculine and feminine things get different pronouns, and even “them” comes in a masculine and a feminine form.

Noun replacedPronounSpanishEnglish
masculine singularlo¿El pan? Lo compro yo.The bread? I'll buy it.
feminine singularla¿La tarta? La hace mi madre.The cake? My mother's making it.
masculine plurallos¿Los billetes? Los tiene Pablo.The tickets? Pablo has them.
feminine plurallas¿Las llaves? No las encuentro.The keys? I can't find them.

So you always need to know the gender of the Spanish noun: la tarta is feminine (the cake → la), el coche is masculine (the car → lo), even though both are just “it” in English.

Before the verb, not after

English puts “it” after the verb: “I open it,” “I'm waiting for her.” Spanish puts the pronoun in front: lo abro, la espero. Each pronoun is a separate, full word.

¿La ventana? Ahora la abro.The window? I'll open it right now.

Lo can also stand for a whole idea, where English often says nothing at all. It gives you the most useful phrases in the lesson: No lo sé (I don't know), Lo entiendo (I understand).

", "

Me, te, nos, os: when it's people

For people, you use the full set. Me, te, nos, os are the same as for the reflexive verbs you already know (me levanto, te duchas).

PronounEnglishSpanishEnglish
meme¿Me llamas mañana?Will you call me tomorrow?
teyouTe espero en la plaza.I'll wait for you in the square.
lo / lahim / her¿Conoces a Marta? — Sí, la conozco.Do you know Marta? — Yes, I know her.
nosusMis abuelos nos invitan a comer.My grandparents are inviting us to lunch.
osyou (plural)Chicos, os veo a las ocho.Guys, I'll see you at eight.
los / lasthemMis primos son simpáticos: los invito a cenar.My cousins are nice: I'm inviting them to dinner.

The personal a disappears when you use the pronoun: Conozco a Marta becomes La conozco.

Leísmo in Madrid

In Madrid and central Spain, you'll often hear le instead of lo for a man: ¿Conoces a Pablo? — Sí, le conozco. It's accepted for a male person. You just need to recognize it; you can say lo, which is correct everywhere.

Don't confuse this with the le of gustar (le gusta, he or she likes it). With gustar, the pronouns are le and les for everyone; for a direct object, a woman is always la: I see her, I know her.

", "

Where does the pronoun go?

This is the big difference from English: the pronoun goes right before the conjugated verb.

SentenceSpanishEnglish
StatementLo compro.I buy it.
NegativeNo lo compro.I don't buy it.
Question¿Lo compras?Do you buy it?
With a question word¿Dónde lo compras?Where do you buy it?

The no goes before the pronoun, never between the pronoun and the verb: No la conozco, not “la no conozco.”

And with an infinitive?

With querer, poder, tener que + infinitive, you'll hear two positions, both correct: Lo quiero comprar or Quiero comprarlo (attached to the end of the infinitive, no space). For now, just know that it exists; here we're practicing the pronoun before the conjugated verb.

¿Las gafas? Siempre las pierdo. ¿Y tú? ¿Dónde las pones?My glasses? I'm always losing them. What about you? Where do you put them?
¿Mi móvil? No lo encuentro. ¿Lo tienes tú?My phone? I can't find it. Do you have it?

To find the right pronoun, ask yourself two questions: is the noun masculine or feminine in Spanish? Singular or plural? Las llaves → las, el paraguas → lo, los regalos → los.

es-u05-l5.title: Review: talking about your people
es-u05-l5.why: This review wraps up the unit on the people around us: it brings together possessives, describing people, gustar and direct object pronouns, with nothing new. You should be able to introduce your family and friends, say what they like and how often you see them, before moving on to the present tense in motion.
es-u05-l5.json:
{"lessons": ["

Introducing your people

This lesson doesn't introduce anything new: it brings together everything you need to talk about your family and friends. Start with the possessives.

PossessiveExamples
mi / mismi hermano, mis primas
tu / tustu madre, tus abuelos
su / sussu marido (de Ana), sus hijos (de usted)
nuestro, nuestra, nuestros, nuestrasnuestra familia, nuestros padres
vuestro, vuestra, vuestros, vuestrasvuestro piso, vuestras hijas

A reminder of the traps: no article (mi casa), an -s when the thing owned is plural (mi becomes mis), and su, which covers “his, her, its, their, your.”

Describing: ser, tener, llevar

VerbTo talk aboutExample
seridentity, looks, personalityMi tía es baja y muy alegre.
tenerhair, eyes, beard; ageTiene el pelo blanco y setenta años.
llevarclothes, glassesSiempre lleva un sombrero.
estarhow someone is right now, locationHoy está cansada. Está en Cádiz.
Mi hermano mayor se llama Javier. Es alto, moreno y tiene barba. Es muy trabajador, pero un poco serio. Vive en Valencia con su pareja.My older brother's name is Javier. He's tall, dark-haired and has a beard. He's very hardworking, but a bit serious. He lives in Valencia with his partner.

To talk about resemblance: Me parezco a mi padre, Mi hermana y yo nos parecemos mucho. And don't forget the personal a before a person: Conozco a su hermano. Remember too that age goes with tener: Spanish “has” seventy years where English “is” seventy.

", "

What they like

With gustar, encantar and interesar, the thing that's liked is the subject: the verb agrees with it.

Who?PronounVerbWhat?
A mi padrelegustael fútbol.
A mis primoslesencantanlos videojuegos.
A nosotrosnosinteresala historia.
¿A vosotrososgustacocinar?

Three traps to watch for

  • The pronoun is required even when you name the person: A Lucía le gusta, never “a Lucía gusta.”
  • Plural if the thing that's liked is plural: Le gustan los perros.
  • Before one or more infinitives, singular: Le gusta leer y pasear.

Reacting

Someone saysYou answer
A mi madre le encanta bailar.A la mía también. / A la mía no.
A mi hijo no le gustan las verduras.A mi hija tampoco. / A mi hija sí.

In the right-hand column, la mía means “mine”: you can understand it without using it yet. To react simply, say A mi madre también.

", "

Avoiding repetition

When you talk about your people, you quickly end up repeating the same names. Direct object pronouns go before the conjugated verb:

PersonPronounExample
mi abueloloLo visito los domingos.
mi sobrinalaLa veo poco.
mis primoslosLos llamo todas las semanas.
mis amigaslasLas invito a cenar el sábado.
yo / túme / teMi madre me llama todos los días. ¿Te llama tu madre?
nosotros / vosotrosnos / osMis tíos nos invitan. ¿Os invitan a vosotros?
Tengo una sobrina, Ana. La quiero mucho, pero la veo poco porque vive en Lugo. Le encanta dibujar y siempre me da sus dibujos.I have a niece, Ana. I love her very much, but I don't see her much because she lives in Lugo. She loves drawing and she always gives me her drawings.

Notice the difference in this text between la quiero (direct object: I love her) and le encanta (with encantar: she loves it, it delights her).

What about Mexico?

You'll meet lots of Latin American Spanish speakers in Spain. A few differences to recognize:

  • In Mexico, people often say mis papás and mi mamá for “my parents” and “my mom.”
  • In Latin America, vosotros isn't used: people say ustedes (¿A ustedes les gusta?) even among friends.
  • No leísmo: for a man, it's always lo (Lo conozco).

You can stick with the Spanish of Spain: mis padres, vosotros, os. You'll be understood everywhere.

es-u06-l1.title: Right now: estar + gerund
es-u06-l1.why: This lesson opens the unit on the present in motion: estar + gerund for what's happening right now, the handful of irregular gerunds, and seguir + gerund. It rounds out the simple present you've used since the start and sets up the near future with ir a + infinitive.
es-u06-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Estoy trabajando: what's happening right now

To say “I'm working,” Spanish uses estar + gerund: Estoy trabajando. Good news: this works just like the English “be + -ing.” Whenever you talk about what's going on at this very moment, this is the form to use. Just remember that the “be” here is always the verb for states and location, never the one for identity.

Forming the gerund

Take off the infinitive ending and add -ando for -ar verbs, -iendo for -er and -ir verbs. That's the Spanish “-ing.” The gerund never changes: no gender, no number.

InfinitiveStemGerund
hablarhabl-hablando
trabajartrabaj-trabajando
comercom-comiendo
hacerhac-haciendo
escribirescrib-escribiendo
salirsal-saliendo

Estar is conjugated, the gerund stays the same

PersonestarExample
yoestoyestoy hablando
túestásestás comiendo
él, ella, ustedestáestá escribiendo
nosotros, nosotrasestamosestamos cenando
vosotros, vosotrasestáisestáis haciendo
ellos, ellas, ustedesestánestán saliendo
¿Qué estás haciendo? — Estoy cocinando.What are you doing? — I'm cooking.

Unlike the English “-ing” form, the Spanish gerund is never used as a noun (“swimming is fun”) or as an adjective (“a sleeping baby”). Here, it always goes with estar (or seguir, below). And don't forget the accents on estás, está, estáis, están.

", "

Irregular gerunds

There aren't many, and they follow two simple rules.

1. -yendo after a vowel

When the stem ends in a vowel, -iendo becomes -yendo: an i between two vowels is written y.

InfinitiveGerund
leerleyendo
oíroyendo
traertrayendo
iryendo

2. Stem-changing -ir verbs

The -ir verbs that change their vowel in the present also change it in the gerund, but in a smaller step: e → i and o → u.

InfinitiveGerund
pedir (pido)pidiendo
decir (digo)diciendo
repetir (repito)repitiendo
servir (sirvo)sirviendo
seguir (sigo)siguiendo
vestirse (me visto)vistiéndose
preferir (prefiero)prefiriendo
dormir (duermo)durmiendo

Stem-changing -ar and -er verbs stay regular: pensar → pensando, volver → volviendo, empezar → empezando.

With a reflexive verb

The pronoun goes before estar: Me estoy duchando. You can also attach it to the end of the gerund, with a written accent to keep the stress in place: Estoy duchándome. Both are correct; the first is the simpler one.

Los niños se están vistiendo y el bebé está durmiendo.The kids are getting dressed and the baby is sleeping.

Learn three gerunds that come up all the time: leyendo, durmiendo, diciendo. ¿Qué estás diciendo? = What are you saying? What are you talking about?

", "

Simple present or estar + gerund?

The simple present describes a habit or a general truth; estar + gerund describes an action in progress, or a temporary situation. It's the same distinction English makes.

SpanishEnglish
Trabajo en un banco.I work at a bank (that's my job).
Hoy estoy trabajando en casa.Today I'm working from home (not usually).
Leo mucho.I read a lot (in general).
Estoy leyendo un libro muy bueno.I'm reading a really good book (right now).

For a quick question, you'll also hear the simple present: ¿Qué haces? (what are you up to?); but on the phone, to find out what someone is doing at this very moment, ¿Qué estás haciendo? is very natural.

Here's where English and Spanish part ways: this form isn't used with ser, tener or estar itself: Estoy en casa, Tengo hambre. With ir and venir, Spanish prefers the simple present, where English uses “-ing”: Ya voy (I'm coming!). And an English “-ing” for a future plan (“I'm leaving tomorrow”) is never the -ndo form in Spanish.

Seguir + gerund: “still,” “keep on”

Seguir (sigo, sigues, sigue, seguimos, seguís, siguen) + gerund says that an action is continuing. English says “still” or “keep (on) doing.”

Sigo estudiando español.I'm still studying Spanish.
¿Sigues viviendo en Sevilla?Do you still live in Seville?

After seguir, never an infinitive and never an “a”: Sigo trabajando, not “sigo a trabajar” or “sigo trabajar.” Think of English “keep working,” with the “-ing.”

es-u06-l2.topic: near future with ir a; time expressions
es-u06-l2.why: After estar + gerund for what's happening right now, this lesson lets you talk about the near future with ir a + infinitive, pensar + infinitive and the present for schedules. With time expressions, you can finally talk about your plans, while you wait for the future and past tenses of level A2.

{"lessons": ["

Voy a cenar: the near future

Just like English “going to”, Spanish talks about plans with the verb “to go” + infinitive: Voy a cenar con Lucía (I'm going to have dinner with Lucía). The structure is the same as in English: ir conjugated, then a (like “to”), then the infinitive.

Personirir a + infinitive
yovoyvoy a trabajar
túvasvas a comer
él, ella, ustedvava a salir
nosotros, nosotrasvamosvamos a viajar
vosotros, vosotrasvaisvais a venir
ellos, ellas, ustedesvanvan a dormir
¿Qué vas a hacer este fin de semana? — Voy a visitar a mis abuelos.What are you going to do this weekend? — I'm going to visit my grandparents.

Negation and pronouns

No goes in front of ir: No voy a salir esta noche. Pronouns can go in front of ir or attach to the end of the infinitive: Lo voy a comprar = Voy a comprarlo. With a reflexive verb: Me voy a duchar = Voy a ducharme.

The English speaker's trap: English says “I'm going to”, with “-ing”, so it's tempting to use estar + gerund (“estoy yendo a cenar”). Don't: for a plan, Spanish uses the simple present of “ir”. And don't drop the a either: “voy cenar” is wrong. And vamos a + infinitive is also used to suggest something, like “let's”: ¡Vamos a ver! (Let's see!)

", "

When? Time expressions

These expressions place your plan in time. They go at the beginning or at the end of the sentence, as in English.

SpanishEnglish
esta tarde / esta nochethis afternoon / tonight
mañanatomorrow
mañana por la mañanatomorrow morning
pasado mañanathe day after tomorrow
este fin de semanathis weekend
la semana que vienenext week
el próximo mes / el mes que vienenext month
el año que vienenext year
dentro de dos díasin two days
dentro de un mesin a month

Watch out for two traps:

  • Mañana means “tomorrow”, and la mañana means “the morning”: so “tomorrow morning” is mañana por la mañana.
  • English “in two days” has two meanings, and Spanish splits them. Two days from now: dentro de dos días. En dos días means “within two days” (the time it takes to do something).
Dentro de tres semanas vamos a ir a Granada.In three weeks, we're going to go to Granada.

Pensar + infinitive: to plan to, to intend to

Pensar (pienso, piensas, piensa, pensamos, pensáis, piensan) followed directly by an infinitive means “to plan to”, “to intend to”. No a here.

Pienso cambiar de trabajo el año que viene.I'm planning to change jobs next year.

Próximo agrees with the noun (English adjectives never change, Spanish ones do): el próximo mes, la próxima semana. Both forms, la próxima semana and la semana que viene, are equally natural.

", "

The present for a fixed schedule

As in English, the present is often used for a future that's already organized: a timetable, an appointment, a schedule. Where English uses “I'm having dinner…” for an arrangement, Spanish simply uses the simple present.

SpanishEnglish
El tren sale a las ocho.The train leaves at eight.
Mañana trabajo hasta las seis.Tomorrow I'm working until six.
El concierto empieza a las nueve.The concert starts at nine.
El sábado ceno con mis padres.On Saturday I'm having dinner with my parents.

Ir a + infinitive rather stresses an intention or something you can see coming: Voy a llamar a Pablo (I've decided to call him), ¡Va a llover! (it's going to rain, look at the sky).

El avión sale a las siete, así que voy a dormir en el aeropuerto.The plane leaves at seven, so I'm going to sleep at the airport.

Talking about your coming weekend

Este fin de semana voy a estar muy ocupada. El sábado por la mañana voy a hacer la compra y por la tarde voy a ver una película con Laura. El domingo como con mi familia.This weekend I'm going to be very busy. On Saturday morning I'm going to do the grocery shopping, and in the afternoon I'm going to see a movie with Laura. On Sunday I'm having lunch with my family.

The Spanish simple future (cenaré, I will have dinner) also exists, but you'll see it later. In everyday life, ir a + infinitive and the present are enough to talk about your plans.

es-u06-l3.title: Linking your ideas
es-u06-l3.topic: simple connectors: y/e, o/u, pero, porque, cuando, también, además, entonces
es-u06-l3.why: After estar + gerund and ir a + infinitive, this lesson teaches you to link your sentences: y/e, o/u, pero/sino, porque, cuando and storytelling connectors. You move from isolated sentences to a short, smooth account of your routine, which prepares you for the big review conversation.

{"lessons": ["

Y, o, pero: little words that change shape

Y (and), o (or) and pero (but) are used just like in English. But y and o change shape in front of certain sounds, to avoid two identical vowels running together.

Y becomes e before the “ee” sound

In front of a word that starts with i- or hi- (the h is silent), y becomes e:

SpanishEnglish
padre e hijofather and son
español e inglésSpanish and English
Lucía e InésLucía and Inés
geografía e historiageography and history

Exception: in front of hie-, pronounced like “yeh”, you keep y: agua y hielo (water and ice).

O becomes u before the “o” sound

In front of a word that starts with o- or ho-, o becomes u: siete u ocho, uno u otro, mujer u hombre.

Pero or sino?

English has only one “but”. Spanish has two:

  • pero adds a contrasting idea: Es caro, pero me gusta (it's expensive, but I like it).
  • sino corrects something after a negative: “not this, but that”. No es rojo sino verde. No vivo en Madrid sino en Toledo.
No hablo italiano sino francés, pero entiendo un poco el italiano.I don't speak Italian but French, but I understand a bit of Italian.

The test: if you can say “not… but rather…”, it's sino. Otherwise, it's pero. Don't confuse sino (one word) with si no (if… not).

", "

Porque, por qué, cuando

Porque and ¿por qué?

You've already seen them: ¿por qué?, two words with an accent, asks the question (why?); porque, one word with no accent, gives the answer (because).

¿Por qué estudias español? — Porque mi pareja es de Murcia.Why are you studying Spanish? — Because my partner is from Murcia.

Cuando + present: habits

Cuando (when), with no accent, links two habitual actions. As in English, you use the present on both sides.

SpanishEnglish
Cuando llego a casa, me ducho.When I get home, I take a shower.
Cuando hace calor, vamos a la playa.When it's hot, we go to the beach.
Leo cuando estoy en el metro.I read when I'm on the subway.

In a question, ¿cuándo? takes an accent: ¿Cuándo comes? In a sentence that links two ideas, no accent: Como cuando tengo hambre.

Careful: cuando + present is for habits. For a future moment (“when I'm in Madrid next month”), English still uses the present, but Spanish uses another mood, the subjunctive, which you'll see later. For now, stick to habits.

", "

Telling your day smoothly

To link the steps of a routine, here are the most useful connectors.

SpanishEnglish
primerofirst
luegothen, next
despuésafter that, afterwards
más tardelater
entoncesso, then
ademásbesides, what's more
tambiénalso, too
al finalin the end, finally

Después de, antes de + infinitive

In front of a noun or an infinitive, después and antes take de: después de comer (after eating), antes de dormir (before sleeping), después del trabajo (after work). English uses the “-ing” form after “after” and “before”; Spanish always uses the infinitive after a preposition, never the gerund.

Primero me levanto y desayuno. Luego voy a la oficina en metro. Después de comer, tomo un café con mis compañeros. Cuando salgo del trabajo, voy al gimnasio o paseo un poco. Al final, ceno y leo antes de dormir.First I get up and have breakfast. Then I go to the office by subway. After lunch, I have a coffee with my coworkers. When I leave work, I go to the gym or go for a little walk. Finally, I have dinner and read before going to sleep.

Además and después have a written accent. Además means “besides, what's more”: it adds an argument in the same direction. Entonces is also used to draw a conclusion, like “so”: Estoy cansado, entonces voy a dormir.

es-u06-l4.title: False friends and first expressions
es-u06-l4.topic: common false friends and everyday expressions
es-u06-l4.why: Before the big review of the basics, this lighter lesson defuses the false friends that trip up English speakers (embarazada, constipado, éxito, largo…) and gives you the expressions that make a conversation sound natural in Spain: vale, venga, ¡qué pena!, no pasa nada.
es-u06-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

False friends that trip up English speakers

Spanish and English share thousands of words from Latin, so you can often guess what a word means. That's a gift, but also a trap: some words look familiar and mean something completely different. Here are the most common ones, and the most embarrassing.

SpanishMeansWatch out
embarazadapregnantembarrassed → avergonzada
constipado / constipadahaving a cold, congestedconstipated → estreñido
exquisito / exquisitadelicious (a dish)used mostly for food
la salidathe exitfrom salir (to go out), not a “sale”
el éxitosuccessexit → la salida
largo / largalongnot “large”! wide → ancho
contestarto answerto contest, dispute → discutir, protestar
la carpetathe folder, the bindercarpet, rug → la alfombra
el vasothe glass (for drinking)vase → el jarrón
la ropaclothesnot “rope”! a dress → el vestido
molestarto bother, to disturbnothing to do with “molest”
quitarto take off, to removeto quit → dejar, salir de

The most famous one: an English speaker who wants to say “I'm embarrassed” and says estoy embarazado announces… that he's pregnant. For embarrassment, say me da vergüenza (I'm embarrassed), and learn it as a set phrase.

", "

Examples so you never get them wrong again

The best way to lock in a false friend is to see it in an everyday sentence.

Mi hermana está embarazada: ¡voy a ser tío!My sister is pregnant: I'm going to be an uncle!
No voy a trabajar hoy: estoy muy constipado.I'm not going to work today: I have a really bad cold.
La tortilla de tu madre está exquisita.Your mother's tortilla is delicious.
Perdone, ¿dónde está la salida?Excuse me, where's the exit?
Su restaurante tiene mucho éxito.His restaurant is very successful.
Esta calle es muy larga, pero no es muy ancha.This street is very long, but it isn't very wide.
Te escribo, pero nunca contestas.I write to you, but you never answer.
¿Me das un vaso de agua? Los papeles están en la carpeta verde.Can you give me a glass of water? The papers are in the green folder.
¿Te molesta la música? — No, no me molesta.Does the music bother you? — No, it doesn't bother me.
Me quito la chaqueta porque hace calor.I'm taking off my jacket because it's hot.

Notice that molestar works like gustar: the thing that bothers you is the subject (me molesta el ruido, me molestan los coches).

Learn false friends in pairs: largo / ancho, la salida / el éxito, el vaso / el jarrón. Linking the trap with the right word helps you stop mixing them up. Two more classics for later: actual means “current”, not “actual”, and la librería is a bookstore, not a library.

Everyday expressions

These little words come up in every conversation in Spain. Knowing them will make you sound much more natural.

ExpressionMeaningExample
valeOK, all right¿Quedamos a las ocho? — Vale.
vengacome on!; OK then; right, bye¡Venga, vamos! / Venga, hasta luego.
¡qué guay!so cool! awesome! (informal)¿Vas a Ibiza? ¡Qué guay!
¡qué pena!what a shame!¿No puedes venir? ¡Qué pena!
no pasa nadano worries, it's fine— Lo siento. — No pasa nada.
¡ojo!watch out! careful!¡Ojo, el suelo está mojado!
¿qué tal?how are you? how's it going?¡Hola! ¿Qué tal?
de nadayou're welcome— Gracias. — De nada.
¡qué rico!so tasty! yum!¡Qué rica está la paella!

A few details

  • Vale is typically Spanish: you'll hear it ten times a minute. In Latin America, people tend to say está bien or ok.
  • ¡Qué guay! is informal and specific to Spain. In Mexico, people say ¡qué padre!, in Argentina ¡qué bueno!
  • ¡Qué pena! means “what a pity”, nothing to do with pain or a penalty: it's light.
  • Rico means “rich”, but for food it means “tasty”; it agrees with the noun: ¡Qué ricas están las croquetas!

The pattern ¡qué + adjective! works with lots of words: ¡Qué bonito! (how beautiful!), ¡Qué raro! (how weird!), ¡Qué bien! (great!). Don't forget the opening ¡ and the accent on qué.

es-u06-l5.title: Basics review: ten minutes of conversation
es-u06-l5.why: This big review wraps up the basics level: it brings together the regular and irregular present, ser / estar, gustar, pronouns, estar + gerund and ir a + infinitive in one long conversation. You should be able to keep going for ten minutes with a stranger about your life, your tastes and your plans before tackling the past at level A2.
es-u06-l5.json:
{"lessons": ["

The present in all its forms

You've reached the end of the basics level. This lesson introduces nothing new: it gathers what you need to hold a real conversation. It all starts with the present.

Regular endings

Personhablarcomervivir
yohablocomovivo
túhablascomesvives
él, ella, ustedhablacomevive
nosotros, nosotrashablamoscomemosvivimos
vosotros, vosotrashabláiscoméisvivís
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablancomenviven

Irregular verbs to know by heart

TypeForms
Irregular first personhago, pongo, salgo, tengo, vengo, digo, doy, sé, conozco, me parezco
Completely irregularsoy, eres, es…; estoy, estás, está…; voy, vas, va…
e → iequiero, pienso, prefiero, empiezo, cierro
o → uepuedo, duermo, vuelvo, encuentro, cuesta
e → ipido, repito, sirvo, sigo

Remember the “boot”: nosotros and vosotros keep the vowel of the infinitive (podemos, queréis, pedimos).

Ser, estar and estar + gerund

English has only “to be”; Spanish splits it in two, and also uses the second one for actions in progress.

FormUseExample
seridentity, job, origin, personalitySoy profesora. Es de Bilbao.
estarlocation, temporary stateEstoy cansado. ¿Dónde está el baño?
estar + gerundaction in progressEstoy preparando la cena.
seguir + gerundaction that's still going onSigo viviendo en Bilbao.

In conversation, the subject is usually left out, because the verb ending already says who: Trabajo en un hotel is enough, no need for “I”. Use yo only to insist or to contrast: Yo trabajo, y él estudia.

", "

Likes, pronouns and plans

To…You sayRemember
Say what you likeMe gusta el cine. Me encantan los pintxos.The verb agrees with the thing you like.
Talk about other people's likesA mi pareja le gusta correr.a + person + le / les
ReactA mí también. A mí tampoco. A mí sí. A mí no.también after a yes, tampoco after a no
Avoid repeating¿El vino? Lo compro yo. ¿Conoces a Ana? La conozco.lo, la, los, las before the verb
Talk about your plansVoy a viajar a Asturias. Pienso aprender a cocinar.ir a + infinitive; pensar + infinitive
Give a scheduleLa cena empieza a las nueve.present
Talk about your familyMi hermana y su marido viven en Getafe.mi, tu, su, nuestro, vuestro

Linking your sentences

A smooth conversation links ideas together: y / e, o / u, pero, sino (after a negative), porque, cuando, además, entonces, luego, después, al final.

Soy de Valencia, pero vivo en Bilbao porque mi pareja es de aquí. Me encanta la ciudad y, además, la comida es exquisita. El año que viene vamos a buscar un piso más grande.I'm from Valencia, but I live in Bilbao because my partner is from here. I love the city and, what's more, the food is delicious. Next year we're going to look for a bigger apartment.

In this text, más grande (bigger) is a set phrase: comparisons will be covered at level A2. You already know everything else.

", "

Keeping a conversation going for ten minutes

Holding a conversation doesn't mean understanding everything: it means asking questions, reacting, buying time and asking for help without panicking.

Questions that get the conversation going

SpanishEnglish
¿De dónde eres?Where are you from?
¿A qué te dedicas?What do you do (for a living)?
¿Dónde vives? ¿Te gusta vivir aquí?Where do you live? Do you like living here?
¿Qué te gusta hacer los fines de semana?What do you like to do on weekends?
¿Tienes hermanos? ¿Cómo son?Do you have any brothers or sisters? What are they like?
¿Qué vas a hacer en verano?What are you going to do this summer?

Reacting, buying time, asking for help

To…You say
React¿En serio? ¡Qué guay! ¡Qué pena! ¡Qué bien! Vale.
Buy timePues… Bueno… A ver…
Say you don't understandPerdona, no entiendo. ¿Puedes repetir, por favor?
Ask someone to speak slowly¿Puedes hablar más despacio?
Look for a word¿Cómo se dice « ... » en español? ¿Qué significa « ... »?
Bounce the question back¿Y tú? ¿Y a ti?

Perdona (informal, with tú) and perdone (formal, with usted) are worth learning as set phrases. And never forget to send the question back: ¿Y tú? after a simple question, ¿Y a ti? after a question with gustar. English uses “And you?” for both, Spanish doesn't.

— Me encanta el teatro. ¿Y a ti? — A mí también, pero prefiero el cine.— I love the theater. And you? — Me too, but I prefer the movies.

In Spain, people interrupt each other and talk loudly: it's not rude, it's enthusiasm! Feel free to drop in a ¡Qué guay! or an ¿En serio? while the other person is talking.
