es-u07-l1.title: The present perfect: he hablado
es-u07-l1.topic: pretérito perfecto; regular participles; hoy, esta semana, ya, todavía no, alguna vez
es-u07-l1.why: The first past tense of the course: after the present, ir a + infinitive and estar + gerund, you discover the pretérito perfecto, built like the English present perfect. The lesson focuses on what differs from English (always haber, never anything between haber and the participle, used in Spain for anything that happened today or this week) and prepares the contrast with the indefinido in the next lesson.
es-u07-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

He hablado: haber + participle

Good news: the pretérito perfecto is built just like the English present perfect (“I have spoken”), with an auxiliary in the present followed by a past participle. The auxiliary is haber, a verb used almost only for this (“to have” in the sense of owning is always tener).

hablarcomervivir
yohe habladohe comidohe vivido
túhas habladohas comidohas vivido
él, ella, ustedha habladoha comidoha vivido
nosotros, nosotrashemos habladohemos comidohemos vivido
vosotros, vosotrashabéis habladohabéis comidohabéis vivido
ellos, ellas, ustedeshan habladohan comidohan vivido

The participle: -ado or -ido

-ar verbs take -ado: trabajar → trabajado, llegar → llegado. -er and -ir verbs take -ido: comer → comido, salir → salido. Even verbs that are irregular in the present often have a regular participle: ir → ido, ser → sido, estar → estado, tener → tenido, poder → podido, querer → querido.

Three things to watch

  • Always haber, never tener, even though English uses “have” for both: he ido (I've gone), ha llegado (he has arrived), me he levantado (I've gotten up).
  • The participle never changes, just like in English: Marta ha llegado, las chicas han salido, la he llamado (I've called her).
  • Never separate haber from the participle. English says “I have already eaten”, “I have not seen”; in Spanish, pronouns and no go in front of haber, and nothing goes in between.
No lo he comprado. Me he duchado.I haven't bought it. I've taken a shower.

“I've gotten up” = me he levantado: the pronoun, then he, then the participle in -o, whether you're a man or a woman. Never “he me levantado”.

", "

A past that still touches today

The perfecto is used for a past connected to the present, a bit like the English present perfect: an action done in a period that isn't over yet (today, this week, this year), or a life experience with no specific date. But Spain, and especially Madrid, goes further than English: it uses it for anything that happened today, even with a precise time like “this morning”, where English switches to the past simple. For “yesterday” or “last year”, Spanish uses another tense, the indefinido, which you'll see in the next lesson.

Time markerExampleTranslation
hoyHoy he trabajado en casa.I've worked from home today.
esta mañanaEsta mañana he desayunado con Pablo.This morning I had breakfast with Pablo.
esta semanaEsta semana hemos comido fuera tres veces.This week we've eaten out three times.
este añoEste año he viajado mucho.This year I've traveled a lot.
yaYa he terminado.I've already finished.
todavía noTodavía no he comido.I haven't eaten yet.
nuncaNunca he estado en Cádiz.I've never been to Cádiz.
alguna vez¿Has probado alguna vez el pulpo?Have you ever tried octopus?

Ya or alguna vez: “already” or “ever”

English separates these two ideas, and so does Spanish. Ya means it's done: Ya he comido (I've already eaten, no need to do it anymore). Alguna vez asks whether it has happened at least once in your life: ¿Has estado alguna vez en Sevilla? You answer with nunca, una vez, dos veces, muchas veces.

¿Has comido ya? — No, todavía no.Have you eaten yet? — No, not yet.
¿Has estado alguna vez en Sevilla? — Sí, dos veces.Have you ever been to Seville? — Yes, twice.

Nunca at the beginning of a sentence is used without no: Nunca he estado en Cádiz. Placed after the verb, it needs no in front: No he estado nunca en Cádiz. Yes, a double negative: in Spanish it's correct.

In Latin America, and in a few regions of Spain (Galicia, Asturias, the Canary Islands), the perfecto is used much less. This course follows the usage of Madrid.

", "

Eight irregular participles

The vast majority of participles are regular. Here are the eight most common irregular ones: learn them by heart, because they come up all the time. Just like English “done”, “said” or “written”, they don't follow the rule (dicho / said, escrito / written).

InfinitiveParticipleExampleTranslation
hacerhecho¿Qué has hecho hoy?What have you done today?
decirdicho¿Qué ha dicho Marta?What did Marta say?
vervistoEsta semana he visto dos películas.This week I've seen two movies.
escribirescritoYa he escrito el correo.I've already written the email.
volvervueltoMis padres todavía no han vuelto.My parents haven't come back yet.
ponerpuesto¿Dónde has puesto las llaves?Where have you put the keys?
abrirabiertoHoy han abierto un bar nuevo.A new bar opened today.
romperrotoLos niños han roto un vaso.The kids have broken a glass.

Hecho is spelled with an h: it's the participle of hacer. And when the ending -ido follows an a, an e or an o, it takes a written accent: leer → leído, oír → oído.

All together

Hoy me he levantado temprano, he escrito tres correos y he vuelto a casa a las seis.Today I got up early, wrote three emails and came back home at six.
¿Has visto a Javier esta semana? — No, todavía no lo he visto.Have you seen Javier this week? — No, I haven't seen him yet.

Notice the a in front of Javier: it's the “personal a” you already know (he visto a Javier, but he visto la película). And the pronoun lo always goes in front of haber.

es-u07-l2.title: The simple past: el indefinido
es-u07-l2.topic: pretérito indefinido of regular verbs; ayer, el año pasado, en 2019
es-u07-l2.why: After the perfecto, here's the other big past tense, the indefinido, the one used for yesterday, last week or last year. The lesson nails down the regular endings, the written accent (hablo / habló), the spellings llegué, busqué, empecé, and above all the choice between perfecto and indefinido depending on the time marker, before the irregular verbs of the next lesson.
es-u07-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

The endings of the indefinido

The pretérito indefinido is the equivalent of the English simple past (“she spoke”, “we ate”): a completed action, used all the time in everyday speech. For regular verbs, there's one set of endings for -ar and a single shared set for -er and -ir.

hablarcomervivir
yohablécomíviví
túhablastecomisteviviste
él, ella, ustedhablócomióvivió
nosotros, nosotrashablamoscomimosvivimos
vosotros, vosotrashablasteiscomisteisvivisteis
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablaroncomieronvivieron

The written accent changes everything

The yo and él forms have a written accent on the last syllable. Without it, the word becomes a different tense:

PresentIndefinido
hablo: I speakhabló: he spoke
trabajo: I worktrabajó: she worked
llego: I arrivellegó: he arrived

For nosotros, -ar and -ir verbs have the same form in the present and in the indefinido: hablamos, vivimos. The time marker makes the difference: Ayer hablamos con Carmen (yesterday we spoke with Carmen).

Another very common trap, even among Spaniards: the tú form never takes a final -s. You write hablaste, comiste, not “hablastes”.

", "

A finished time

The indefinido tells of an action completed in a period that's also over, cut off from the present: yesterday, last week, last year, in 2019. It's the partner of the perfecto from the previous lesson: the time marker decides, much like the English choice between “I worked” and “I've worked”.

Time markerExampleTranslation
ayerAyer cené con Lucía.Yesterday I had dinner with Lucía.
anocheAnoche volvimos tarde.Last night we came back late.
anteayerAnteayer llovió mucho.The day before yesterday it rained a lot.
el lunes pasadoEl lunes pasado empecé un curso.Last Monday I started a course.
la semana pasadaLa semana pasada trabajé mucho.Last week I worked a lot.
el año pasadoEl año pasado viajaron a Italia.Last year they traveled to Italy.
en 2019, en agostoEn 2019 viví en Londres.In 2019 I lived in London.
hace dos añosHace dos años conocí a Marta.Two years ago I met Marta.

Perfecto or indefinido?

Ask yourself just one question: is the period over? If it's still going on (hoy, esta semana, este año), it's the perfecto. If it's over (ayer, la semana pasada, el año pasado), it's the indefinido.

Period not over: perfectoPeriod over: indefinido
Hoy he comido paella.Ayer comí paella.
Esta semana he trabajado mucho.La semana pasada trabajé mucho.
Este año he viajado a Roma.El año pasado viajé a Roma.

Hace + length of time = “ago”, but it comes first: hace dos años (two years ago), hace una semana (a week ago). Don't confuse it with hay, which means “there is, there are”.

In Latin America, people use the indefinido almost everywhere, even with “today”, just like American English: Hoy comí paella. In Madrid, people say Hoy he comido paella.

", "

Spelling: llegué, busqué, empecé

In the yo form, the ending -é forces some verbs to change a letter to keep the same sound. It's only a matter of spelling: the pronunciation doesn't change.

Verbs ending in…ChangeExamples (yo)But (él)
-garg → gullegué, pagué, juguéllegó, pagó, jugó
-carc → qubusqué, saqué, toquébuscó, sacó, tocó
-zarz → cempecé, crucé, comencéempezó, cruzó, comenzó

Without the u, “llegé” would be pronounced with a jota (the throaty h sound); without the qu, “buscé” would be read with the sound of z. And in Spanish you almost never write ze or zi: you write ce, ci.

Ayer llegué tarde, busqué un taxi y pagué veinte euros.Yesterday I arrived late, looked for a taxi and paid twenty euros.

No more stem changes!

Good news: the -ar and -er verbs that change their stem in the present are completely regular in the indefinido. The “boot” disappears:

PresentIndefinido
vuelvo (volver)volví, volvió
pienso (pensar)pensé, pensó
encuentro (encontrar)encontré, encontró
empiezo (empezar)empecé, empezó
juego (jugar)jugué, jugó

-ir verbs like pedir or dormir change a little in the third person: you'll see them in the next lesson, along with the big irregular verbs (ser, ir, tener, hacer…).

es-u07-l3.title: Irregular indefinidos
es-u07-l3.topic: indefinido of ser/ir, tener, estar, hacer, poder, poner, venir, decir, querer, saber, dar
es-u07-l3.why: After the regular endings, this lesson gives you the irregular indefinidos of the verbs you need most to tell a story: ser and ir, tener, estar, hacer, poder, poner, venir, decir, querer, saber, dar, plus leyó, durmió, pidió. With them, you can finally talk about a vacation or a memorable day, while avoiding the typical mistakes (fuí, hico, dijieron).

{"lessons": ["

Fui, fuiste, fue: ser and ir

Surprise: in the indefinido, ser and ir have exactly the same forms. The context tells you which verb it is, and in practice you'll almost never get it wrong. (English “to be” and “to go” are irregular in the past too: was, went.)

ser / irdarver
yofuidivi
túfuistedisteviste
él, ella, ustedfuediovio
nosotros, nosotrasfuimosdimosvimos
vosotros, vosotrasfuisteisdisteisvisteis
ellos, ellas, ustedesfuerondieronvieron
El sábado fui a Toledo. Fue un día increíble.On Saturday I went to Toledo. It was an amazing day.

In the first sentence, fui + a + place: it's ir. In the second, fue + adjective: it's ser.

Dar is an -ar verb, but in the indefinido it takes the -er / -ir endings, like ver: di, diste, dio. These very short forms have no written accent.

Classic mistake: writing “fuí” or “dió”. One-syllable forms don't take an accent: fui, fue, di, dio, vi, vio.

", "

Tuve, estuve, hice: irregular stems

Many very common verbs change their stem in the indefinido, a bit like English “have → had”, “do → did”. The good news is that they all share the same endings, with no written accent: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron.

InfinitiveStemyoél, ella, usted
tenertuv-tuvetuvo
estarestuv-estuveestuvo
poderpud-pudepudo
ponerpus-pusepuso
sabersup-supesupo
hacerhic-hicehizo
venirvin-vinevino
quererquis-quisequiso
decirdij-dijedijo
tenerhacerdecir
yotuvehicedije
tútuvistehicistedijiste
él, ella, ustedtuvohizodijo
nosotros, nosotrastuvimoshicimosdijimos
vosotros, vosotrastuvisteishicisteisdijisteis
ellos, ellas, ustedestuvieronhicierondijeron

The traps

  • hizo is spelled with a z (not “hico”) to keep the sound.
  • decir gives dijeron, with no i: “dijieron” is a mistake.
  • No written accent: tuve, tuvo, hice, pudo, unlike regular verbs (hablé, habló).

English “I was”, “it was” has two Spanish versions: estuve for a place (estuve en Cádiz), fui / fue for identity or a judgment (fue fantástico, it was fantastic). It's the ser and estar rule you already know.

", "

Leyó, durmió, pidió: only in the third person

Some verbs are regular everywhere except in the third person singular and plural. For all the other persons, you conjugate normally.

TypeVerbsyoélellos
i → yleer, creer, oírleíleyóleyeron
o → udormirdormídurmiódurmieron
e → ipedir, repetir, servir, seguir, preferirpedípidiópidieron
Anoche dormí mal, pero mi hermano durmió diez horas.Last night I slept badly, but my brother slept ten hours.
En el restaurante pedí pescado y Marta pidió paella.At the restaurant I ordered fish and Marta ordered paella.

For leer, the i between two vowels becomes y: you write leyó, never “leió”. Same for creer (creyó) and oír (oyó).

Telling a memorable day

El verano pasado fuimos a Mallorca. Estuvimos diez días en un pueblo, hicimos muchas excursiones y un día vimos delfines. ¡Fue increíble!Last summer we went to Mallorca. We stayed ten days in a village, went on lots of excursions, and one day we saw dolphins. It was amazing!

Make a list of the ten most useful yo forms and repeat them out loud: fui, estuve, tuve, hice, pude, puse, vine, dije, quise, supe. Everything else follows from them.

es-u07-l4.title: Review: telling about a weekend
es-u07-l4.why: The review of the unit on the past: you bring together the perfecto and the indefinido, regular and irregular, and learn to choose between them using the time marker. With primero, luego, después and al final, you can tell about a whole weekend smoothly, like on Monday morning at the office.

{"lessons": ["

Perfecto or indefinido: the time marker decides

You now have two tenses for the past: “I've done” and “I did”. English has the same pair and the logic is close, with one big difference: Spain uses the perfecto for anything that happened today, even “this morning” once the morning is over. The principle: is the period in which the action happened over or not?

Perfecto: period not overIndefinido: period over
hoy (today)ayer, anteayer, anoche
esta mañana, esta tardeel lunes, el sábado pasado
esta semana, este mesla semana pasada, el mes pasado
este año, este veranoel año pasado, en 2019, en agosto
ya, todavía nohace dos días, hace un año
nunca, alguna vez, muchas vecesun día, el verano de 2018
Esta mañana he desayunado en casa, pero ayer desayuné en una cafetería.This morning I had breakfast at home, but yesterday I had it in a café.

The weekend case

On Monday, the weekend is over: people ask ¿Qué tal el fin de semana? ¿Qué hiciste? and answer in the indefinido: El sábado fui al cine. On Sunday evening, on the other hand, it isn't over yet: Este fin de semana he descansado mucho.

If you're unsure, look for the time marker in the sentence. No marker at all? If the action has just happened or still affects the present (¿Qué ha dicho?, He perdido las llaves), use the perfecto, just like “What has he said?” or “I've lost my keys” in English. If you're telling a story that's over and done with, use the indefinido.

", "

Telling things in order

To tell about your weekend, you need a few little words that organize the story. They work like their English equivalents and usually go at the beginning of the sentence.

SpanishEnglishExample
primerofirstPrimero desayunamos en el hotel.
luegothen, nextLuego fuimos al Retiro.
despuésafter that, afterwardsDespués comimos en un bar.
más tardelaterMás tarde vimos una película.
al finalin the end, finallyAl final volvimos a casa a las doce.

Después de + infinitive = “after …ing”: Después de comer, dimos un paseo (after eating, we went for a walk). English uses the -ing form, Spanish a plain infinitive.

A weekend, told

El sábado me levanté tarde. Primero hice la compra, luego comí con mis padres y después fui al cine con Elena. Al final volví a casa muy cansado. Hoy he dormido hasta las diez.On Saturday I got up late. First I did the grocery shopping, then I had lunch with my parents, and after that I went to the movies with Elena. In the end I came home very tired. Today I slept until ten.

The whole Saturday story is in the indefinido; only the last sentence, with hoy, switches to the perfecto (even though English says “slept” here).

Watch the meaning of comer: in Spain, it means “to eat”, but also “to have lunch” (the midday meal, around 2 p.m.): comí con mis padres = I had lunch with my parents. La comida is lunch. Dinner is la cena.

es-u08-l1.title: When I was little: the imperfect
es-u08-l1.why: After the perfecto and the indefinido, here's the third past tense, the imperfecto, used to describe things and talk about past habits: what English says with “used to”, “would” or “was …ing”. With only three irregular verbs (era, iba, veía), you can talk about your childhood, your school and your vacations at your grandparents', before learning to combine it with the indefinido.
es-u08-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

The imperfect: a very regular conjugation

The imperfecto has no single English equivalent: it covers “I used to play”, “I would play (every summer)”, “I was playing” and often a plain “I played” when it means a habit or a description. The good news: it's the easiest tense in Spanish, with two sets of endings, one for -ar and one for -er / -ir.

jugarcomervivir
yojugabacomíavivía
tújugabascomíasvivías
él, ella, ustedjugabacomíavivía
nosotros, nosotrasjugábamoscomíamosvivíamos
vosotros, vosotrasjugabaiscomíaisvivíais
ellos, ellas, ustedesjugabancomíanvivían

What to watch

  • -ar verbs are spelled with a b: jugaba, hablaba, never with a v.
  • Only the nosotros form of -ar verbs has an accent: jugábamos, estábamos.
  • For -er and -ir, every form has an accent on the í: comía, vivíamos, teníais.
  • The yo and él forms are identical (jugaba): add the subject if the sentence isn't clear.

No stem changes in the imperfect: jugar → jugaba, dormir → dormía, querer → quería. And you already know quería: it's the polite “I'd like” you use in cafés and shops.

", "

Only three irregular verbs: era, iba, veía

In the whole language, only three verbs are irregular in the imperfect. Even tener, hacer or estar, so complicated in the indefinido, are perfectly regular here: tenía, hacía, estaba.

serirver
yoeraibaveía
túerasibasveías
él, ella, ustederaibaveía
nosotros, nosotraséramosíbamosveíamos
vosotros, vosotraseraisibaisveíais
ellos, ellas, ustedeseranibanveían
De pequeño era muy tímido, iba al colegio a pie y veía dibujos animados todas las tardes.As a kid, I was very shy, I used to walk to school and I watched cartoons every afternoon.

And hay? In the imperfect, it becomes había: En mi pueblo había un río. (In my village there was a river.) Just one form, even before a plural: había muchos niños (there were lots of kids).

Compare with the indefinido from the previous lessons: fui (I went, once) / iba (I used to go, I was going); tuve (I had, I got, at one point) / tenía (I had, over a period).

", "

When to use it

The imperfect describes the past and talks about things that happened repeatedly. Here's the trap for English speakers: English often uses the plain past for these (“When I was a kid, I played outside”), but Spanish needs the imperfect. The test: if you could say “used to”, “would” or “was …ing”, use the imperfect (“I used to do” → hacía); if you're describing how things were, use it too.

UseExampleTranslation
a past habitDe pequeña jugaba en la calle.As a little girl, I used to play in the street.
a descriptionLa casa era grande y tenía un jardín.The house was big and had a garden.
the weatherHacía calor y el cielo estaba azul.It was hot and the sky was blue.
ageTenía diez años.I was ten years old.
the timeEra la una. Eran las ocho.It was one o'clock. It was eight o'clock.

Habit markers

de pequeño / de pequeña, de niño / de niña (as a child, when I was little), antes (before, in the past), siempre, a menudo (often), todos los veranos, los domingos, cuando era joven.

Note: de pequeño replaces a whole clause, like English “as a child”. No need to say “cuando yo era pequeño”, even though that's correct too.

Soler + infinitive

To say “to usually do” or “used to”, Spanish has a verb: soler. In the imperfect, it's regular: solía, solías, solía, solíamos, solíais, solían.

Los domingos solíamos comer en casa de mis abuelos.On Sundays we used to have lunch at my grandparents' house.

For age, Spanish uses tener: tenía diez años (literally “I had ten years”), never “era diez años”, even though English says “I was ten”. And for the time, era la una but eran las dos, as in the present.

es-u08-l2.title: Imperfect or indefinido?
es-u08-l2.why: You now know the indefinido and the imperfecto; this lesson teaches you to combine them in the same sentence, using what English already does with “was …ing” and the simple past. Background and event, an interrupted action (estaba durmiendo cuando sonó el teléfono), habit or one-off fact, and the verbs that change meaning (conocí, supe, no quise): it's the key to telling stories in the past.
es-u08-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

The background and the event

Spanish chooses between the imperfecto and the indefinido depending on the role the action plays in the story. Think of a movie: the imperfect is the background, the setting; the indefinido is the actions that move the story forward.

Imperfecto: the backgroundIndefinido: the event
Llovía… (it was raining)… cuando salí (when I went out).
Hacía sol… (it was sunny)… y fuimos a la playa (and we went to the beach).
Había mucha gente… (there were lots of people)… y no encontramos mesa (and we didn't find a table).
Era tarde… (it was late)… y cogimos un taxi (and we took a taxi).

The background answers the questions “what was it like?”, “what was the weather like?”, “what was going on?”. The event answers “what happened?”.

Eran las once, hacía frío y las calles estaban vacías. Entonces sonó mi móvil.It was eleven o'clock, it was cold and the streets were empty. Then my phone rang.

The English speaker's trick: “was …ing” and “used to” point to the imperfect: “it was raining” → llovía. A step in the story (“what happened next?”) points to the indefinido: “it rained (all day)” → llovió. Be careful with the English simple past, which can be either: “The house was big” is background (imperfect), “I was there for two hours” is a finished event (indefinido).

", "

An interrupted action: estaba durmiendo cuando…

For an action in progress when something else happens, Spanish very often uses estar in the imperfect + gerund, exactly like English “I was sleeping”. You already know estoy durmiendo; just put estar in the imperfect.

estar + gerund
yoestaba durmiendo
túestabas durmiendo
él, ella, ustedestaba durmiendo
nosotros, nosotrasestábamos durmiendo
vosotros, vosotrasestabais durmiendo
ellos, ellas, ustedesestaban durmiendo
Estaba durmiendo cuando sonó el teléfono.I was sleeping when the phone rang.

You can also simply say Dormía cuando sonó el teléfono: both are correct. What matters is that the interrupted action is in the imperfect and the interruption in the indefinido.

Habit or one-off

Habit: imperfectoOnce: indefinido
Los domingos comíamos en casa de mi abuela.El domingo pasado comimos en un restaurante.
Siempre íbamos a la playa en coche.El verano de 2010 fuimos en tren.
De pequeño me levantaba a las siete.Ayer me levanté a las diez.

Time markers help you: siempre, todos los días, los domingos, de pequeño call for the imperfect; ayer, un día, el domingo pasado, en 2015 call for the indefinido. In English, “we would eat at my grandma's on Sundays” is a habit too: imperfect.

", "

Verbs that change meaning

A few verbs don't mean quite the same thing in the imperfect and in the indefinido. English makes the same distinction, but with different words.

VerbImperfectoIndefinido
conocerconocía a Pablo: I knew Pabloconocí a Pablo: I met Pablo
sabersabía la verdad: I knew the truthsupe la verdad: I found out the truth
tenertenía un coche: I had a cartuve un accidente: I had an accident
quererquería salir: I wanted to go outno quise salir: I refused to go out
poderpodía ir: I could gopude ir: I managed to go
Conocí a Laura en 2018, en un concierto. Entonces no sabía hablar español.I met Laura in 2018, at a concert. Back then, I couldn't speak Spanish.
Ayer supe que Jorge tenía un hermano gemelo.Yesterday I found out that Jorge had a twin brother.

English “to meet” covers two Spanish verbs. Meeting someone for the first time is conocí a + person (with the personal a). Meeting up with someone you already know is something else: vi a Marta (I saw Marta, I met up with Marta).

es-u08-l3.title: Telling a story
es-u08-l3.topic: organizing a story in the past; time connectors
es-u08-l3.why: The last step of the unit on memories: you combine the three past tenses in a real story, with the connectors that give it rhythm (un día, de repente, mientras, al cabo de un rato, por fin, al final). You also learn to react when someone tells you a story (¡No me digas!, ¿Y qué pasó?, ¡Qué fuerte!), which is essential in a conversation in Spain.

{"lessons": ["

Words for telling a story

A good story is a series of well-linked events. These little words organize your story in time; most of them have a direct English equivalent.

SpanishEnglishExample
un díaone dayUn día fuimos de excursión a la sierra.
de repentesuddenly, all of a suddenDe repente empezó a llover.
entoncesthen, soEntonces llamamos a un taxi.
mientraswhileMientras esperábamos, hablamos con una señora.
al cabo de un ratoafter a whileAl cabo de un rato llegó el autobús.
por finat last (what a relief!)Por fin encontramos el hotel.
al finalin the endAl final fue un viaje estupendo.
al día siguientethe next dayAl día siguiente volvimos a casa.

Two pairs to keep apart

  • English “finally” covers two Spanish expressions. Por fin expresses relief after a wait: “at last!”. Al final simply says how the story ends: “in the end”.
  • Mientras introduces an action that lasts, so it's usually in the imperfect (mientras esperaba, while I was waiting). De repente introduces a sudden event, so it's in the indefinido (de repente sonó el móvil).

“The next day” is al día siguiente; don't confuse it with pasado mañana (the day after tomorrow). And al cabo de works with any length of time: al cabo de dos horas, al cabo de una semana.

", "

Three past tenses in one story

To tell an anecdote, you combine the three tenses you know. Each one has its role:

  • the imperfecto sets the scene: the weather, the place, what was going on;
  • the indefinido moves the story forward: the actions, the events;
  • the perfecto connects the story to today: a comment, a consequence for this year or this week.
Un día de agosto íbamos en coche por Galicia. Hacía calor y estábamos perdidos. De repente vimos a un señor en la carretera y paramos el coche. Al final nos invitó a comer en su casa. Este año hemos vuelto a su pueblo y hemos comido otra vez con él.One day in August we were driving through Galicia. It was hot and we were lost. Suddenly we saw a man on the road and stopped the car. In the end he invited us to lunch at his house. This year we've gone back to his village and had lunch with him again.
VerbTenseRole
íbamos, hacía, estábamosimperfectothe background
vimos, paramos, invitóindefinidothe events
hemos vuelto (este año)perfectothe link with today

The perfecto only appears if you come back to the present, with a time marker like este año or esta semana. A story that's over and done with, with no link to today, is told only with the imperfect and the indefinido.

", "

Reacting to a story

When someone tells you an anecdote in Spain, people react a lot, and out loud! These little phrases show you're listening and keep the story going.

ReactionMeaningRegister
¿Y qué pasó?And what happened?everyday
¿Y entonces?And then?everyday
¿En serio?Really? Seriously?everyday
¡No me digas!No way! You don't say!everyday
¡Qué fuerte!That's crazy! Wow!informal (Spain)
¡Qué miedo!How scary!everyday
¡Qué suerte!How lucky!everyday
¡Qué mala suerte!What bad luck!everyday
¡Menos mal!Thank goodness! Phew!everyday

¡No me digas! is a set phrase: grammatically, it's a negative command (“don't tell me”), a form you'll study later. For now, just learn it as it is.

— Y de repente el coche se paró en medio de la carretera. — ¡No me digas! ¿Y qué pasó?— And suddenly the car stopped in the middle of the road. — No way! And what happened?

¡Qué fuerte! is very common among young Spaniards, but it's informal: avoid it with your doctor or in a formal work situation. ¡Menos mal!, on the other hand, works everywhere.

At the station: buying a ticket

In Spain, people take the train a lot: the AVE (the high-speed train) links Madrid to Seville, Barcelona or Valencia in under three hours, and the cercanías serves the suburbs of the big cities. In Madrid, the main station is called Atocha.

Buenos días. Quería un billete de ida y vuelta para Sevilla.Good morning. I'd like a round-trip ticket to Seville.
¿Para qué día? — Para el viernes, por la mañana.For what day? — For Friday, in the morning.

You recognize the polite phrase quería (I'd like): it's the imperfect of querer, which you now know how to conjugate. You say a ticket para Sevilla (the destination) or a Sevilla: both are correct.

El billete means both “the train ticket” and “the bill” (banknote). In Latin America, a train ticket is often el boleto or el pasaje.

Understanding a timetable

For timetables, the present is enough, as in English (el tren sale a las ocho, the train leaves at eight). Two verbs do all the work: salir (to leave) and llegar (to arrive).

  • la salida = departure; la llegada = arrival (careful, la salida also means “the exit”).

  • directo = direct; hacer transbordo = to change trains, to make a connection.
  • ¿Cuánto dura el viaje? = How long is the trip?

In stations and announcements, times are given on the 24-hour clock: a las catorce treinta (14:30, 2:30 p.m.). In conversation, people quickly go back to a las dos y media.

The Madrid subway (the metro) is big and easy to use. The lines have a number and a color, and people say la línea 1, la línea 3. To travel, you top up a tarjeta de transporte (transit card).

To give a route, Spanish uses the present, as you already did for giving walking directions: coges, cambias, te bajas.

In Spain, coger is the normal verb for “taking” a means of transportation. In several Latin American countries, people prefer tomar (tomar el bus), because coger has a vulgar meaning there.

es-u09-l2.title: At the hotel
es-u09-l2.why: The second stage of the trip: after the train, the hotel. You book a room, check in at the front desk and ask your questions politely with usted, reusing the phrase quería and telling time; it also directly prepares the usted imperative (next lesson) and complaints (last lesson of the unit).

{"lessons": ["

Booking a room

To book by phone or at the front desk, a few phrases are enough. You already know the most useful one: quería (I'd like).

SpanishEnglish
Quería reservar una habitación.I'd like to book a room.
una habitación individuala single room
una habitación doblea double room
con dos camas / con cama de matrimoniowith two beds / with a double bed
con desayuno / con media pensiónwith breakfast / with half board (breakfast and dinner)
¿Para cuántas noches?For how many nights?
¿A nombre de quién?Under what name?
Tengo una reserva a nombre de…I have a reservation under the name…

On the phone

Recepción, buenos días. — Buenos días. Quería reservar una habitación doble para el fin de semana.Front desk, good morning. — Good morning. I'd like to book a double room for the weekend.
¿Para cuántas noches? — Para dos noches, del viernes al domingo.For how many nights? — For two nights, from Friday to Sunday.

Vocabulary note: la habitación means “the room” (in a hotel or a home), nothing to do with “habitat”. And “the reservation” is la reserva in Spain; in Latin America you also hear la reservación.

", "

At the front desk: being polite with usted

At a hotel, the staff address guests formally, and guests do the same. English has just one “you”, so the politeness is all in the verb form. Reminder: usted is conjugated like él / ella, in the third person singular; ustedes (you, plural) is conjugated like ellos.

TúUstedEnglish
¿Puedes…?¿Puede…?Can you…?
¿Tienes…?¿Tiene…?Do you have…?
¿Necesitas algo?¿Necesita algo?Do you need anything?
¿Me puedes decir…?¿Me puede decir…?Can you tell me…?
Aquí tienes.Aquí tiene.Here you go (handing something over).

Guests' questions

¿A qué hora es el desayuno?What time is breakfast?
¿Está incluido el desayuno?Is breakfast included?
¿Me puede decir la contraseña del wifi?Could you tell me the wifi password?
¿A qué hora tengo que dejar la habitación?What time do I have to check out?

Incluido agrees like an adjective (in English it never changes, in Spanish it does): el desayuno está incluido, la cena está incluida, las bebidas están incluidas. You use estar because it's a state, the result of a decision.

In Spain, young people quickly switch to tú, even with strangers. But at a hotel front desk, usted remains the rule on both sides: it's the safer choice for you too.

", "

During your stay

Once you've checked in, here's the vocabulary you'll use every day at the hotel.

SpanishEnglishExample
la recepciónthe front desk, receptionLa recepción está abierta toda la noche.
la llave / la tarjetathe key / the key cardAquí tiene la tarjeta de la habitación.
el ascensorthe elevatorEl ascensor está a la izquierda.
la plantathe floor (level)Su habitación está en la tercera planta.
la toallathe towel¿Me puede dar otra toalla?
el aire acondicionadothe air conditioningLa habitación tiene aire acondicionado.
las vistas al marthe sea viewQuería una habitación con vistas al mar.
el comedorthe dining roomEl desayuno es en el comedor.

For floors, Spanish uses ordinal numbers: la primera planta, la segunda, la tercera, la cuarta, la quinta. The ground floor is la planta baja, so careful if you're American: the “primera” floor is one floor up, what you'd call the second floor. People also say el piso: el tercer piso.

Tengo una reserva a nombre de Martin. — Sí, una habitación doble con desayuno, en la quinta planta. Aquí tiene la llave.I have a reservation under the name Martin. — Yes, a double room with breakfast, on the fifth floor. Here's your key.

When you arrive, you'll be asked for el DNI o el pasaporte: the DNI (Documento Nacional de Identidad) is the Spanish ID card. For an ID document in general, people say el documento de identidad.

es-u09-l3.title: The imperative: giving directions
es-u09-l3.topic: affirmative imperative with tú and usted; irregular imperatives
es-u09-l3.why: Until now, you gave directions using the present; now you finally discover the affirmative imperative, for tú (habla, sigue, and the eight irregular ones ven, ve, sal, haz, di, pon, ten, sé) and for usted (siga, gire, vaya, venga, haga). With attached pronouns (siéntate, cógelo), you can give directions, a recipe or instructions, whether traveling or at home.

{"lessons": ["

The imperative with tú

In English, a command is just the bare verb (“speak”, “turn”), whoever you're talking to. Spanish has different forms for tú and usted. Good news: for tú, the regular affirmative imperative is identical to the third person singular of the present, the él form. So you already know almost all the forms, including those of stem-changing verbs.

InfinitivePresent (él)Imperative (tú)Example
hablarhablahablaHabla despacio, por favor.
girargiragiraGira a la derecha.
cruzarcruzacruzaCruza la plaza.
cogercogecogeCoge la primera calle.
seguirsiguesigueSigue todo recto.
volvervuelvevuelveVuelve pronto.
cerrarcierracierraCierra la puerta.

Eight irregular imperatives

Eight very common verbs have a short form, often just one syllable. They're so frequent that you'll learn them quickly.

venirirsalirhacerdecirponertenerser
venvesalhazdipontensé
comegogo out, leavedo, makesay, tellputhave, holdbe
Ven aquí, pon la mesa y haz la ensalada, por favor.Come here, set the table and make the salad, please.

Sé (be) has an accent, like sé (I know): Sé bueno (be good). For vosotros, the imperative has another form (hablad, venid): you'll see it later.

", "

The imperative with usted

To address someone formally, Spanish borrows a form of the subjunctive, a mood English barely uses and that you'll study in detail later. For now, just learn it as the usted imperative. The principle: take the yo form of the present, drop the -o and “swap” the vowel: -ar → -e, -er / -ir → -a.

InfinitivePresent (yo)Imperative (usted)
hablarhablohable
girargirogire
comercomocoma
subirsubosuba
seguirsigosiga
volvervuelvovuelva
cogercojocoja
venirvengovenga
hacerhagohaga
tenertengotenga
ponerpongoponga
salirsalgosalga
decirdigodiga
irvoyvaya (irregular)

The spelling adapts, just like in llegué, busqué, empecé: cruzar → cruce, llegar → llegue, buscar → busque.

Perdone, ¿para ir a la estación? — Siga todo recto, cruce la plaza y gire a la izquierda.Excuse me, how do I get to the station? — Go straight ahead, cross the square and turn left.

You were already using this imperative without knowing it: perdone (excuse me) comes from perdonar. For several people addressed formally (ustedes), just add -n: sigan, giren, vengan.

", "

Attached pronouns: siéntate, levántese, cógelo

In the affirmative imperative, pronouns don't go in front of the verb: they attach to the end, making a single word. To keep the stress in the same place, you often add a written accent.

InfinitiveTúUstedEnglish
sentarsesiéntatesiéntesesit down
levantarselevántatelevánteseget up, stand up
coger (el billete)cógelocójalotake it
abrir (la puerta)ábrelaábralaopen it
ponerse (el abrigo)pontepóngaseput on (your coat)

In the kitchen: a recipe

Pela las patatas y córtalas en trozos pequeños. Pon aceite en la sartén, fríe las patatas y añade los huevos batidos.Peel the potatoes and cut them into small pieces. Put oil in the frying pan, fry the potatoes and add the beaten eggs.

The negative: just for recognizing

Careful: in the negative, the imperative changes completely (no cruces, no gire). You'll study it later; for now, just learn to recognize it: No gire a la izquierda = “Don't turn left”.

The pronoun attaches to the imperative, but stays in front of conjugated forms: Lo coges (you take it) / Cógelo (take it). In a command, the pronoun comes after the verb, just like “take it” in English; the difference is that Spanish writes it as one word.

es-u09-l4.title: When Something Goes Wrong
es-u09-l4.topic: complaining and solving a problem politely
es-u09-l4.why: Last lesson of the travel unit: when something goes wrong, the learner can report a problem, politely ask for a solution with the phrase ¿Podría…?, and say they've forgotten or lost something (se me ha olvidado). They also learn to make themselves understood at the doctor's and the pharmacy, reusing the perfecto, usted and the imperative from the previous lesson.

{"lessons": ["

Reporting a problem politely

Broken air conditioning, a mistake on the bill, a room that hasn't been cleaned: when you travel, you need to know how to complain without being rude. In Spain, people stay direct but courteous, and they almost always start with Perdone.

To say…In Spanish
it doesn't workNo funciona el aire acondicionado. / La ducha no funciona.
there's a problem with…Hay un problema con la factura.
there's no…No hay agua caliente. / No hay toallas.
it's dirtyLa habitación está sucia.
there's a lot of noiseHay mucho ruido en la calle.
I'd like to make a complaintQuería hacer una reclamación.

Asking for a solution: ¿Podría…?

¿Podría…? (could you…?) is the most polite way to ask for something. It's a conditional, a tense you'll study later: for now, just learn it as a set phrase, followed by an infinitive, exactly like English \"could you + verb\".

¿Podría llamar a un técnico, por favor?Could you call a technician, please?
¿Podría cambiar las toallas?Could you change the towels?

What the staff will say

Lo siento mucho (I'm very sorry), Perdone las molestias (sorry for the inconvenience), Ahora mismo (right away), No se preocupe (don't worry, a negative form you just need to recognize).

In Spain, every business must have a hoja de reclamaciones, an official complaint form. Just asking for it often solves the problem! Watch out: the word reclamación means \"complaint,\" not \"reclamation.\"

", "

Se me ha olvidado, se me ha perdido

To say you forgot or lost something by accident, Spanish speakers use a very common construction. Take it as a set expression: se me ha olvidado (I forgot), se me ha perdido (I lost), se me ha roto (I broke).

Se me ha olvidado el pasaporte en el hotel.I left my passport at the hotel.

Word for word: \"the passport has gotten forgotten on me.\" That's why the verb agrees with the thing forgotten, not with the person:

One thingSeveral things
Se me ha olvidado la llave.Se me han olvidado las llaves.
Se me ha perdido el móvil.Se me han perdido las gafas.
Se me ha roto el vaso.Se me han roto los vasos.

For someone else, you only change me: ¿Se te ha olvidado algo? (did you forget something?), se nos ha perdido el perro (we've lost the dog).

You can also say He olvidado el pasaporte or He perdido las llaves: that's correct, but more neutral. Se me ha olvidado stresses that it wasn't your fault, it just happened, a bit like English \"the glass broke\" instead of \"I broke the glass\"!

", "

At the doctor's and the pharmacy

To say where it hurts, Spanish uses doler, which works like gustar: the body part is the subject (\"my head hurts,\" not \"I hurt my head\"). So me duele for one thing, me duelen for several.

SymptomIn Spanish
I have a headacheMe duele la cabeza.
my feet hurtMe duelen los pies.
I have a sore throatMe duele la garganta.
I have a feverTengo fiebre.
I have a coughTengo tos.
I have a cold (man / woman)Estoy resfriado / resfriada. (or constipado / constipada)
I feel dizzyEstoy mareado / mareada.

Remember the false friend: constipado means \"having a cold,\" not \"constipated\"!

The doctor's advice

The doctor addresses the patient formally and gives advice in the usted imperative you've just learned:

Abra la boca. Tome una pastilla cada ocho horas, beba mucha agua y descanse.Open your mouth. Take a pill every eight hours, drink lots of water and get some rest.

At the pharmacy

Buenos días. ¿Tiene algo para el dolor de garganta? — Sí, tenemos un jarabe muy bueno: tome una cucharada dos veces al día.Good morning. Do you have anything for a sore throat? — Yes, we have a very good syrup: take one spoonful twice a day.

In Spain, pharmacies have a glowing green cross, and at night there's always a farmacia de guardia (on-duty pharmacy). False friend alert: la receta means \"the prescription\" (and also a cooking \"recipe\"), never a \"receipt.\"

es-u10-l1.title: Le, les and se: indirect object pronouns
es-u10-l1.topic: indirect object pronouns; le / les → se before lo, la
es-u10-l1.why: The lesson moves from direct object pronouns (lo, la) to the indirect pronouns le / les, then to double pronouns like me lo, se lo, with the rule "le lo → se lo" that trips up every learner. It opens the unit on pronouns and prepares the next lesson, where these pronouns attach to the infinitive, the gerund and the imperative.
es-u10-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

To whom? Indirect object pronouns

You already know the direct object pronouns lo, la, los, las (I see him = lo veo). The indirect object answers the question \"to whom?\": I give a book to Marta → I give her a book. English uses the same words for both (\"I see him,\" \"I give him a book\"), but Spanish doesn't: \"to him / to her\" is le and \"to them\" is les.

PersonDirect (whom? what?)Indirect (to whom?)
yomeme
tútete
éllole
ellalale
ustedlo, lale
nosotros, nosotrasnosnos
vosotros, vosotrasosos
elloslosles
ellaslasles
ustedeslos, lasles

Good news: you already know these pronouns! They're the ones you use with gustar: me gusta, le gusta, les gusta. \"It's pleasing to me, to him\": that's an indirect object.

The big trap: le = to him, to her

Only in the 3rd person does le differ from the direct pronoun. Le escribo means \"I write to him / to her\"; \"I write it\" (the letter) is la escribo. And le works for a man as well as a woman: le escribo a Pablo, le escribo a Marta. So don't translate \"her\" automatically: ask yourself \"her, or to her?\"

Where does it go?

Unlike English, the pronoun goes before the conjugated verb, and in the perfect tense before haber:

Le he regalado un libro.I've given him (or her) a book.
No les digo nada.I don't tell them anything.
¿Le traigo la cuenta?Shall I bring you the check? (usted)

With usted, le also means \"to you\": that's why the market vendor asks you ¿Le pongo algo más?

", "

The double: le escribo a mi madre

Here's a habit that surprises English speakers: Spanish likes to say the indirect object twice. You use the pronoun le or les and the noun introduced by a.

Le escribo un mensaje a mi madre.I'm writing a message to my mother. (word for word: \"I'm writing her a message to my mother\")
¿Les has dicho la verdad a tus padres?Have you told your parents the truth?

In English, that extra \"her\" would be a mistake; in Spanish, it's the most natural sentence. And in two cases, the double is required:

  • when a + person comes first: A mi hermana le regalo un libro (just like A Marta le gusta el cine);
  • with a mí, a ti, a él, a ella… used for emphasis or to make things clear: Le escribo a ella, no a él.

Verbs that take an indirect object

VerbExampleTranslation
darLe doy mi número a Lucía.I give Lucía my number.
decir¿Qué le dices?What do you say to him (or her)?
regalarLes regalo flores.I give them flowers (as a gift).
prestar, dejar¿Me dejas tu paraguas?Will you lend me your umbrella?
devolverTe devuelvo las llaves mañana.I'll give you back the keys tomorrow.
enviar, mandarOs mando las fotos.I'll send you (all) the photos.
contarLe cuento todo a mi abuela.I tell my grandmother everything.
explicar¿Nos explicas el ejercicio?Can you explain the exercise to us?
enseñarTe enseño mi piso.I'll show you my apartment.
pedirLe pido ayuda a Javier.I ask Javier for help.
preguntarLe pregunto la hora.I ask him (or her) the time.

Pedir or preguntar? Both mean \"to ask,\" but you pide for a thing (help, a coffee, a favor) and you pregunta for information (the time, the way). Both take le or les. And in Spain, dejar very often means \"to lend\": ¿Me dejas tu bici?

", "

Two pronouns: me lo, te la, se lo

When there are two pronouns, Spanish always puts the indirect one first, then the direct one, and both go before the verb:

¿El libro? Te lo presto.The book? I'll lend it to you.
¿Las fotos? Nos las envía Diego.The photos? Diego is sending them to us.

English says \"I'll lend it to you\"; Spanish says, word for word, \"to-you it I lend.\" With me, te, nos, os, just remember: indirect, then direct, always in that order.

The golden rule: le lo → se lo

Le and les can never come right before lo, la, los, las. They turn into se:

SentenceOne pronounTwo pronouns
Doy el libro a Pablo.Le doy el libro.Se lo doy.
Doy la llave a Marta.Le doy la llave.Se la doy.
Regalo los libros a mis primos.Les regalo los libros.Se los regalo.
Devuelvo las llaves a la vecina.Le devuelvo las llaves.Se las devuelvo.

Se never changes: it means to him, to her, to you (usted), to them. To be clear, add a él, a ella, a usted, a ellos:

Se lo explico a ella.I'll explain it to her.

A three-step method: 1) find the direct object (what?) and pick lo, la, los, las to match its gender and number; 2) find the indirect object (to whom?); 3) if it's le or les, replace it with se. This se has nothing to do with the one in reflexive verbs like levantarse.

—¿Quién te regaló el reloj? —Me lo regaló mi abuela.— Who gave you the watch? — My grandmother gave it to me.

es-u10-l2.title: Where do pronouns go?
es-u10-l2.topic: pronouns with the infinitive, the gerund and the imperative
es-u10-l2.why: After indirect and double pronouns, this lesson settles where they go with the infinitive, the gerund and the imperative, and above all the written accent that appears when they attach to the verb (dímelo, comprándolo, dártelo). It lets the learner ask for help and give instructions naturally, just before the big pronoun review.
es-u10-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

With an infinitive: two possible positions

With a single conjugated verb, you already know the pronoun goes in front: Lo compro. But with ir a, querer, poder, tener que, deber + infinitive, Spanish gives you a choice:

Before the conjugated verbAttached to the infinitiveTranslation
Lo voy a comprar.Voy a comprarlo.I'm going to buy it.
La quiero ver.Quiero verla.I want to see her.
Te puedo ayudar.Puedo ayudarte.I can help you.
Me tengo que duchar.Tengo que ducharme.I have to take a shower.
Le debes escribir.Debes escribirle.You should write to him (or her).

Both sentences are correct and mean the same thing. Careful: attached means attached, as one single word: comprarlo, not \"comprar lo.\"

What's impossible

  • The pronoun never goes between the two verbs: voy lo a comprar doesn't exist.
  • It never goes right before a separate infinitive: voy a lo comprar is wrong.
  • Two pronouns stay together: Te lo voy a dar or Voy a dártelo, never one pronoun on each side (te voy a darlo is wrong).

The accent that appears

With one pronoun attached to the infinitive, no accent: comprarlo, verla, decirte. With two pronouns, the word gets longer and the stressed syllable becomes the third from the end: you write the accent. dar → dártelo, decir → decírselo, explicar → explicártelo.

", "

With the gerund: leyéndolo

Same freedom with estar or seguir + gerund (the \"-ing\" form): the pronoun goes before the conjugated verb, or attaches to the gerund.

BeforeAttached to the gerundTranslation
Lo estoy leyendo.Estoy leyéndolo.I'm reading it.
La estamos arreglando.Estamos arreglándola.We're fixing it.
Me estoy duchando.Estoy duchándome.I'm taking a shower.
Se lo estoy explicando.Estoy explicándoselo.I'm explaining it to him (or her).

Here, you need a written accent from the very first pronoun. Why? The gerund is stressed on -an- or -en- (comprando, leyendo). Add a syllable, and that vowel becomes the third from the end: com-prán-do-lo. In Spanish, a word stressed there always carries a written accent.

Say the word out loud: the stress never moves. You say comPRANdo, so comPRÁNdolo. The written accent is simply there to show it once the word gets longer.

Accent summary

FormOne pronounTwo pronouns
infinitivecomprarlo (no accent)comprártelo
gerundcomprándolocomprándotelo
tú imperativecómpralocómpratelo

And if you can't decide between the two positions, remember that putting the pronoun before the conjugated verb is always possible and avoids accents: Lo estoy leyendo.

", "

In the imperative: dímelo, cómpralo, siéntate

In the affirmative imperative, there's no choice: the pronouns attach to the end of the verb, a bit like English \"tell me,\" but as one single word and always in the order indirect + direct: dímelo = \"tell-me-it,\" i.e. tell it to me.

Verb + pronoun(s)túustedTranslation
comprar + locómpralocómprelobuy it
ayudar + meayúdameayúdemehelp me
sentarsesiéntatesiéntesesit down
decir + me + lodímelodígamelotell it to me
dar + me + lodámelodémelogive it to me
dar + se + lodáselodéselogive it to him / her
poner + loponlopóngaloput it (there)
hacer + lohazlohágalodo it
traer + me + lotráemelotráigamelobring it to me

The accent: a simple rule

  • One-syllable verb + one pronoun: no accent (dime, hazlo, ponlo, dale).
  • In every other case, write an accent on the verb's stressed syllable: cómpralo, llámame, siéntate, dímelo, dáselo.

Handy for asking for help or giving instructions:

¿Las cajas? Súbelas al tercero, por favor.The boxes? Take them up to the third floor, please.
Rellene el formulario y fírmelo aquí.Fill out the form and sign it here.

In the negative, which you'll learn later, the pronouns move back in front of the verb (no lo compres). For now, just remember the affirmative.

es-u10-l3.title: Pronouns: the big picture
es-u10-l3.topic: lo, la, le, se, double pronouns in the present and the past
es-u10-l3.why: This review lesson brings together all the pronouns seen since A1 (reflexive, direct, indirect, double) and runs them through every tense and form the learner knows, from the present to the imperative. It closes the pronoun unit with step-by-step replacement exercises and a dialogue about a surprise birthday party.
es-u10-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

All the pronouns at a glance

You now have all the pieces of the puzzle. Here's the complete table:

SubjectReflexiveDirectIndirectAfter a preposition
yomemememí (conmigo)
túteteteti (contigo)
élselole (se)él
ellaselale (se)ella
ustedselo, lale (se)usted
nosotros, nosotrasnosnosnosnosotros, nosotras
vosotros, vosotrasosososvosotros, vosotras
ellosselosles (se)ellos
ellasselasles (se)ellas
ustedesselos, lasles (se)ustedes

Direct or indirect? Ask the question

  • \"Whom? What?\" → direct: Veo la película → la veo.
  • \"To whom?\" → indirect: Escribo a Marta → le escribo.

English \"him\" and \"her\" won't help you here, since \"I help her\" and \"I ask her\" look exactly the same. A few verbs to watch:

VerbSpanishEnglish
ayudar a alguienla ayudo (direct)I help her
llamar a alguienlo llamo (direct)I call him
invitar a alguienlos invito (direct)I invite them
preguntar a alguienle pregunto (indirect)I ask him / her
gustar, encantarle gusta (indirect)he / she likes it
dolerle duele la cabeza (indirect)he / she has a headache

The a before a person doesn't mean \"indirect\"! It's often just the \"personal a\" (Conozco a Marta). Only the question \"to whom?\" counts: ayudar a Marta = to help Marta → la ayudo.

", "

Replacing step by step

Take a sentence and replace the nouns one at a time:

Regalo un reloj a mi padre. → Le regalo un reloj. → Se lo regalo.I'm giving my father a watch. → I'm giving him a watch. → I'm giving it to him.

Here's the same sentence in every tense and form you know:

FormSentenceTranslation
presentSe lo regalo.I give it to him.
perfectoSe lo he regalado.I've given it to him.
indefinidoSe lo regalé ayer.I gave it to him yesterday.
imperfectoSe lo regalaba cada año.I used to give it to him every year.
ir a + infinitiveSe lo voy a regalar. / Voy a regalárselo.I'm going to give it to him.
gerundSe lo estoy envolviendo. / Estoy envolviéndoselo.I'm wrapping it for him.
tú imperativeRegálaselo.Give it to him.
usted imperativeRegáleselo.Give it to him. (formal)

Watch the gender: English just says \"it,\" but el reloj is masculine, so lo. The pronoun always matches the gender of the Spanish noun.

The participle doesn't change

Good news: just like in English (\"the flowers, I've given them\"), the participle after haber never changes: ¿Las flores? Se las he regalado. Never \"regaladas\"!

¿Las invitaciones? Ya las he enviado.The invitations? I've already sent them.
", "

Traps to avoid

  • Le lo doesn't exist. Before lo, la, los, las, le and les turn into se: Se lo digo.
  • Indirect first. \"I give it to him\" is se lo doy, and \"you tell it to me\" is me lo dices.
  • Both pronouns together. Te lo voy a dar or voy a dártelo, never one pronoun on each side.
  • Accents. Two pronouns on an infinitive (dártelo), one or more pronouns on a gerund (haciéndolo), the imperative of a verb with more than one syllable (cómpralo).
  • The double. Le escribo a mi madre sounds natural; and when an object comes first, you repeat it with a pronoun: A mi madre le escribo, El pan lo compro yo.

Leísmo in Madrid

In Madrid, you'll often hear le instead of lo for a man: A Pablo le conozco desde niño (instead of lo conozco). It's accepted for a male person, but you should use lo: it's always correct.

Reflexive se, or the se of se lo?

Pablo se pone el jersey. → Se lo pone.Pablo puts on his sweater. → He puts it on.
Doy el jersey a Pablo. → Se lo doy.I give the sweater to Pablo. → I give it to him.

In the first example, se is the pronoun of ponerse (the verb is in the 3rd person); in the second, it replaces le (the verb is in the 1st person). The verb always tells you which one it is.

es-u11-l1.title: The simple future
es-u11-l1.topic: forming and using the future tense
es-u11-l1.why: After ir a + infinitive, seen from the very basics, the lesson introduces the simple future, which is built on the infinitive, with its ten irregular verbs (tendré, haré, diré…) and its typically Spanish use for guesses (estará en casa). It opens the unit "Plans and politeness" and provides the stem that the conditional will reuse in the next lesson.
es-u11-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

The future: infinitive + an ending

Good news: the Spanish future is easy to build. Where English adds \"will\" in front of the verb, Spanish keeps the whole infinitive and adds an ending to it (hablar + é = I will speak). And the endings are the same for all three verb groups!

hablarcomervivir
yohablarécomeréviviré
túhablaráscomerásvivirás
él, ella, ustedhablarácomerávivirá
nosotros, nosotrashablaremoscomeremosviviremos
vosotros, vosotrashablaréiscomeréisviviréis
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablaráncomeránvivirán

Every form has a written accent except the nosotros form (hablaremos). Easy landmarks: -é for \"I will,\" -á for \"he / she will,\" -án for \"they will.\" And the endings sound like the present of the verb haber (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han) glued onto the infinitive.

Reflexive verbs keep their pronoun in front: Me levantaré temprano (I'll get up early). Stem-changing verbs don't change at all, since you start from the infinitive: volveré, dormiré, pediré, empezaré.

El año que viene viviré en Sevilla y trabajaré en un hotel.Next year, I'll live in Seville and work in a hotel.
¿Cenaréis con nosotros el sábado?Will you (all) have dinner with us on Saturday?
", "

Irregular verbs: same endings, different stem

About ten very common verbs change their stem but keep the normal endings. They fall into three families:

FamilyInfinitiveFuture (yo)English
the e of the infinitive drops outpoderpodréI'll be able to
sabersabréI'll know
quererquerréI'll want
haber (hay)habráthere will be
a d replaces the voweltenertendréI'll have
salirsaldréI'll go out, I'll leave
venirvendréI'll come
ponerpondréI'll put
two one-offshacerharéI'll do, I'll make
decirdiréI'll say

Why the d? Try saying \"tenré\" quickly: the n and r clash, so Spanish slips a d in between to smooth it out: vendré, tendré. Just like diré, they're shorter than the infinitive, not longer.

tenerhacerdecir
yotendréharédiré
tútendrásharásdirás
él, ella, ustedtendráharádirá
nosotros, nosotrastendremosharemosdiremos
vosotros, vosotrastendréisharéisdiréis
ellos, ellas, ustedestendránharándirán

Hay becomes habrá, always singular, even with a plural noun (\"there will be\"): Mañana habrá mucha gente (never \"habrán\"). And querré is spelled with two r's.

", "

When to use the future

UseExampleTranslation
distant or less certain planAlgún día viviré en la costa.Someday, I'll live on the coast.
prediction, weatherMañana lloverá en el norte.Tomorrow it will rain in the north.
promiseTe llamaré esta noche, te lo prometo.I'll call you tonight, I promise.
guess about the present—¿Dónde está Ana? —Estará en casa.— Where's Ana? — She must be at home.

The future of guessing

Here's a use that English only has in a few phrases (\"that'll be the mailman\"): Spanish uses the future all the time to make a guess about right now. Estará en casa = \"she's probably at home.\" ¿Qué hora será? = \"I wonder what time it is.\" Tendrá unos cuarenta años = \"he must be about forty.\"

Future or ir a + infinitive?

In everyday speech in Spain, for a near, decided plan, people prefer ir a: Esta tarde voy a estudiar. The simple future sounds more distant, less certain or more solemn (promises, forecasts, resolutions). It's a bit like the difference between \"I'm going to leave\" and \"I shall leave.\"

Si + present, then the future

Just like in English, never use the future after si (if): use the present, and put the future in the other half of the sentence.

Si llueve, nos quedaremos en casa.If it rains, we'll stay home.

Useful time markers: mañana, pasado mañana, el año que viene, dentro de dos años, algún día, pronto, en el futuro, seguramente.

es-u11-l2.title: The conditional
es-u11-l2.why: Built on the future stem, the conditional finally lets the learner ask politely (¿Podrías…? ¿Te importaría…?), express wishes (me gustaría) and give advice (deberías, yo que tú). The lesson keeps to these everyday uses, without if-clauses, and prepares the invitations of the next lesson.
es-u11-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

The conditional: future stem + -ía

The conditional is the Spanish \"would.\" It uses the same stem as the future (the infinitive) and adds the imperfect endings of -er and -ir verbs: -ía, -ías, -ía… So hablaría = I would speak, in a single word.

hablarcomervivir
yohablaríacomeríaviviría
túhablaríascomeríasvivirías
él, ella, ustedhablaríacomeríaviviría
nosotros, nosotrashablaríamoscomeríamosviviríamos
vosotros, vosotrashablaríaiscomeríaisviviríais
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablaríancomeríanvivirían

The written accent is on the í, in every person.

Irregular verbs: exactly the same as the future

InfinitiveFutureConditionalEnglish
tenertendrétendríaI'd have
salirsaldrésaldríaI'd go out
venirvendrévendríaI'd come
ponerpondrépondríaI'd put
poderpodrépodríaI could
sabersabrésabríaI'd know
quererquerréquerríaI'd want
hacerharéharíaI'd do, I'd make
decirdirédiríaI'd say
haber (hay)habráhabríathere would be

Don't mix it up with the imperfect: comía (I was eating, I used to eat) / comería (I would eat). The conditional keeps the whole infinitive: comería. Careful with English \"would\" meaning \"used to\" (\"as a kid, I would eat there every Sunday\"): that's the imperfect in Spanish, not the conditional!

", "

Asking politely and saying what you'd like

You already know quería and ¿podría…? as set phrases. Here's the whole system:

To…SentenceTranslation
ask a friend for a favor¿Podrías ayudarme con la maleta?Could you help me with my suitcase?
ask formally (usted)¿Podría decirme la hora?Could you tell me the time?
ask very gently¿Te importaría cerrar la ventana?Would you mind closing the window?
express a wishMe gustaría aprender a bailar.I'd like to learn to dance.
a very strong wishMe encantaría vivir en Barcelona.I'd love to live in Barcelona.
a preferencePreferiría quedarme en casa.I'd rather stay home.

Me gustaría: works like gustar

Gustar and encantar keep their usual construction: me gustaría, te gustaría, le gustaría, nos gustaría, os gustaría, les gustaría. With an infinitive, the verb stays singular: A mis padres les gustaría viajar. With a plural noun, it becomes plural: Me gustarían unas vacaciones tranquilas.

When you answer ¿Te importaría…?, careful: No, para nada or Claro que no mean \"no, I don't mind at all,\" so it's actually a yes! Exactly like English: \"Would you mind? — No, not at all.\"

", "

Giving advice

PhraseExampleTranslation
deberías + infinitiveDeberías descansar más.You should rest more.
tendrías que + infinitiveTendrías que ir al médico.You ought to see a doctor.
yo que tú + conditionalYo que tú, hablaría con ella.If I were you, I'd talk to her.
yo en tu lugar + conditionalYo en tu lugar, no diría nada.In your place, I wouldn't say anything.
sería mejor + infinitiveSería mejor salir temprano.It would be better to leave early.

Yo que tú is the most typical expression of spoken Spanish: word for word \"I that you,\" meaning \"if I were you.\" With usted: Yo que usted, cogería un taxi.

Deberías is softer than debes (you must), exactly like \"you should\" is softer than \"you must.\"

Estás agobiada: yo que tú, me tomaría unos días de vacaciones.You're swamped: if I were you, I'd take a few days off.

As in English, the conditional also shows up in sentences with \"if\" (\"if I had time, I would travel\"). But after si, Spanish uses another tense you'll learn later: for now, keep the conditional for politeness, advice and wishes.

es-u11-l3.title: Suggesting, accepting, declining
es-u11-l3.why: The lesson puts the future and the conditional to work in social life: suggesting an outing (¿Te apetece…? ¿Qué tal si…?), accepting, politely declining with an excuse, and setting up a meeting with quedar. It wraps up the unit "Plans and politeness" before moving on to comparisons and shopping.
es-u11-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Making a suggestion

PhraseExampleTranslation
¿Te apetece + infinitive or noun?¿Te apetece ir al cine?Do you feel like going to the movies?
¿Qué tal si + present?¿Qué tal si cenamos fuera?How about we eat out?
¿Por qué no + present?¿Por qué no vamos a la playa?Why don't we go to the beach?
¿Vienes…? ¿Vamos…?¿Vienes a la fiesta de Marta?Are you coming to Marta's party?
¿Quedamos…?¿Quedamos el sábado?Shall we meet up on Saturday?

Apetecer: the \"feel like\" verb

Apetecer works like gustar: me apetece, te apetece, os apetece… and agrees with the thing you feel like: ¿Te apetece un café? / ¿Te apetecen unas tapas? It's the most Spanish way to suggest something. In Latin America, people tend to say ¿Tienes ganas de…? or ¿Quieres…?

The \"if\" trap: use the present!

In English, you might suggest with a past tense: \"What if we went to the movies?\" In Spanish, use the present: ¿Qué tal si vamos al cine? or ¿Y si vamos al cine?

Quedar: to meet up

Quedar is the magic verb for going out in Spain: ¿Quedamos? (shall we meet up?), ¿A qué hora quedamos?, ¿Dónde quedamos?, Quedamos en la plaza a las ocho. Quedar con alguien = to meet up with someone, to have plans with them: He quedado con Marta.

Una cita is a doctor's appointment or a romantic date. Between friends, you simply say quedar.

", "

Accepting and declining

To acceptTranslation
¡Vale!Okay!
¡Genial! / ¡Estupendo!Great! / Wonderful!
¡Me parece bien!Sounds good!
¡Buena idea!Good idea!
¡Claro que sí!Of course!
¡Me encantaría!I'd love to!
¡Venga, vamos!Come on, let's go!

Declining politely: always give an excuse

A blunt \"no\" is very rude in Spain. You apologize, give a reason, and often suggest something else. The essential little phrase: es que… (\"it's just that…\"), which introduces the excuse.

To declineTranslation
Lo siento, no puedo, es que tengo que trabajar.Sorry, I can't, it's just that I have to work.
¡Qué pena! Ese día no puedo.What a shame! I can't that day.
Me encantaría, pero estoy muy cansada.I'd love to, but I'm really tired.
Gracias, pero hoy no me apetece mucho.Thanks, but I don't really feel like it today.
Otro día será.Maybe another time.

Me encantaría, pero… is the most elegant way to say no: the conditional softens everything, just like \"I'd love to, but…\"

", "

Suggesting something else and setting the time

SentenceTranslation
¿Y si lo dejamos para el sábado?What if we put it off until Saturday?
¿Qué tal el domingo?How about Sunday?
¿Te viene bien el martes?Does Tuesday work for you?
Mejor otro día.Another day would be better.
¿Podríamos quedar un poco más tarde?Could we meet a little later?

Venir bien works like gustar: ¿Te viene bien? (does that work for you?), El jueves no me viene bien. Dejar para = to put off until: Lo dejamos para mañana.

Meeting up, Spanish style

You set the place and the time: Quedamos a las nueve en la puerta del cine (\"outside the movie theater\" is often en la puerta de). And don't forget Spanish hours: quedar a las diez para cenar is perfectly normal!

You can reuse the future and the conditional to confirm or give a heads-up:

Vale, allí estaré. Llegaré un poco tarde, es que salgo del trabajo a las ocho.Okay, I'll be there. I'll be a little late, it's just that I get off work at eight.

es-u12-l1.title: Comparing
es-u12-l1.why: The lesson provides every tool for comparing: más / menos… que, tan… como, tanto… como, the irregular forms mejor, peor, mayor, menor, the superlative and the very expressive -ísimo. It opens the unit "Comparing and choosing" and feeds straight into the next lesson, where learners compare clothes in stores.
es-u12-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

More, less, as… as

ComparisonSpanishExampleTranslation
moremás… queMadrid es más grande que Valencia.Madrid is bigger than Valencia.
lessmenos… queEl tren es menos caro que el avión.The train is less expensive than the plane.
equal (adjective, adverb)tan… comoSevilla es tan bonita como Granada.Seville is as pretty as Granada.
equal (noun)tanto, tanta, tantos, tantas… comoTengo tantos amigos como tú.I have as many friends as you.
equal (verb)verb + tanto comoTrabajo tanto como tú.I work as much as you.

English helps you here: \"as… as\" is tan… como, never que (that one is for \"than\"): tan alto como yo. And tanto agrees with the noun that follows: tanta gente, tantos pisos, tantas habitaciones.

Que yo, que tú

English says \"taller than me,\" but after que and como, Spanish uses subject pronouns: más alto que yo, tan simpática como tú. Never \"que mí\" or \"como ti.\"

Más de + number

Before a number, \"more than\" is más de: Hay más de cien personas. Cuesta menos de veinte euros. But to compare two things, it's que: Gana más que yo.

To make a comparison stronger, add mucho (much, a lot) or un poco (a little): Valencia es mucho más tranquila que Madrid. El piso es un poco más caro.

", "

Mejor, peor, mayor, menor… and the superlative

AdjectiveComparativeExample
bueno, bienmejorEsta paella es mejor que la de ayer.
malo, malpeorHoy hace peor tiempo que ayer.
grande (age)mayorMi hermana es mayor que yo.
pequeño (age)menorPablo es menor que su primo.

Mejor and peor don't change in the feminine, but take -es in the plural: los mejores restaurantes. For quality, you don't say \"más bueno\" but mejor, just like \"better\" and not \"more good.\"

For age, use mayor and menor: mi hermano mayor = my older brother; in everyday speech in Spain, you'll also hear mi hermano pequeño for a younger brother. For size, keep más grande, más pequeño: Mi piso es más grande que el de Javier. And to make it stronger: mucho mejor (much better), never \"muy mejor.\"

The superlative: el más… de

Article + noun + más or menos + adjective + de.

Madrid es la ciudad más grande de España.Madrid is the biggest city in Spain.
Es el barrio más tranquilo de la ciudad.It's the quietest neighborhood in the city.

Two differences from English: the adjective comes after the noun (el barrio más tranquilo, word for word \"the neighborhood most quiet\"), and \"in\" becomes de. With mejor and peor, the adjective goes before the noun: el mejor restaurante del barrio, la peor habitación del hotel.

", "

-ísimo: really, really…

To say \"very\" more strongly than muy, spoken Spanish loves the suffix -ísimo. Drop the final vowel of the adjective and add -ísimo, -ísima, -ísimos, -ísimas:

AdjectiveWith -ísimoTranslation
carocarísimosuper expensive
buenobuenísimoexcellent, delicious
guapaguapísimagorgeous
grandegrandísimohuge
muchomuchísimoa whole lot
ricoriquísimodelicious
largolarguísimoreally long
fácilfacilísimosuper easy

-ísimo always carries the written accent, and it's the only one in the word: fácil loses its accent in facilísimo. Watch the spelling, which keeps the same sound: rico → riquísimo, largo → larguísimo.

Never put muy before -ísimo: \"muy carísimo\" is impossible, since carísimo already means \"really, really expensive.\"

Comparing cities

Valencia es más barata que Barcelona, pero tan animada como Madrid.Valencia is cheaper than Barcelona, but as lively as Madrid.
En verano hace muchísimo calor en Sevilla; en Bilbao llueve mucho más.In summer it's extremely hot in Seville; in Bilbao it rains much more.

es-u12-l2.title: Out shopping
es-u12-l2.why: The lesson takes the learner shopping: clothing and shoe sizes, trying things on (¿Puedo probármelo?), saying how something fits with quedar, choosing with este, ese, aquel, paying, returning and exchanging. It recycles attached pronouns and comparatives just before the big A2 review.
es-u12-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

In the store: asking and trying on

In Spain, the salesperson (el dependiente, la dependienta) often speaks to you with tú, especially in clothing stores. You can do the same, or use usted in a more traditional shop.

You want to…You sayTranslation
ask for an item¿Tienen esta camisa en la talla 40?Do you have this shirt in a size 40?
another color¿La tenéis en azul?Do you have it in blue?
another size¿Tienes una talla más? / ¿Una talla menos?Do you have one size up? / One size down?
shoesCalzo un 39. ¿Tienen este número?I'm a size 39. Do you have this size?
try something on¿Puedo probármelo?Can I try it on?
the fitting room¿Dónde están los probadores?Where are the fitting rooms?

Talla or número?

English says \"size\" for everything, but Spanish has two words. La talla is a clothing size (la 38, la M); el número is a shoe size. To give your shoe size, use calzar: calzo un 42 (I'm a size 42).

Probarse + pronoun

Probarse (to try on) is reflexive, and you know how to attach pronouns to the infinitive: ¿Puedo probármelo? (the sweater), ¿Puedo probármela? (the jacket), ¿Puedo probármelos? (the shoes). Two pronouns, so a written accent! You can also say ¿Me lo puedo probar?

Probar without a pronoun means \"to taste, to try (food)\": ¿Puedo probar el queso? And in the imperative, the salesperson will tell you: Pruébatelo (try it on).

", "

Me queda bien: the verb quedar

To say a piece of clothing \"fits well\" or \"is too big,\" Spanish uses quedar, which works like gustar: the person is an indirect pronoun, and the verb agrees with the item of clothing.

SpanishTranslation
Esta chaqueta me queda bien.This jacket looks good on me.
La falda me queda corta.The skirt is too short on me.
Estos zapatos me quedan pequeños.These shoes are too small for me.
Los pantalones te quedan largos.The pants are too long on you.
¿Qué tal me queda?How does it look on me?
Te queda genial.It looks great on you.

The adjective agrees with the item of clothing: la falda → corta, los zapatos → pequeños. Note: me queda grande already means \"it's too big for me\"; no need for \"demasiado.\"

Los pantalones is plural in Spanish, just like \"pants\" in English: Estos pantalones me quedan bien. And don't mix it up with quedar = to meet up (¿Quedamos?): the context makes it clear.

Comparing to choose

La azul me queda mejor que la negra.The blue one looks better on me than the black one.
Este jersey es más bonito, pero es carísimo.This sweater is nicer, but it's super expensive.
", "

Este, ese, aquel, then paying and exchanging

English has \"this\" and \"that.\" Spanish has three demonstratives, depending on distance:

Near me (aquí)Near you (ahí)Far from both of us (allí)
masculine singularesteeseaquel
feminine singularestaesaaquella
masculine pluralestosesosaquellos
feminine pluralestasesasaquellas
neuterestoesoaquello

The same forms work as pronouns, with no accent: Me llevo este (I'll take this one). The neuter esto, eso, aquello refers to something you don't name: ¿Qué es esto?

Careful: este ends in -e but estos ends in -os (not \"estes\"); and aquel has no -o in the masculine singular.

Paying, returning, exchanging

SpanishTranslation
¿Cómo va a pagar? / ¿Cómo vas a pagar?How would you like to pay? (usted / tú)
Con tarjeta. / En efectivo.By card. / In cash.
¿Está rebajado?Is it on sale?
Quería devolver esta camisa.I'd like to return this shirt.
¿Tiene el ticket?Do you have the receipt?
¿Me la puede cambiar por otra talla?Can you exchange it for another size?

The big sales (las rebajas) start in Spain in early January and early July: the stores go crazy!
