es-u18-l2.title: B1 review: a real conversation
es-u18-l2.why: This big review brings together all of level B1 (opinion and the subjunctive, hypotheses, the past conditional, storytelling tenses, relative pronouns, por / para, reported speech) around a long conversation about work, life plans and a trip to Latin America. In a conversation, nobody expects perfection: people expect you to get your meaning across and keep the exchange going. But these structures make the difference between “survival” Spanish and a real B1.

Traps for English speakers

Here are the most common mistakes English speakers make at level B1. Reread your messages with this list in mind.

AvoidSayWhy
Si tendría tiempo…Si tuviera tiempo…Never the conditional after si (just like “if I would”).
Cuando llegas mañana…Cuando llegues mañana…Cuando + a future event = present subjunctive, even though English uses the plain present.
Quiero tú venir.Quiero que vengas.“I want you to…” = querer que + subjunctive.
Me dijo venir.Me dijo que viniera.A reported command = que + subjunctive.
Espero que estás bien.Espero que estés bien.Esperar que always takes the subjunctive.
Estudio por aprobar.Estudio para aprobar.Purpose (“in order to”) = para + infinitive.
El libro leo es bueno.El libro que leo es bueno.The relative que can never be dropped.
Según a el estudio…Según el estudio…Según takes no preposition, unlike “according to.”
La gente son simpáticos.La gente es simpática.La gente is feminine singular, unlike “people are.”
Conozco Marta.Conozco a Marta.A person as direct object takes the personal a.

A reflex to keep

Before conjugating, ask yourself two questions: which time (present, past linked to the present, finished past, past of the past, future) and which mood (a fact = indicative; a wish, a doubt, a future after cuando = subjunctive; a hypothesis = conditional). These two questions settle most hesitations.

", "

Keeping a conversation going

Speaking isn't just making correct sentences: it's also keeping things going, reacting and buying time. These little words bring your Spanish to life.

To…Spanish
buy timePues… / A ver… / Bueno… / ¿Cómo te diría?
keep it going¿Y tú qué opinas? / ¿Y qué pasó después? / ¿En serio?
react¡Qué envidia! / ¡No me digas! / ¡Qué fuerte! / ¡Qué bien!
add nuanceDepende. / Por un lado…, por otro… / No estoy del todo de acuerdo.
rephraseO sea… / Es decir… / Lo que quiero decir es que…

In Spain, after a meal with family or friends, people stay at the table chatting for hours: it's the sobremesa. It's the perfect moment to practice everything you've learned.

Next stop: Latin America

If you travel to Peru, Colombia or Mexico, your Spanish from Spain will be understood everywhere. A few differences worth knowing so you can understand the people you talk to:

In SpainIn Latin AmericaEnglish
vosotros tenéisustedes tienenyou (all) have
el cocheel carro, el autothe car
el móvilel celularthe cell phone
el ordenadorla computadorathe computer
conducirmanejarto drive
coger el autobústomar el autobústo take the bus

In several Latin American countries, the verb coger has a vulgar meaning. There, say tomar instead: tomar un taxi, tomar el autobús.

{"lessons": ["

We read from right to left

Hebrew is written and read from right to left. There are no capital or lowercase letters, and the alphabet, the alef-bet, has only consonants: 22 letters.

The vowels are small marks, dots and dashes, placed under or above the letters: the niqqud. Children's books and textbooks use it; newspapers and street signs almost never do. To start with, you'll always have the vowels.

שָׁלוֹםshalom: hello, goodbye, peace

The right reflex: always start with the letter furthest to the right.

", "

Your first five letters

LetterNameSound
שׁshinsh (dot at the top right)
לlamedl
מmemm
םfinal memm, at the end of a word
הhelight h, silent at the end of a word
וֹvav + doto

Five letters have a special form at the end of a word. The first one: מ becomes ם, as in שָׁלוֹם and שָׁם (there).

The trap: ה at the end of a word is not pronounced. מָה is read simply \"ma\".

", "

The vowels a and o

MarkSoundExample
מָ / מַ (a dash or a small T under the letter)a (as in father)מָה ma
לוֹ (dot on the vav)o (as in more)לוֹ lo

The vowel is read after the letter that carries it: מָ = ma. Then you put the syllables together:

שָׁ + לוֹ + םsha + lo + m = shalom

To ask how someone is: מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ? to a man, מָה שְׁלוֹמֵךְ? to a woman. Hebrew always distinguishes between a masculine \"you\" and a feminine \"you\". The answer is טוֹב, תּוֹדָה: fine, thanks.

LetterNameSound
אalefsilent: it only carries the vowel
בּbetb (with the dot)
בvetv (without the dot)
תtavt
יyody

אַ is read simply a: the letter א makes no sound at all, it just holds the vowel.

The dot in בּ is called the dagesh. It changes the sound: בּ = b, ב = v. The v in \"Tel Aviv\" is a ב without a dot.

", "

The vowel i and the family

A dot under the letter is read i (like the ee in see): מִ = mi. It's often followed by a י: מִי (who?).

אִמָּאima: mom
אַבָּאaba: dad

Israelis, adults included, call their parents this way. There is no verb \"to be\" in the present tense: you say \"dad at-the-home\".

אַבָּא בַּבַּיִת.Dad is at home. [aba ba-bayit]

בְּ (in, at) attaches to the word; with the article \"the\", it becomes בַּ: בַּבַּיִת, at home (literally \"in the house\"); בַּיָּם, at the sea.

", "

You: אַתָּה or אַתְּ?

To say \"you\", Hebrew first asks: are you talking to a man or to a woman?

HebrewPronunciationMeaning

Shabbat (שַׁבָּת) begins on Friday evening. People greet each other with שַׁבָּת שָׁלוֹם [shabbat shalom], \"a peaceful Shabbat\".

LetterNameSound

The dot in דּ (the dagesh) changes nothing: דּ and ד are always read d. Only a few letters change their sound with the dot, like בּ (b) and ב (v).

MarkSoundExample
נֵ (two dots side by side: tsere)eנֵר ner, candle

he-u02-l1.title: K, kh, and g: כּ כ ך ק ג
he-u02-l1.topic: כּ (k) and כ ך (kh); ק (k); ג (g)
he-u02-l1.why: Start of the second unit: the sounds k, kh and g, with the letter כ that changes its sound depending on the dot, and the final ך. You can finally read מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ, and you discover that the adjective comes after the noun.

{"lessons": ["

K, kh and g: five new forms

LetterNameSound
כּkafk (with the dot)
כkhafkh (without the dot)
ךfinal khafkh, at the end of a word
קkufk
גgimelg, always hard as in \"go\"

The kh sound doesn't exist in English: it's a raspy breath from the back of the throat, like the ch in Scottish \"loch\" or German \"Bach\". It's a bit like the throaty Hebrew r, only with more friction.

מֶלֶךְmelekh: king

ג is always read g, never j as in \"gem\": גְּלִידָה is read glida (ice cream), not \"jlida\".

", "

Two k's, two kh's

Like בּ / ב, the letter kaf changes its sound depending on the dot: כּ = k, כ = kh. And ק also makes k: כֶּלֶב (kelev, dog) and קָר (kar, cold) start with the same sound. Only the spelling tells them apart, like \"c\" and \"k\" in English (cat, kit): learn each word with its letter.

The final ך is always read kh. Sometimes it carries a kamats: לְךָ is read lekha (to you, to a man); לָךְ is read lakh (to you, to a woman). You can finally read מָה שְׁלוֹמְךָ? and מָה שְׁלוֹמֵךְ?.

תּוֹדָה לְךָ! / תּוֹדָה לָךְ!Thank you! (lit. thanks to you; to a man / to a woman) [toda lekha! / toda lakh!]

A famous exception: in כָּל הַכָּבוֹד (well done!), כָּל is read kol, not \"kal\". You'll hear it often in the app!

", "

Big, cold, here

The adjective goes AFTER the noun, and it agrees: כֶּלֶב גָּדוֹל (a big dog), כַּלְבָּה גְּדוֹלָה (a big female dog). Still no verb \"to be\": הַכֶּלֶב גָּדוֹל, the dog is big.

כָּאן קָר.It's cold here. [kan kar]

After הַ (the), the next letter usually takes a dot (not א or ר: הָאִישׁ): so הַכֶּלֶב is read ha-kelev, with a k. גַּן is the garden, the park… and also kindergarten!

he-u02-l2.title: Z, s, and the silent letter ע
he-u02-l2.why: Three more letters: ז, ס and ע, the second silent letter after א. You learn to point things out and ask with זֶה / זֹאת and מָה זֶה, while discovering that every Hebrew noun has a gender, which you learn along with the word.
he-u02-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Three new letters: ז, ס, ע

LetterNameSound
זzayinz
סsamekhs
עayinsilent, like א

Watch the shapes: ז looks like ו, with a little head that sticks out; ס is rounded at the bottom, while ם is square.

סוּסsus: horse
עִירir: city

Some Israelis pronounce ע from deep in the throat; most don't do anything with it. For you: it's silent.

", "

Two silent letters, two s's

You now know two silent letters: א and ע. They only carry the vowel: אִ and עִ are both read i. Between two vowels, the transliteration marks them with an apostrophe: מִסְעָדָה [mis'ada], restaurant.

For the s sound, there's ס, and another letter you'll see soon: ש with the dot on the left. Another spelling matter!

סַבָּא וְסַבְתָּאgrandpa and grandma [saba ve-savta]

In סַבְתָּא, the ב has no dot: you read savta, not \"sabta\". Israelis call their grandparents saba and savta.

", "

זֶה and זֹאת: this is…

To point something out: זֶה (ze) before a masculine word, זֹאת (zot) before a feminine word. Still no verb \"to be\". To ask, you say מָה זֶה? (what is this?).

זֶה סוּס.This is a horse. [ze sus]
זֹאת מִסְעָדָה.This is a restaurant. [zot mis'ada]

English nouns have no gender, but every Hebrew noun does, so learn it with each word: מִסְעָדָה (restaurant) is feminine, like most words ending in a. And עִיר (city) is feminine, even without a final a.

זֹאת עִיר גְּדוֹלָה.This is a big city. [zot ir gdola]

The dot at the top left of זֹ is a holam: o, as in לֹא.

he-u02-l3.title: Throat sounds and ts: ח ט צ ץ
he-u02-l3.why: Four more letters: ח, ט and the ts (צ ץ). It's time to take stock of the letters that sound the same, and to greet people depending on the time of day with טוֹב, which you can finally read in full.

{"lessons": ["

The throat and the ts: ח, ט, צ, ץ

LetterNameSound
חkhetkh, like כ without a dot
טtett, like ת
צtsadits
ץfinal tsadits, at the end of a word

Don't confuse ח and ה: in ה, the left leg doesn't touch the roof; in ח, it does.

לֶחֶםlekhem: bread
עֵץets: tree

In English, the ts sound only shows up in the middle or at the end of a word (\"cats\", \"pizza\"); in Hebrew, it's common, even at the start of a word: צִ = tsi.

", "

Letters that sound the same

SoundLettersExamples
khח כ ךחָלָב khalav, מֶלֶךְ melekh
tט תטוֹב tov, תּוֹדָה toda
kק כּקָר kar, כֶּלֶב kelev
silentא עאֶרֶץ erets, עֵץ ets
vב ותֵּל אָבִיב, דָּוִד
sס (and soon שׂ)סוּס sus

When speaking, there's no difference at all. When writing, you have to know which letter to use: it's like the f sound in English, spelled \"f\" in \"fan\" but \"ph\" in \"phone\". Learn each word with its spelling.

Under ח or ע, the shva often becomes a small a (hataf patah): חֲבֵרָה (khavera, friend, f.), the feminine of חָבֵר (khaver).

", "

Good morning, good evening, good night

טוֹב (good), which you've recognized since the first lesson, is finally fully readable. It's used to greet people depending on the time of day:

בֹּקֶר טוֹב! — בֹּקֶר אוֹר!Good morning! — Good morning! (in the morning; the reply means \"morning of light\") [boker tov! — boker or!]
עֶרֶב טוֹבgood evening [erev tov]
לַיְלָה טוֹבgood night [layla tov]

The adjective agrees: לֶחֶם טוֹב (good bread), חֲבֵרָה טוֹבָה (a good friend, f.). At the table, people say בְּתֵאָבוֹן! (enjoy your meal!); \"on the table\" is עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.

לַיְלָה (night) is masculine despite its final a: you say לַיְלָה טוֹב, never \"tova\".

he-u02-l4.title: Letters with two sounds: בּ ב, כּ כ, פּ פ ף
he-u02-l4.topic: the dagesh: בּ/ב, כּ/כ, פּ/פ; final ף
he-u02-l4.why: The letter פ, which is read p or f, lets you take stock of the dagesh, the dot that changes the sound of בּ/ב, כּ/כ and פּ/פ. You also learn to ask where something is and to order politely.

{"lessons": ["

New letter: פּ, פ and ף

LetterNameSound
פּpep (with the dot)
פfef (without the dot)
ףfinal fef, at the end of a word

פ looks like כ, with a little tongue hanging inside. Its final form ף goes down below the line, like ך and ן.

פֹּהpo: here
סֵפֶרsefer: book
כֶּסֶףkesef: money

פֹּה (po, here) and פֶּה (pe, mouth): only one vowel tells them apart! פֹּה means the same thing as כָּאן.

", "

The dagesh: a dot that changes the sound

Three letters change their sound depending on the dot (the dagesh):

LetterNameSound
בּbetb
בvetv
כּkafk
כ ךkhaf, final khafkh
פּpep
פ ףfe, final fef

A simple rule of thumb: at the start of a word, these letters almost always have the dot (b, k, p); in the middle or at the end, after a vowel, often not (v, kh, f).

פֶּה — יָפֶהpe: mouth — yafe: beautiful
כֶּלֶב — מֶלֶךְkelev: dog — melekh: king
בַּיִת — תֵּל אָבִיבbayit: house — Tel Aviv

In the other letters (דּ, תּ, גּ, מּ…), the dot doesn't change the sound: אִמָּא is read ima, פִּתָּה is read pita.

", "

Where? Here! Open, closed

אֵיפֹה הַסֵּפֶר? — פֹּה!Where is the book? — Here! [eifo ha-sefer? — po!]
הַמִּסְעָדָה פְּתוּחָה?Is the restaurant open? [ha-mis'ada ptukha?]
לֹא, הִיא סְגוּרָה.No, it's closed. [lo, hi sgura]

A small a under a final ח is read BEFORE the letter: פָּתוּחַ is read pa-tu-akh (open). In the feminine, no more trap: פְּתוּחָה, ptukha.

To order politely, add בְּבַקָּשָׁה (bevakasha, please): קָפֶה, בְּבַקָּשָׁה.

Words borrowed from other languages often keep their sound: טֶלֶפוֹן (telefon), קָפֶה (kafe). The פ without a dot really does make f.

{"lessons": ["

Shin or sin?

LetterNameSound
שׁshinsh (dot at the top right)
שׂsins (dot at the top left)

It's the same letter; only the dot changes. A trick: dot on the right (יָמִין, yamin, right) = sh; dot on the left (שְׂמֹאל, smol, left) = s. And שְׂמֹאל itself starts with a sin!

שָׁלוֹם — שָׂמֵחַshalom: hello — same'akh: happy
שֶׁמֶשׁ — עֶשֶׂרshemesh: sun — eser: ten

Without vowels (on the street, in the newspaper), nothing tells shin and sin apart: you recognize the word. And in שָׂמֵחַ, as in פָּתוּחַ, the a under the final ח is read before it: sa-me-akh.

", "

The five final letters

Five letters change their shape at the end of a word. Don't panic: the sound doesn't change.

LetterNameSound
ךfinal khafkh: מֶלֶךְ
םfinal memm: שָׁלוֹם
ןfinal nunn: גַּן
ףfinal fef: כֶּסֶף
ץfinal tsadits: עֵץ

Four of them go down below the line (ך, ן, ף, ץ); ם, on the other hand, is a closed square.

The normal form comes back as soon as the letter is no longer at the end: מֶלֶךְ but מַלְכָּה (malka, queen).

", "

The whole alef-bet

Here are the 22 letters in order. The word alef-bet comes from the names of the first two: אָלֶף, בֵּית.

א ב ג ד ה ו ז ח ט י כ ל מ נ ס ע פ צ ק ר ש תalef, bet, gimel, dalet, he, vav, zayin, khet, tet, yod, kaf, lamed, mem, nun, samekh, ayin, pe, tsadi, kuf, resh, shin, tav

With the sin, you can wish people all sorts of things:

שָׁנָה טוֹבָה!Happy New Year! (at the Jewish New Year, in the fall) [shana tova!]

שָׂמֵחַ agrees: a man says אֲנִי שָׂמֵחַ, a woman אֲנִי שְׂמֵחָה (smekha).

The 22 letters

", "

Traps to avoid

Letters that look alike: ב / כ (the bet has a little foot at the bottom right), ד / ר (corner or rounded), ה / ח (left leg detached or attached), ו / ז / ן, ס / ם.

SoundLettersExample
tת טתְּמוּנָה, טוֹב
kכּ קכֶּלֶב, קָר
khכ ך חמֶלֶךְ, לֶחֶם

sס שׂסוּס, שָׂמֵחַ
silentא עאֶרֶץ, עֵץ

The dagesh changes the sound of only three letters: בּ / ב, כּ / כ, פּ / פ. The five final forms ך ם ן ף ץ are only used at the end of a word.

For a new word, always do the same thing: letter by letter, from right to left, each letter with its vowel. צִ־פּוֹר → tsi-por, a bird.

", "

יֵשׁ and אֵין: there is, I have

יֵשׁ (yesh) means \"there is / there are\"; אֵין (ein), \"there isn't / there aren't\". With לִי (to me), it gives \"I have\": יֵשׁ לִי, literally \"there is to me\".

יֵשׁ לִי אָח וְאָחוֹת.I have a brother and a sister. [yesh li akh ve-akhot]
אֵין לִי כֶּלֶב.I don't have a dog. [ein li kelev]
יֵשׁ לְךָ חָתוּל? / יֵשׁ לָךְ חָתוּל?Do you have a cat? (to a man / to a woman) [yesh lekha khatul? / yesh lakh khatul?]

To introduce someone: זֶה אִיתַי (this is Itai), זֹאת נֹעָה (this is Noa).

Hebrew has no word for \"a\", and nothing like \"any\" after the negative: אֵין לִי כֶּלֶב, literally \"there isn't to me dog\".

he-u03-l1.why: A first step toward reading "the Israeli way": full spelling replaces some of the dots with the letters ו, י, ה and א. Each word is shown with and then without vowels, to prepare for reading without niqqud in the next lesson.
he-u03-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Reading without the dots

Open an Israeli newspaper, look at a street sign or a message on a phone: no niqqud. Israelis read without vowels, a bit like you do when you recognize \"thx\" or \"pls\" in a text message: you know the word, you don't need to see all of it.

To help the reader, spelling without vowels, full spelling (כְּתִיב מָלֵא, ktiv male), keeps or adds four letters that act as vowels: ו, י, ה and א.

With vowelsWithout vowelsSound
שָׁלוֹםשלוםshalom
תּוֹדָהתודהtoda
טוֹבטובtov
מִימיmi
הוּאהואhu

Good news: in these words, the ו for o and u, and the י for i, are already letters. When the dots go away, they stay.

Without the dots, the dagesh disappears too: ב can be read b or v, כ k or kh, פ p or f. It's the word you know that tells you: אבא is read aba, כלב is read kelev.

", "

ו and י: o, u, i

Without niqqud, the language adds a letter where there was only a dot. The o is written ו, the u is written ו, the i is often written י:

SoundWith vowelsWithout vowelsMeaning
oבֹּקֶרבוקרmorning [boker]
oנֹעָהנועהNoa [No'a]
uשֻׁלְחָןשולחןtable [shulkhan]
iסִפּוּרסיפורstory [sipur]
iעִתּוֹןעיתוןnewspaper [iton]
e (sometimes)בֵּיצָהביצהegg [beitsa]

A few exceptions: some very common little words keep their short form, לא, זאת, פה (lo, zot, po), and sometimes the i stays invisible: ישראל (Israel), עברית (ivrit, Hebrew).

The trap: a ו can be read o, u… or v! דוד is read dod (uncle) or David. And two וו in the middle of a word make a v: טלוויזיה (televizya).

", "

ה and א: a and e at the end of a word

The a and the e usually leave no trace in the middle of a word: שַׁבָּת becomes שבת, כֶּלֶב becomes כלב, יֶלֶד becomes ילד. That's where an English speaker gets stuck: all you see is three consonants. An Israeli reader adds the vowels of the word they know in their head.

At the end of a word, a silent ה or א often signals a or e:

End of wordWith vowelsWithout vowelsSound
ה = aתּוֹדָהתודהtoda
ה = aיַלְדָּהילדהyalda
ה = eקָפֶהקפהkafe
ה = eמוֹרֶהמורהmore
א = aסָבָאסבאsaba

As a result: מורה is read more (a male teacher) or mora (a female teacher). Context decides: that will be the topic of the next lesson.

The א also stays in the middle of words, always silent: מְאוֹד is written מאוד (me'od).

he-u03-l2.topic: guessing the vowels from context and word patterns
he-u03-l2.why: On to real reading without vowels, with three strategies: recognizing frequent words, spotting the prefixes ו ה ב ל מ ש, and guessing verbs from the present-tense pattern (כּוֹתֵב / כּוֹתֶבֶת). Sentences are given with and without niqqud, so you can read a menu or a sign the way people do in Israel.

{"lessons": ["

Words you recognize at a glance

An Israeli reader doesn't decode letter by letter: they recognize frequent words like pictures, exactly as you do with \"the\" or \"and\" in English. Learn them first without vowels:

Without vowelsWith vowelsMeaning
אניאֲנִיI, me [ani]
הוא / היאהוּא / הִיאhe / she [hu / hi]
זה / זאתזֶה / זֹאתthis (is), it's (m. / f.) [ze / zot]
מה / מימָה / מִיwhat? / who? [ma / mi]
כן / לאכֵּן / לֹאyes / no [ken / lo]
ישיֵשׁthere is [yesh]
טוב / מאודטוֹב / מְאוֹדgood / very [tov / me'od]

Without the dots, ש can be shin or sin: יש is read yesh, but ישראל is read yisra'el. Once again, it's the word you know that decides.

", "

Little attached words: ו ה ב ל מ ש

In Hebrew, \"and\", \"the\", \"in\", \"to\", \"from\" and \"that\" are not separate words: a single letter attaches to the front of the word. Without vowels, spot this prefix first, then read the word that's left.

PrefixMeaningWith vowelsWithout vowelsSound
וandסָבָא וְסַבְתָּאסבא וסבתאsaba ve-savta
הtheהַבַּיִתהביתha-bayit
בin, atבַּבַּיִתבביתba-bayit
לto, towardלַיָּםליםla-yam
מfromמֵהַבַּיִתמהביתme-ha-bayit
שthat, whoyou'll see it latershe

With ב and ל, the ה of \"the\" disappears: you write בבית (ba-bayit, in the house), never בהבית.

The trap: not every first letter is a prefix! In שלום, בית, לילה or מאוד, it's part of the word. If, once you remove the letter, what's left isn't a word you know, it's not a prefix.

", "

Patterns: a mold for the present tense

Many verbs in the present tense follow the same mold: a ו after the first letter, read o, then an e. In the feminine, you add a ת at the end: -et. In English, the present changes a little with the person (I write, she writes); in Hebrew, it doesn't change with the person at all, but with gender: אֲנִי לוֹמֵד (a man), אֲנִי לוֹמֶדֶת (a woman).

With vowelsWithout vowelsSoundMeaning
כּוֹתֵב / כּוֹתֶבֶתכותב / כותבתkotev / kotevetwrite(s)
לוֹמֵד / לוֹמֶדֶתלומד / לומדתlomed / lomedetlearn(s)

he-u03-l3.why: The geresh lets you write the sounds dj, j and tch, which Hebrew doesn't have, and opens the door to the many international words of everyday Israeli life. You also learn to write your own name in Hebrew, just before the big alef-bet review.

{"lessons": ["

The geresh: a little mark that changes the sound

Hebrew has no letter for the j in \"jeans\", for the s in \"pleasure\" or for the ch in \"chips\". For words from other languages, you add a little mark after the letter, the geresh (׳). In our transliteration, dj is the j of \"jeans\", j is the s of \"pleasure\", and tch is the ch of \"chips\":

LetterNameSoundExample
ג׳gimel + gereshdj, like the j in \"jeans\"גִ׳ינְס djins, jeans
ז׳zayin + gereshj, like the s in \"pleasure\"זָ׳קֶט jaket, a jacket
צ׳tsadi + gereshtch, like the ch in \"chips\"צִ׳יפְּס tchips, French fries

The vowel stays under the letter, and the geresh goes right after it: גִ׳ is read dji. Without the geresh, you get the usual sounds back: ג = g, ז = z, צ = ts.

On a phone, Israelis often type a simple apostrophe: ג'ינס. It's the same word.

", "

International words

Lots of everyday words are international: you read them, and you understand them right away.

HebrewSoundMeaning
פִּיצָהpitsapizza
טַקְסִיtaksitaxi
אוֹטוֹבּוּסotobusbus
בַּנְקbankbank
אִינְטֶרְנֶטinternetinternet
סְטוּדֶנְט / סְטוּדֶנְטִיתstudent / studentitstudent (m. / f.)
אוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָהuniversitauniversity

Where an English speaker slips up: many of these words came into Hebrew through Russian, German or other European languages, not through English. So you say מוּזִיקָה (muzika), with a z sound and a final a, and שׁוֹקוֹלָד (shokolad), with sh and a clearly pronounced final d. And a borrowed word takes the Hebrew feminine: סְטוּדֶנְטִית.

אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְטִית בָּאוּנִיבֶרְסִיטָה.I'm a student at the university. (a woman is speaking) [ani studentit ba-universita.]
", "

Your name in Hebrew

A foreign name is written the way it's pronounced, with the closest Hebrew letters. Here are some French names (like Léo's):

NameIn HebrewSound
Julieז׳וּלִיJuli: j = ז׳
Georgesז׳וֹרְז׳Jorj: ז׳ twice
CharlesשַׁרְלSharl: the French ch = שׁ
MichelמִישֶׁלMishel
LéoלֵאוֹLéo

Write what you hear, not how the name is spelled in English: in French, the ch of \"Charles\" sounds like sh, so it needs no geresh, שׁ already makes that sound. The English Charles, with the ch of \"chips\", would take tsadi + geresh; John and Jessica start with gimel + geresh (dj). The geresh is only for dj, j and tch. And the French u (in Julie) doesn't exist in Hebrew: Julie becomes \"Zhoo-lee\" [Juli].

אֲנִי ז׳וּלִי, מִפָּרִיז.I'm Julie, from Paris. [ani Juli, mi-Pariz.]

The same little mark is also used to write numbers with letters: יוֹם א׳ (yom alef) is Sunday, the first day of the Israeli week.

{"lessons": ["

The 22 letters at a glance

You now know the whole alef-bet. The most useful things to remember: the letters that sound the same, and the ones that change their sound with the dot (dagesh).

SoundLettersWatch out
silentא עonly carry the vowel
b / vבּ / בwith the dot: b; without: v
vב וtwo letters for v
kכּ קsame sound
khכ ך חsame raspy sound (like the ch in \"loch\")
p / fפּ / פ ףwith the dot: p; without: f
tת טsame sound
sס שׂsame sound; שׂ has the dot on the left
shשׁdot on the right

hהsilent at the end of a word

The five final forms, always at the end of a word: ך ם ן ף ץ. And the three sounds from elsewhere, with the geresh: ג׳ (dj), ז׳ (j), צ׳ (tch).

SoundWith niqqudWithout niqqudExample

he-u04-l1.title: Who are you? Pronouns and gender
he-u04-l1.topic: all the personal pronouns; masculine and feminine nouns
he-u04-l1.why: First lesson of level A1: you complete the set of pronouns (we, you, they, in the masculine and the feminine) and learn how to form the feminine of nouns for people. With job names, you can already say who you are and ask who someone else is, still without the verb "to be."

{"lessons": ["

All the pronouns

You already know אֲנִי, אַתָּה, אַתְּ, הוּא and הִיא. Here is the plural. Just like in the singular, Hebrew distinguishes masculine and feminine everywhere… except for \"I\" and \"we.\"

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
אֲנִיaniI, me
אַתָּה / אַתְּata / atyou (m.) / you (f.)
הוּא / הִיאhu / hihe / she
אֲנַחְנוּanakhnuwe
אַתֶּם / אַתֶּןatem / atenyou, plural (m.) / you, plural (f.)
הֵם / הֵןhem / henthey (m.) / they (f.)

English uses one \"you\" for everything; Hebrew has four: one man, one woman, several men, several women. The plural forms are only for groups: there is no formal \"you,\" so with one person you simply say אַתָּה or אַתְּ. In Israel everyone talks this way, even to the doctor or at the bank.

A mixed group takes the masculine: Avi and Noa together are הֵם. In everyday speech, many Israelis even say אַתֶּם and הֵם to a group of women.

", "

Masculine and feminine nouns

Nouns for people almost always have two forms (like actor / actress in English, but for nearly every word). You can recognize the feminine by its ending:

MasculineFeminineEnding
מוֹרֶה moreמוֹרָה moraa, written ָה
תַּלְמִיד talmidתַּלְמִידָה talmidaa, written ָה
חָבֵר khaverחֲבֵרָה khaveraa, written ָה
סְטוּדֶנְט studentסְטוּדֶנְטִית studentitit, written ִית
מֶלְצַר meltsarמֶלְצָרִית meltsaritit, written ִית
מְהַנְדֵּס mehandesמְהַנְדֶּסֶת mehandesetet, written ֶת
זַמָּר zamarזַמֶּרֶת zameretet, written ֶת

So remember: the feminine ends in a (ָה) or in t (ִית, ֶת). Sometimes a vowel changes along the way, as in מְהַנְדֵּס → מְהַנְדֶּסֶת: learn both forms together.

In the plural, the masculine ends in ִים (im) and the feminine in וֹת (ot):

חֲבֵרִים / חֲבֵרוֹתfriends (m.) / friends (f.) [khaverim / khaverot]
אֲנַחְנוּ תַּלְמִידִים.We are students. [anakhnu talmidim]
", "

Jobs: מִי אַתָּה?

No verb \"to be\" in the present, and no article before a job. English says \"I am a doctor\"; Hebrew simply says \"I doctor.\"

אֲנִי רוֹפֵא.I'm a doctor. (a man speaking) [ani rofe]
אֲנִי רוֹפְאָה.I'm a doctor. (a woman speaking) [ani rof'a]

Watch out, this is the trap for English speakers: in Hebrew, the word changes according to who is speaking. A woman says אֲנִי מוֹרָה, a man says אֲנִי מוֹרֶה.

To ask: מִי אַתָּה? to a man, מִי אַתְּ? to a woman (who are you?). And to say \"me too\": גַּם אֲנִי. The word גַּם goes before the word it goes with.

גַּם אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְטִית!Me too, I'm a student! (a woman speaking) [gam ani studentit!]

מִי אַתָּה? is direct. Among young people at a party, it's natural; otherwise, the easiest thing is to introduce yourself first: אֲנִי…, וְאַתָּה?

he-u04-l2.title: Where are you from?
he-u04-l2.topic: מֵאֵיפֹה; prefixes מִ־ בְּ־; nationalities m./f.
he-u04-l2.why: After pronouns and jobs, you learn to say where you're from and where you live, with the little attached words מִ (from) and בְּ (in). Nationalities in the masculine and feminine complete your introduction.
he-u04-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Where are you from?

You know אֵיפֹה (eifo, where?). Attach מֵ (from) to it and you get מֵאֵיפֹה (me-eifo): where from? As always, no verb: literally \"from where you?\"

מֵאֵיפֹה אַתָּה? / מֵאֵיפֹה אַתְּ?Where are you from? (to a man / to a woman) [me-eifo ata? / me-eifo at?]
אֲנִי מִצָּרְפַת, מִפָּרִיז.I'm from France, from Paris. [ani mi-tsarfat, mi-pariz]

To say where you live, learn this expression as a whole. The word גָּר is a verb: you'll see all its forms in unit 5. For now, just remember that a man says גָּר (gar) and a woman says גָּרָה (gara).

אֵיפֹה אַתָּה גָּר? / אֵיפֹה אַתְּ גָּרָה?Where do you live? (to a man / to a woman) [eifo ata gar? / eifo at gara?]
אֲנִי גָּרָה בְּתֵל אָבִיב.I live in Tel Aviv. (a woman speaking) [ani gara be-tel aviv]

To add a nuance: אֲנִי מִפָּרִיז, אֲבָל אֲנִי גָּר בְּתֵל אָבִיב. The word אֲבָל (aval) means \"but.\"

", "

Two little attached words: בְּ and מִ

English says \"in Paris,\" \"in France\" and \"from Paris,\" \"from France,\" with a separate word. Hebrew also has just one word for each idea, but it is always glued to the front of the noun, and there is never an article before a country:

PrefixMeaningExample
בְּ (be)in, at: where you areבְּתֵל אָבִיב, בְּצָרְפַת, בְּקָנָדָה
מִ (mi)from: where you come fromמִתֵּל אָבִיב, מִצָּרְפַת, מִקָּנָדָה

Look closely at מִ: it adds a dot (dagesh) to the next letter. That's why מִפָּרִיז is read mi-pariz, with a real p.

Before א, ה, ח, ע and ר, which don't take that dot, מִ becomes מֵ (me):

מֵאִיטַלְיָה, מֵחֵיפָה, מֵרוֹמָאfrom Italy, from Haifa, from Rome [me-italya, me-kheifa, me-roma]

Jerusalem gets shortened in speech: בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם is said birushalayim (in Jerusalem), and מִירוּשָׁלַיִם mirushalayim (from Jerusalem).

", "

Nationalities

Nationalities are adjectives: they agree with the person. The masculine ends in ִי (i); the feminine in ִיָּה (iya) or in ִית (it). You have to learn which one, word by word.

CountryMasculineFeminine
צָרְפַת tsarfatצָרְפָתִי tsarfatiצָרְפָתִיָּה tsarfatiya
יִשְׂרָאֵל yisra'elיִשְׂרְאֵלִי yisre'eliיִשְׂרְאֵלִית yisre'elit
אִיטַלְיָה italyaאִיטַלְקִי italkiאִיטַלְקִיָּה italkiya
גֶּרְמַנְיָה germanyaגֶּרְמָנִי germaniגֶּרְמָנִיָּה germaniya
קָנָדָה kanadaקָנָדִי kanadiקָנָדִית kanadit
אָמֶרִיקָה amerikaאֲמֵרִיקָאִי amerika'iאֲמֵרִיקָאִית amerika'it
רוֹן יִשְׂרְאֵלִי, וְנֹעָה צָרְפָתִיָּה.Ron is Israeli, and Noa is French. [Ron yisre'eli, ve-No'a tsarfatiya]

Hebrew has no capital letters: not for countries, not for names, not for nationalities (which English capitalizes). And in conversation you'll often hear israeli rather than yisre'eli.

he-u04-l3.title: Numbers from 0 to 10
he-u04-l3.topic: numbers in the feminine (for counting); phone numbers; age
he-u04-l3.why: The numbers from 0 to 10, in the form used for counting, let you give a phone number and say a child's age with בֶּן / בַּת. This is the foundation for numbers, which unit 6 will extend up to 100.
he-u04-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Counting from 0 to 10

Here are the numbers as you say them for counting, giving a phone number or an age.

NumberHebrewPronunciation
0אֶפֶסefes
1אַחַתakhat
2שְׁתַּיִםshtayim
3שָׁלוֹשׁshalosh
4אַרְבַּעarba
5חָמֵשׁkhamesh
6שֵׁשׁshesh
7שֶׁבַעsheva
8שְׁמוֹנֶהshmone
9תֵּשַׁעtesha
10עֶשֶׂרeser

The traps: four numbers start with sh (שָׁלוֹשׁ, שֵׁשׁ, שֶׁבַע, שְׁמוֹנֶה); עֶשֶׂר has a שׂ (dot on the left) that is read s; and שֵׁשׁ (6) and שֶׁבַע (7) come one after the other: don't mix them up.

Hebrew numbers also have a masculine form (אֶחָד, שְׁנַיִם…), used with masculine nouns. You'll see it later; for counting, you always use the form in this table, which is the feminine form.

", "

Your phone number

Israelis give their number digit by digit, in three groups. A cell phone number starts with אֶפֶס חָמֵשׁ (05):

אֶפֶס חָמֵשׁ שְׁתַּיִם, שָׁלוֹשׁ אַרְבַּע שֶׁבַע, אֶפֶס אַחַת תֵּשַׁע שְׁמוֹנֶה052-347-0198 [efes khamesh shtayim, shalosh arba sheva, efes akhat tesha shmone]

To ask for someone's number, learn this question as a whole; you'll understand its parts (הַ and שֶׁלְּךָ) later:

מָה הַמִּסְפָּר שֶׁלְּךָ? / מָה הַמִּסְפָּר שֶׁלָּךְ?What's your number? (to a man / to a woman) [ma ha-mispar shelkha? / ma ha-mispar shelakh?]

The word מִסְפָּר (mispar) means both \"number\" as in a phone number and \"number\" as in counting.

", "

How old are you?

In English, you \"are\" a certain age. In Hebrew, you're the \"son\" or \"daughter\" of a number of years: בֶּן (ben, son) for a boy or a man, בַּת (bat, daughter) for a girl or a woman. And כַּמָּה (kama) means \"how many / how much.\"

בֶּן כַּמָּה אַתָּה?How old are you? (to a boy) [ben kama ata?]

he-u04-l4.topic: the article הַ־; the adjective after the noun and its agreement; זֶה / זֹאת
he-u04-l4.why: The article הַ, the adjective placed after the noun, and its agreement: everything you need to describe a house, a city or people. You also learn to tell "the big house" apart from "the house is big," just before the unit review.
he-u04-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

The article: הַ

Hebrew has just one article, הַ (ha), which means \"the.\" It is glued to the front of the word. And there is no word for \"a / an\": \"a house\" is simply בַּיִת.

Without articleWith articleMeaning
בַּיִת bayitהַבַּיִת ha-bayita house / the house
דִּירָה diraהַדִּירָה ha-diraan apartment / the apartment
סְטוּדֶנְט studentהַסְּטוּדֶנְט ha-studenta student / the student
אִישׁ ishהָאִישׁ ha-isha man / the man
עִיר irהָעִיר ha-ira city / the city
רְחוֹב rekhovהָרְחוֹב ha-rekhova street / the street

Do you see the dot that appears in the letter after הַ (הַדִּירָה, הַסְּטוּדֶנְט)? Before א, ע and ר, which don't take it, the article is written הָ. Before ה and ח, it usually stays הַ, without a dot: הַחֶדֶר (the room). In every case, it's pronounced ha.

You already know the article without realizing it: בַּבַּיִת (at home) is בְּ + הַ + בַּיִת, merged into a single word.

", "

The adjective follows the noun

In English, the adjective comes before the noun: \"a big house.\" In Hebrew it's the other way around, and it's simple: the adjective always comes after the noun, \"a house big.\" And it agrees in gender and number:

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.Meaning
גָּדוֹלגְּדוֹלָהגְּדוֹלִיםגְּדוֹלוֹתbig
קָטָןקְטַנָּהקְטַנִּיםקְטַנּוֹתsmall
יָפֶהיָפָהיָפִיםיָפוֹתbeautiful
נֶחְמָדנֶחְמָדָהנֶחְמָדִיםנֶחְמָדוֹתnice, friendly
בַּיִת גָּדוֹל, דִּירָה קְטַנָּה, חֲבֵרִים נֶחְמָדִיםa big house, a small apartment, nice friends [bayit gadol, dira ktana, khaverim nekhmadim]

With the article, the adjective takes it too: literally \"the house the big.\"

הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל, הַדִּירָה הַקְּטַנָּהthe big house, the small apartment [ha-bayit ha-gadol, ha-dira ha-ktana]

English nouns have no gender, so learn each noun's gender along with the word: דִּירָה (an apartment) is feminine. And עִיר (city) is feminine even though it doesn't look it: עִיר גְּדוֹלָה.

", "

\"The house is big\" and זֶה / זֹאת / אֵלֶּה

Without the verb \"to be,\" everything depends on the article. Compare:

HebrewMeaningThe article
בַּיִת גָּדוֹלa big housenowhere
הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹלthe big houseon both words
הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל.The house is big.only on the noun

To present something: זֶה (ze) before a masculine noun, זֹאת (zot) before a feminine noun, אֵלֶּה (ele) in the plural. Here too, no article: \"this is a…\"

זֶה חֶדֶר שָׁקֵט. זֹאת עִיר יָפָה. אֵלֶּה הַשְּׁכֵנִים.This is a quiet room. This is a beautiful city. These are the neighbors. [ze kheder shaket. zot ir yafa. ele ha-shkhenim]

Hebrew has no \"it\": for things, you say הוּא or הִיא depending on the noun's gender: הַחֶדֶר? הוּא קָטָן. (The room? It's small. Literally: \"he small.\") Remember: חֶדֶר is masculine in Hebrew.

he-u04-l5.title: Review: introducing yourself
he-u04-l5.why: Review of unit 4: pronouns, gender, nationalities, numbers, the article and adjectives, all brought together in a real encounter in Tel Aviv. After this lesson, you can introduce yourself and ask the same questions; unit 5 then opens up the present tense of verbs.

Introducing yourself in a few sentences

With this unit, you can already introduce yourself fully, without a single conjugated verb (apart from the expression גָּר / גָּרָה). Pick the column that fits you:

A man saysA woman saysMeaning

אֲנִי צָרְפָתִי, מִפָּרִיז.אֲנִי צָרְפָתִיָּה, מִפָּרִיז.I'm French, from Paris.

The four reflexes of this unit: no verb \"to be\"; no word for \"a / an\"; the adjective after the noun; and everything agrees with the person, including when you're the one speaking.

To a manTo a womanMeaning

he-u05-l1.title: The present tense: four forms
he-u05-l1.topic: the present tense of regular verbs (pa'al): m. sg., f. sg., m. pl., f. pl.
he-u05-l1.why: Your first lesson on verbs: the Hebrew present tense has only four forms, depending on the gender and number of the subject, on the model of כּוֹתֵב (to write). It opens the unit "The present tense," reusing the pronouns and vocabulary from the unit "Introducing yourself."
he-u05-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Four forms, depending on gender

In English, the present changes with the person: I write, but she writes. In Hebrew, the present doesn't care about the person but about the gender and number of the subject. The result: just four forms, like an adjective.

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
אֲנִי, אַתָּה, הוּא
ani, ata, hu		אֲנִי, אַתְּ, הִיא
ani, at, hi		אֲנַחְנוּ, אַתֶּם, הֵם
anakhnu, atem, hem		אֲנַחְנוּ, אַתֶּן, הֵן
anakhnu, aten, hen
כּוֹתֵב
kotev		כּוֹתֶבֶת
kotevet		כּוֹתְבִים
kotvim		כּוֹתְבוֹת
kotvot

אֲנִי (I) appears in two columns: a man says אֲנִי כּוֹתֵב, a woman says אֲנִי כּוֹתֶבֶת. The same goes for אֲנַחְנוּ (we).

הִיא כּוֹתֶבֶת.She writes. [hi kotevet]
אֲנַחְנוּ כּוֹתְבִים.We write. [anakhnu kotvim]

The pronoun is required: כּוֹתֵב on its own could mean \"I write,\" \"you write\" or \"he writes.\" So you always say who is writing: אַתָּה כּוֹתֵב, you write (to a man).

", "

The o-e pattern

Most simple verbs have a root of three consonants: כ־ת־ב for \"write.\" In the present, you slip the vowels o and e between them: ko-te-v. Then you add the endings you already know from nouns and adjectives: -et for the feminine, -im and -ot for the plural.

Three more verbs with the same pattern: לוֹמֵד (to learn, to study), עוֹבֵד (to work), אוֹכֵל (to eat).

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
לוֹמֵד
lomed		לוֹמֶדֶת
lomedet		לוֹמְדִים
lomdim		לוֹמְדוֹת
lomdot
עוֹבֵד
oved		עוֹבֶדֶת
ovedet		עוֹבְדִים
ovdim		עוֹבְדוֹת
ovdot
אוֹכֵל
okhel		אוֹכֶלֶת
okhelet		אוֹכְלִים
okhlim		אוֹכְלוֹת
okhlot

In the plural, the middle e disappears: כּוֹתְבִים is read kotvim, not \"kotevim.\"

נֹעָה לוֹמֶדֶת עִבְרִית בָּאוּלְפָּן.Noa is learning Hebrew at the ulpan. [No'a lomedet ivrit ba-ulpan]

English chooses between \"I eat,\" \"I'm eating\" and \"I usually eat.\" Hebrew has just one present form for all three.

", "

Reading and drinking: two small differences

קוֹרֵא (to read) ends in a silent א, which stays everywhere. שׁוֹתֶה (to drink) ends in a ה: in the feminine it becomes -a, and it disappears in the plural.

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
קוֹרֵא
kore		קוֹרֵאת
koret		קוֹרְאִים
kor'im		קוֹרְאוֹת
kor'ot
שׁוֹתֶה
shote		שׁוֹתָה
shota		שׁוֹתִים
shotim		שׁוֹתוֹת

he-u05-l2.title: To live, to get up, to run
he-u05-l2.topic: the present tense of verbs with the vowel a (גָּר, קָם, רָץ)
he-u05-l2.why: Second lesson on the present tense: short verbs like גָּר (to live), which have only two consonants and the vowel a, with a feminine in -a. You use them to talk about your home and your day, reusing the four forms from the previous lesson.

{"lessons": ["

Verbs with two consonants

You already know אֵיפֹה אַתָּה גָּר? (where do you live?). גָּר belongs to a family of very short verbs: two consonants and the vowel a. Their root actually has three letters (ג־ו־ר), but the middle ו disappears in the present.

Three verbs from this family: גָּר (to live), קָם (to get up), רָץ (to run).

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
גָּר
gar		גָּרָה
gara		גָּרִים
garim		גָּרוֹת
garot
קָם
kam		קָמָה
kama		קָמִים
kamim		קָמוֹת
kamot
רָץ
rats		רָצָה
ratsa		רָצִים
ratsim		רָצוֹת
ratsot

Four forms, always by gender and number. In the plural, nothing new: -im and -ot.

The trap: here the feminine ends in -a (גָּרָה, gara), not in -et like כּוֹתֶבֶת.

", "

Coming and putting

Two more very useful short verbs: בָּא (to come, to arrive) and שָׂם (to put, to place). In בָּאָה, both א are silent: ba-a. שָׂם is written with שׂ (dot on the left), which is read s.

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
בָּא
ba		בָּאָה
ba'a		בָּאִים
ba'im		בָּאוֹת
ba'ot
שָׂם
sam		שָׂמָה
sama		שָׂמִים
samim		שָׂמוֹת
samot
הוּא בָּא מִתֵּל אָבִיב.He's coming from Tel Aviv. [hu ba mi-tel aviv]
הִיא שָׂמָה סֵפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.She puts a book on the table. [hi sama sefer al ha-shulkhan]

בָּא means both \"to come\" and \"to arrive\": אַבָּא בָּא! (Dad's here!). With הַבַּיְתָה (toward home), it means \"to come home\": אֲנִי בָּא הַבַּיְתָה, I'm coming home.

", "

My home, my day

אֲנַחְנוּ גָּרִים בְּדִירָה קְטַנָּה.We live in a small apartment. [anakhnu garim be-dira ktana]
יֵשׁ חֶדֶר, מִטְבָּח וּמִרְפֶּסֶת.There's a room, a kitchen and a balcony. [yesh kheder, mitbakh u-mirpeset]
אֲנִי קָם מֻקְדָּם בַּבֹּקֶר.I get up early in the morning (a man speaking). [ani kam mukdam ba-boker]
דָּנָה רָצָה בַּפַּארְק.Dana runs in the park. [Dana ratsa ba-park]
בָּעֶרֶב הֵם בָּאִים הַבַּיְתָה.In the evening, they come home. [ba-erev hem ba'im ha-bayta]

In Israel, almost everyone lives in an apartment, and the מִרְפֶּסֶת (balcony) is the favorite room: people have their coffee there and eat dinner there in summer.

English says \"I get up\" with two words; Hebrew uses a single short verb: אֲנִי קָם.

he-u05-l3.title: Saying no, there is, there isn't
he-u05-l3.topic: לֹא; יֵשׁ / אֵין; questions with הַאִם and intonation
he-u05-l3.why: You learn to make negative sentences with לֹא placed before the verb, to say there is or there isn't (יֵשׁ / אֵין), and to ask questions. With these tools, the present-tense sentences from the two previous lessons turn into real conversations.
he-u05-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Saying no: לֹא

You know לֹא (no). It's also used to make sentences negative, and it's simpler than in English: no \"don't\" or \"doesn't,\" no \"is not,\" just לֹא placed before the verb or adjective.

אֲנִי לֹא עוֹבֵד הַיּוֹם.I'm not working today (a man speaking). [ani lo oved ha-yom]
הִיא לֹא גָּרָה פֹּה.She doesn't live here. [hi lo gara po]
הַדִּירָה לֹא גְּדוֹלָה.The apartment isn't big. [ha-dira lo gdola]

To answer no to a question, people often say לֹא twice: לֹא, אֲנִי לֹא גָּרָה פֹּה (no, I don't live here). That's completely normal.

The trap: English puts \"not\" after \"is\" or \"do\" (\"it is not big\"). In Hebrew, לֹא goes right before the word it negates: \"the apartment not big.\"

", "

There is, there isn't: יֵשׁ, אֵין

יֵשׁ (yesh) means \"there is / there are,\" אֵין (ein) \"there isn't / there aren't.\" They never change: no gender, no number. And since there's no word for \"a,\" \"there is a balcony\" is simply \"there is balcony.\"

יֵשׁ מִרְפֶּסֶת.There's a balcony. [yesh mirpeset]
אֵין חָלָב בַּמְּקָרֵר.There's no milk in the fridge. [ein khalav ba-mekarer]
יֵשׁ פֹּה מַעֲלִית?Is there an elevator here? [yesh po ma'alit?]

You never say לֹא יֵשׁ: the opposite of יֵשׁ is אֵין.

", "

Asking a question

In speech, you just raise your voice at the end, like \"You live here?\" in casual English: אַתָּה גָּר פֹּה? (do you live here?). In careful writing, you can start with הַאִם (a question marker, a bit like \"is it the case that\"): הַאִם יֵשׁ פֹּה מַעֲלִית? The subject is never inverted, and there's no \"do\" or \"does.\"

מִיmiwho?
אֵיפֹהeifowhere?
מָתַיmataiwhen?
לָמָּהlamawhy?
אֵיךְeikhhow?
מָתַי אַתְּ קָמָה?When do you get up? (to a woman) [matai at kama?]
לָמָּה הוּא לֹא בָּא? — כִּי הוּא עוֹבֵד.Why isn't he coming? — Because he's working. [lama hu lo ba? — ki hu oved.]

The question word goes first, then you keep the normal sentence order: \"when you get up?\" To לָמָּה (why), you answer with כִּי (because).

he-u05-l4.title: I want, I like, I can
he-u05-l4.topic: רוֹצֶה, אוֹהֵב, יָכוֹל, צָרִיךְ + infinitive in לִ־
he-u05-l4.why: The verbs want, like, can and have to in the present, followed by an infinitive in לִ־: everything you need to say what you want, like, can or have to do. The infinitives of the unit's verbs are learned here as vocabulary, just before the review.

{"lessons": ["

Want, like, can, have to

These four verbs follow the present-tense rule: four forms, depending on gender and number. רוֹצֶה (to want), אוֹהֵב (to like, to love), יָכוֹל (can, to be able to), צָרִיךְ (to have to, to need to).

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
רוֹצֶה
rotse		רוֹצָה

rotsim		רוֹצוֹת
rotsot
אוֹהֵב
ohev		אוֹהֶבֶת
ohevet		אוֹהֲבִים
ohavim		אוֹהֲבוֹת
ohavot
יָכוֹל

yekhola		יְכוֹלִים
yekholim		יְכוֹלוֹת
yekholot
צָרִיךְ
tsarikh		צְרִיכָה
tsrikha		צְרִיכִים
tsrikhim		צְרִיכוֹת

רוֹצֶה is conjugated like שׁוֹתֶה (final ה), and אוֹהֵב like כּוֹתֵב, with a small a in the plural: אוֹהֲבִים, ohavim.

יָכוֹל and צָרִיךְ have their own pattern: learn their four forms by heart. They have no everyday infinitive; in the exercises, you're given their root (י־כ־ל, צ־ר־ך).

", "

+ the infinitive in ל

As in English, these verbs are followed by an infinitive: \"I want to eat\" = אֲנִי רוֹצֶה לֶאֱכֹל. The Hebrew infinitive starts with ל, a bit like English \"to,\" and it never changes.

InfinitivePronunciationMeaning

לִקְרֹאlikroto read
לִשְׁתּוֹתlishtotto drink
לִישֹׁןlishonto sleep
לֶאֱכֹלle'ekholto eat
לַעֲבֹדla'avodto work
לָגוּרlagurto live
לָקוּםlakumto get up
לָבוֹאlavoto come
לָלֶכֶתlalekhetto go, to walk
לְדַבֵּרledaberto speak

The basic pattern: לִ + the root with o: לִכְתֹּב, לִלְמֹד. Before א or ע, the vowel changes: לֶאֱכֹל, לַעֲבֹד. The short verbs from lesson 2 take לָ: לָגוּר, לָבוֹא. Learn the others as they are.

", "

Saying what you like

הִיא אוֹהֶבֶת לִקְרֹא.She likes to read. [hi ohevet likro]
אֲנַחְנוּ צְרִיכִים לַעֲבֹד הַיּוֹם.We have to work today. [anakhnu tsrikhim la'avod ha-yom]
אַתָּה יָכוֹל לָבוֹא בָּעֶרֶב?Can you come this evening? (to a man) [ata yakhol lavo ba-erev?]
אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצָה לָקוּם!I don't want to get up! (a woman speaking) [ani lo rotsa lakum!]

אוֹהֵב and רוֹצֶה can also take a noun: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב קָפֶה (I like coffee), אֲנִי רוֹצָה תֵּה (I want tea). For a taste in general, Hebrew uses no article, just like English: \"I like coffee.\"

Only the first verb agrees: הֵן רוֹצוֹת לֶאֱכֹל, they (f.) want to eat. The infinitive stays the same for everyone, and לֹא goes before the first verb.

he-u05-l5.title: Review: the present tense
he-u05-l5.why: Review of the unit "The present tense": the four forms of regular verbs and short verbs, negation, יֵשׁ / אֵין, questions, and the modal verbs. You reuse all of it to describe your day, before moving on to everyday life.

{"lessons": ["

The present tense at a glance

Four forms, depending on the gender and number of the subject, never on the person. So the pronoun is required, and a mixed group takes the masculine plural.

m. sg.f. sg.m. pl.f. pl.
כּוֹתֵב
kotev		כּוֹתֶבֶת
kotevet		כּוֹתְבִים
kotvim		כּוֹתְבוֹת
kotvot
שׁוֹתֶה
shote		שׁוֹתָה
shota		שׁוֹתִים
shotim		שׁוֹתוֹת
shotot
גָּר
gar		גָּרָה
gara		גָּרִים
garim		גָּרוֹת
garot
יָכוֹל
yakhol		יְכוֹלָה
yekhola		יְכוֹלִים
yekholim		יְכוֹלוֹת
yekholot

Three patterns to recognize: the o-e pattern (כּוֹתֵב, feminine in -et), verbs ending in ה (שׁוֹתֶה, רוֹצֶה, feminine in -a) and the short verbs (גָּר, קָם, בָּא, feminine in -a). יָכוֹל and צָרִיךְ are in a class of their own.

If you're a woman, all your sentences switch to the feminine: אֲנִי קָמָה, שׁוֹתָה, עוֹבֶדֶת. If you're a man: אֲנִי קָם, שׁוֹתֶה, עוֹבֵד.

", "

No, there is, questions

לֹא goes right before the verb or adjective. יֵשׁ (there is) and אֵין (there isn't) never change. For a question, you raise your voice, or put the question word first: מָה, מִי, אֵיפֹה, מָתַי, לָמָּה, אֵיךְ.

אֲנִי לֹא יָכוֹל לָבוֹא, כִּי אֲנִי עָסוּק.I can't come, because I'm busy. [ani lo yakhol lavo, ki ani asuk]
אֵין זְמַן!There's no time! [ein zman!]
מָתַי אַתֶּם אוֹכְלִים?When do you (pl.) eat? [matai atem okhlim?]

Adjectives like עָיֵף (tired) and עָסוּק (busy) also agree: אֲנִי עֲיֵפָה, I'm tired (a woman speaking). Still with no verb \"to be.\"

", "

Describing your day

With בַּבֹּקֶר (in the morning), בַּצָּהֳרַיִם (at noon), בָּעֶרֶב (in the evening), בַּלַּיְלָה (at night) and אַחַר כָּךְ (then, afterward), you can describe a whole day in the present. Here is Noa's:

כָּל יוֹם אֲנִי קָמָה מֻקְדָּם וְשׁוֹתָה קָפֶה.Every day, I get up early and drink a coffee. [kol yom ani kama mukdam ve-shota kafe]
בַּבֹּקֶר אֲנִי עוֹבֶדֶת, וּבַצָּהֳרַיִם אֲנִי אוֹכֶלֶת פִּתָּה.In the morning I work, and at noon I eat a pita. [ba-boker ani ovedet, u-va-tsohorayim ani okhelet pita]
אַחַר כָּךְ אֲנִי לוֹמֶדֶת עִבְרִית בָּאוּלְפָּן.Then I study Hebrew at the ulpan. [akhar kakh ani lomedet ivrit ba-ulpan]
בָּעֶרֶב אֲנִי אוֹהֶבֶת לִקְרֹא, אֲבָל בַּלַּיְלָה אֲנִי צְרִיכָה לִישֹׁן!In the evening I like to read, but at night I have to sleep! [ba-erev ani ohevet likro, aval ba-layla ani tsrikha lishon!]

Before ב, מ or פ, \"and\" is וּ (u): וּבַצָּהֳרַיִם, and at noon. Elsewhere, it's וְ (ve): וְשׁוֹתָה.

he-u06-l1.title: "To have" in Hebrew: יֵשׁ לִי
he-u06-l1.topic: יֵשׁ לִי / אֵין לִי; ל־ with pronouns (לִי, לְךָ, לָךְ…)
he-u06-l1.why: In Hebrew, "to have" is expressed with יֵשׁ (there is) and the preposition לְ: this lesson teaches you "I have, I don't have" and all the forms לִי, לְךָ, לָךְ… It opens the unit "Everyday life," right after the present tense, with everyday objects and pets.
he-u06-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

No verb \"to have\"

Hebrew has no verb \"to have.\" To say \"I have,\" it takes יֵשׁ (there is), which you already know, and adds לִי (to me): literally, \"there is to me.\"

יֵשׁ לִי כֶּלֶב.I have a dog. [yesh li kelev]

For the negative, יֵשׁ becomes אֵין (there isn't):

אֵין לִי מְכוֹנִית.I don't have a car. [ein li mekhonit]

Watch out: there's no \"don't,\" no \"a\" and no \"any.\" You simply say \"there isn't to me car.\" And never לֹא יֵשׁ: the negative of יֵשׁ is always אֵין.

A question is asked with intonation alone: יֵשׁ לְךָ כֶּלֶב? — כֵּן, יֵשׁ לִי. / לֹא, אֵין לִי.

", "

לְ with pronouns: לִי, לְךָ, לָךְ…

The preposition לְ (to) fuses with the pronoun and takes an ending. Just as with \"you,\" there is one form for a man and one for a woman.

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
לִיlito me
לְךָlekhato you (to a man)
לָךְlakhto you (to a woman)
לוֹloto him
לָהּlato her
לָנוּlanuto us
לָכֶםlakhemto you, plural (men or a mixed group)
לָכֶןlakhento you, plural (women)
לָהֶםlahemto them (m.)
לָהֶןlahento them (f.)

Trap: לוֹ (to him) and לֹא (no) are both pronounced \"lo.\" In speech, the meaning decides; in writing, look at the last letter.

לֹא, אֵין לוֹ זְמַן.No, he doesn't have time. [lo, ein lo zman]

Before a name, לְ is attached too: לְנֹעָה יֵשׁ חָתוּל. (Noa has a cat.) The final ה of לָהּ has a dot (the mappiq): it doesn't change the sound, \"la.\"

", "

My things, my pets

What you own doesn't change יֵשׁ at all: it stays the same for masculine, feminine and plural. Only the adjective agrees, with the object.

יֵשׁ לָהּ מְכוֹנִית חֲדָשָׁה.She has a new car. [yesh la mekhonit khadasha]
יֵשׁ לָנוּ כֶּלֶב גָּדוֹל וַחֲתוּלָה קְטַנָּה.We have a big dog and a little female cat. [yesh lanu kelev gadol va-khatula ktana]

Two everyday expressions: אֵין לִי זְמַן (I don't have time) and אֵין בְּעָיָה (no problem: here without לְ, \"there's no problem\").

Without לְ, יֵשׁ means \"there is\": יֵשׁ חָתוּל בַּבַּיִת (there's a cat in the house). With לְ, it means \"to have\": יֵשׁ לִי חָתוּל (I have a cat).

he-u06-l2.title: Family and "my, your"
he-u06-l2.why: The possessives שֶׁלִּי, שֶׁלְּךָ, שֶׁלָּךְ… are built on the same endings as לִי, לְךָ, which you saw in the previous lesson. You also learn the family words so you can introduce your own family.
he-u06-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Whose? שֶׁל

שֶׁל means \"of,\" in the sense of belonging: הַכֶּלֶב שֶׁל נֹעָה (Noa's dog, literally \"the dog of Noa\"). To ask whose something is: שֶׁל מִי זֶה? (whose is it?)

With pronouns, שֶׁל takes the same endings as the לִי, לְךָ, לָךְ… you've just learned:

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
שֶׁלִּיshelimy, mine
שֶׁלְּךָshelkhayour, yours (to a man)
שֶׁלָּךְshelakhyour, yours (to a woman)
שֶׁלּוֹshelohis
שֶׁלָּהּshelaher, hers
שֶׁלָּנוּshelanuour, ours
שֶׁלָּכֶםshelakhemyour, plural (men or a mixed group)
שֶׁלָּכֶןshelakhenyour, plural (women)
שֶׁלָּהֶםshelahemtheir (m.)
שֶׁלָּהֶןshelahentheir (f.)
שֶׁל מִי זֶה? זֶה שֶׁלִּי.Whose is this? It's mine. [shel mi ze? ze sheli]
", "

\"My house\": the house of mine

The possessive goes after the noun, and the noun takes the article הַ: הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי, literally \"the house of mine.\" Without the article, בַּיִת שֶׁלִּי would rather mean \"a house of mine.\"

הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי גָּדוֹל.My house is big. [ha-bayit sheli gadol]

The good news: two things work just like English:

  • שֶׁלִּי doesn't change with the object, just like \"my\": הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי (my house), הַדִּירָה שֶׁלִּי (my apartment), הַיְלָדִים שֶׁלִּי (my children).
  • \"His\" and \"her\" depend on the owner, not on the object: הַבַּיִת שֶׁלּוֹ (his house), הַבַּיִת שֶׁלָּהּ (her house). Exactly as in English.

With אַבָּא and אִמָּא, Israelis often drop the article: אַבָּא שֶׁלִּי, אִמָּא שֶׁלִּי. Both are fine.

", "

The family

MasculineFeminineMeaning
אַבָּאאִמָּאDad / Mom [aba / ima]
אָחאָחוֹתbrother / sister [akh / akhot]
סָבָאסַבְתָּאgrandfather / grandmother [saba / savta]
דּוֹדדּוֹדָהuncle / aunt [dod / doda]
בֵּןבַּתson / daughter [ben / bat]
יֶלֶדיַלְדָּהboy / girl, child [yeled / yalda]
בַּעַלאִשָּׁהhusband / wife [ba'al / isha]

he-u06-l3.topic: ordering politely; prices; numbers from 11 to 100
he-u06-l3.why: Ordering at a café, asking a price at the market and counting up to 100: everything you need to get by in the most common situations in Israel. The lesson reuses the present of רוֹצֶה and the numbers from 0 to 10.

{"lessons": ["

Ordering politely

In Israel, people order very directly: אֲנִי רוֹצֶה… (a man) or אֲנִי רוֹצָה… (a woman), \"I want.\" With בְּבַקָּשָׁה (please), it's perfectly polite: no need for \"I'd like\" or \"could I have.\"

אֲנִי רוֹצָה קָפֶה הָפוּךְ, בְּבַקָּשָׁה.I'd like a latte, please. [ani rotsa kafe hafukh, bevakasha]

Another very common phrase: אֶפְשָׁר…? (\"is it possible?\") followed by what you want. It never changes, for men and women alike.

אֶפְשָׁר כּוֹס מַיִם?Can I have a glass of water? [efshar kos mayim?]

The waiter asks עוֹד מַשֶּׁהוּ? (anything else?). You answer זֶה הַכֹּל, תּוֹדָה (that's all, thanks).

קָפֶה הָפוּךְ, literally \"upside-down coffee,\" is the frothy milky coffee, a kind of latte, that people drink all over Israel.

", "

Numbers from 11 to 100

From 11 to 19: the unit, slightly shortened, then עֶשְׂרֵה (esre), a bit like \"-teen\" in English. The tens end in ־ִים, like a plural: עֶשְׂרִים (20) comes from עֶשֶׂר (10).

NumberHebrewPronunciation
11אַחַת עֶשְׂרֵהakhat esre
12שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵהshtem esre

14אַרְבַּע עֶשְׂרֵהarba esre
15חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵהkhamesh esre

17שְׁבַע עֶשְׂרֵהshva esre

19תְּשַׁע עֶשְׂרֵהtsha esre
20עֶשְׂרִיםesrim
30שְׁלוֹשִׁיםshloshim
40אַרְבָּעִיםarba'im
50חֲמִשִּׁיםkhamishim
60שִׁשִּׁיםshishim

100מֵאָהme'a

For 21, 35, 42…, the tens come first, as in English, but joined with \"and\": \"twenty and one.\" עֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת (21), שְׁלוֹשִׁים וְחָמֵשׁ (35), אַרְבָּעִים וּשְׁתַּיִם (42: before a shva, וְ becomes וּ, \"u\").

These are the counting forms, like 0 to 10. They're also used for age, with בֶּן as well as with בַּת: הוּא בֶּן עֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת, הִיא בַּת עֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת (he / she is 21).

", "

At the market: how much is it?

At the שׁוּק (shuk, the market), the key question: כַּמָּה זֶה עוֹלֶה? (how much is it?). You can also name the product: כַּמָּה עוֹלֶה קִילוֹ עַגְבָנִיּוֹת? (how much is a kilo of tomatoes?).

The currency is the שֶׁקֶל (shekel), plural שְׁקָלִים (shkalim), symbol ₪. In speech, after a number, Israelis often keep the singular:

זֶה עוֹלֶה עֶשְׂרִים שֶׁקֶל.It costs twenty shekels. [ze ole esrim shekel]

To react: יָקָר! (that's expensive!) or זוֹל! (cheap!). The adjective agrees: הַתַּפּוּחַ יָקָר (the apple is expensive), הָעוּגָה יְקָרָה (the cake is expensive): in Hebrew, apple is masculine and cake is feminine, so learn the gender with each noun!

No \"of\" between the quantity and the product: קִילוֹ עַגְבָנִיּוֹת, literally \"a kilo tomatoes.\"

he-u06-l4.topic: telling time; days of the week (יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן…); Shabbat
he-u06-l4.why: Days numbered starting from Sunday, the Israeli weekend, and telling time with the numbers you already know. With יֵשׁ לִי זְמַן, you can now set up a meeting.

{"lessons": ["

The days: first, second…

In Hebrew, the days of the week have no names: they're numbered starting from Sunday, with יוֹם (day) followed by an ordinal number. Only Saturday has a real name: שַׁבָּת.

DayHebrewPronunciationWord for word
Sundayיוֹם רִאשׁוֹןyom rishonfirst day
Mondayיוֹם שֵׁנִיyom shenisecond day
Tuesdayיוֹם שְׁלִישִׁיyom shlishithird day
Wednesdayיוֹם רְבִיעִיyom revi'ifourth day
Thursdayיוֹם חֲמִישִׁיyom khamishififth day
Fridayיוֹם שִׁשִּׁיyom shishisixth day
SaturdayשַׁבָּתshabatShabbat

The Israeli weekend (סוֹף שָׁבוּעַ, \"end of week\") is Friday and Saturday; יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן (Sunday) is a working day: many people work מִיּוֹם רִאשׁוֹן עַד יוֹם חֲמִישִׁי (from Sunday to Thursday; עַד, ad = until). On Friday evening, many families have dinner together, and people wish each other שַׁבָּת שָׁלוֹם.

\"On Monday,\" \"on Mondays\": בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי (be-yom sheni). To ask what day it is: אֵיזֶה יוֹם הַיּוֹם? — הַיּוֹם יוֹם שְׁלִישִׁי. (Today is Tuesday.)

", "

What time is it?

מָה הַשָּׁעָה? (ma ha-sha'a?), word for word \"what the hour?\" You answer הַשָּׁעָה + the number, with no verb \"to be.\" The word שָׁעָה (hour) is feminine, so you use the counting forms you already know.

הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ.It's three o'clock. [ha-sha'a shalosh]
HebrewPronunciationTime
הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ וְעֶשֶׂרha-sha'a shalosh ve-eser3:10
הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ וָרֶבַעha-sha'a shalosh va-reva3:15
הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִיha-sha'a shalosh va-khetsi3:30
הַשָּׁעָה רֶבַע לְאַרְבַּעha-sha'a reva le-arba3:45 (\"a quarter to four\")

\"At three o'clock\": בְּשָׁלוֹשׁ (be-shalosh), with בְּ attached to the number. In speech, people count from 1 to 12 and add the time of day: עֶשֶׂר בַּלַּיְלָה (ten in the evening).

In וָחֵצִי and וָרֶבַע, \"and\" is written with an a: va-khetsi, va-reva. You'll also hear ve-khetsi.

", "

Morning, noon, evening and night

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
בֹּקֶרbokermorning
צָהֳרַיִםtsohorayimnoon, early afternoon
עֶרֶבerevevening
לַיְלָהlaylanight

\"In the morning,\" \"in the evening\": the article and בְּ merge into בַּ or בָּ. Learn these four expressions as they are: בַּבֹּקֶר, בַּצָּהֳרַיִם, בָּעֶרֶב, בַּלַּיְלָה.

אֲנִי קָם בְּשֶׁבַע בַּבֹּקֶר.I get up at seven in the morning. [ani kam be-sheva ba-boker]

In צָהֳרַיִם, the vowel under ה (a hataf kamats) is read o: tso-ho-ra-yim. And for greetings: בֹּקֶר טוֹב (good morning), עֶרֶב טוֹב (good evening), לַיְלָה טוֹב (good night).

he-u07-l1.title: Where is…?
he-u07-l1.topic: אֵיפֹה; directions (יָשָׁר, יָמִינָה, שְׂמֹאלָה); places in town
he-u07-l1.why: First lesson of the "In Town" unit: asking where a place is, understanding directions, and saying whether it's near or far. It reuses יֵשׁ, the article, and adjective agreement from units 4 and 5.
he-u07-l1.json:
{"lessons": ["

Excuse me, where is…?

To stop someone in the street, you start with סְלִיחָה (slikha, excuse me), then ask your question with אֵיפֹה (eifo, where?). As always in the present tense, there is no verb \"to be\": you say \"where the-bank?\"

סְלִיחָה, אֵיפֹה הַבַּנְק?Excuse me, where is the bank? [slikha, eifo ha-bank?]

Looking for a bank, any bank? Then you ask whether there is one, with יֵשׁ:

סְלִיחָה, יֵשׁ פֹּה בַּנְק?Excuse me, is there a bank here? [slikha, yesh po bank?]
אֵיפֹה יֵשׁ מִסְעָדָה?Where is there a restaurant? [eifo yesh mis'ada?]

Watch out: \"where is a restaurant?\" doesn't work in Hebrew any more than it does in English. With the article הַ, it's a specific place; without the article, you use יֵשׁ (\"is there…?\").

", "

Straight ahead, right, left

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
יָשָׁרyasharstraight ahead
יָמִינָהyaminato the right (rightward)
שְׂמֹאלָהsmolato the left (leftward)
וְאָזve'azand then, next
לְיַדleyadnext to

The final ה of יָמִינָה and שְׂמֹאלָה shows direction: \"toward the right,\" \"toward the left.\" In שְׂמֹאלָה, the dot on the left makes an s (sin) and the א is silent: you simply say \"smola.\"

יָשָׁר, וְאָז יָמִינָה.Straight ahead, and then right. [yashar, ve'az yamina.]
הַבַּנְק לְיַד הַשּׁוּק.The bank is next to the market. [ha-bank leyad ha-shuk.]

Israelis often give directions with no verb at all: \"straight ahead, and then left.\" These little words are all you need.

", "

Is it near or far?

קָרוֹב (near) and רָחוֹק (far) are adjectives: they agree with the place, like גָּדוֹל / גְּדוֹלָה.

MasculineFeminine
nearקָרוֹב karovקְרוֹבָה krova
farרָחוֹק rakhokרְחוֹקָה rekhoka
הַשּׁוּק קָרוֹב, וְהַתַּחֲנָה רְחוֹקָה.The market is near, and the stop is far. [ha-shuk karov, ve-ha-takhana rekhoka.]

With זֶה, you stay in the masculine: זֶה קָרוֹב? (is it near?). For distance, people count in minutes, using the number forms you already know: חָמֵשׁ דַּקּוֹת בָּרֶגֶל (five minutes on foot).

And if you don't know? אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ (a man) / אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדַעַת (a woman): I don't know. Or אֲנִי לֹא מִפֹּה: I'm not from here.

Every Israeli town has its שׁוּק (market): it's often the best landmark when you ask for directions.

he-u07-l2.topic: the prepositions בְּ־ לְ־ מִ־ with the article (בַּ־ לַ־ מֵהַ־); transportation
he-u07-l2.why: You learn to combine בְּ, לְ and מִ with the article (בַּ, לַ, מֵהַ), where Hebrew fuses "in the," "to the," and "from the" into a single word, plus the vocabulary of transportation. It's the foundation for taking the bus or the train in the next lessons.

{"lessons": ["

In the, to the: בַּ־ and לַ־

English keeps \"in\" and \"the\" as two separate words. Hebrew merges them: when בְּ (in, at) or לְ (to, toward) meets the article הַ, the ה disappears and the preposition takes its vowel.

Preposition + articleResultMeaning
בְּ + הַבַּיִתבַּבַּיִת ba-bayitat home (in the house)
בְּ + הַשּׁוּקבַּשּׁוּק ba-shukat the market (inside)
לְ + הַיָּםלַיָּם la-yamto the sea (direction)
לְ + הַתַּחֲנָהלַתַּחֲנָה la-takhanato the stop (direction)

The dot inside the letter (בַּשּׁוּק) stays, just as after הַ. If the article is הָ (before א, ע, ר), the preposition also takes ָ: הָעִיר → בָּעִיר (in town), לָעִיר.

Without the article, the preposition keeps its shva: בְּבַנְק (in a bank), לְחֵיפָה (to Haifa). Before another shva, it becomes בִּ / לִ: לִירוּשָׁלַיִם (lirushalayim, to Jerusalem).

", "

From the: מֵהַ־

מִ (from, since) is the exception: it doesn't swallow the article. It becomes מֵ and the הַ stays.

אֲנִי בָּא מֵהַתַּחֲנָה.I'm coming from the stop. [ani ba me-ha-takhana.]
מֵהַשּׁוּק לַיָּם זֶה עֶשֶׂר דַּקּוֹת.From the market to the sea, it's ten minutes. [me-ha-shuk la-yam ze eser dakot.]

Without the article, you already know it: מִפָּרִיז, מִתֵּל אָבִיב. To sum up: בַּ = in the, לַ = to the, toward the, מֵהַ = from the.

For transportation, Hebrew says \"in the bus\": בָּאוֹטוֹבּוּס (by bus), בָּרַכֶּבֶת (by train), בְּמוֹנִית (by taxi).

", "

The רַב־קַו is the rechargeable card valid throughout the country; drivers generally no longer sell tickets. In most cities, buses and trains don't run during Shabbat, from Friday afternoon to Saturday evening.

he-u07-l3.title: Coming and going
he-u07-l3.topic: הוֹלֵךְ, נוֹסֵעַ, בָּא, חוֹזֵר in the present
he-u07-l3.why: The four verbs of movement in the present, telling apart going on foot (הוֹלֵךְ) and going by vehicle (נוֹסֵעַ), with לְאָן and time words. You reuse the four present-tense forms from unit 5 and the prepositions from the previous lesson.
he-u07-l3.json:
{"lessons": ["

Going: on foot or by vehicle?

In English, you just \"go\" everywhere. Hebrew first asks how: on foot, it's הוֹלֵךְ; by bus, train, or car, it's נוֹסֵעַ.

on foot (לָלֶכֶת)by vehicle (לִנְסֹעַ)
m. sg.הוֹלֵךְ holekhנוֹסֵעַ nose'a
f. sg.הוֹלֶכֶת holekhetנוֹסַעַת nosa'at
m. pl.הוֹלְכִים holkhimנוֹסְעִים nos'im
f. pl.הוֹלְכוֹת holkhotנוֹסְעוֹת nos'ot

These are the four forms you already know (כּוֹתֵב, כּוֹתֶבֶת…). The little dash (a) under the final ע of נוֹסֵעַ is read just before it: nose-a.

אֲנִי הוֹלֶכֶת לַשּׁוּק, וְהוּא נוֹסֵעַ לְחֵיפָה.I'm going to the market (on foot), and he's going to Haifa. [ani holekhet la-shuk, ve-hu nose'a le-Kheifa.]

The destination takes לְ: לַשּׁוּק, לְחֵיפָה, לִירוּשָׁלַיִם. The one very common exception: הַבַּיְתָה (habayta), \"home,\" with the direction ה you saw in יָמִינָה.

", "

Coming and coming back

to come (לָבוֹא)to come back, return (לַחֲזֹר)
m. sg.בָּא baחוֹזֵר khozer
f. sg.בָּאָה ba'aחוֹזֶרֶת khozeret
m. pl.בָּאִים ba'imחוֹזְרִים khozrim
f. pl.בָּאוֹת ba'otחוֹזְרוֹת khozrot
הִיא חוֹזֶרֶת הַבַּיְתָה מֵהָעֲבוֹדָה.She's coming home from work. [hi khozeret habayta me-ha-avoda.]

English gets by with \"where,\" adding \"to\" or \"from\" at the end of the sentence; Hebrew has three separate words: אֵיפֹה? (where are you?), לְאָן? (where are you going to?), מֵאֵיפֹה? (where are you from?).

לְאָן אַתָּה נוֹסֵעַ?Where are you going? (to a man) [le'an ata nose'a?]

The trap: using אֵיפֹה for a destination. If you're moving, it's לְאָן.

", "

Now, today, tomorrow

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
עַכְשָׁוakhshavnow
הַיּוֹםhayomtoday
מָחָרmakhartomorrow

he-u07-l4.title: Asking politely
he-u07-l4.topic: אֶפְשָׁר…?; בְּבַקָּשָׁה; the everyday imperative (תַּגִּיד, תַּגִּידִי)
he-u07-l4.why: With no formal "you," Hebrew is polite in other ways: אֶפְשָׁר, תּוּכַל / תּוּכְלִי and a few soft imperatives learned as set phrases. This lesson prepares the role-play in the review.
he-u07-l4.json:
{"lessons": ["

No formal \"you\": how do you stay polite?

Like English, Hebrew has no formal \"you\": you speak the same way to everyone, the driver, the shop assistant, your boss. Politeness comes from the way you ask. The magic word: אֶפְשָׁר…? (efshar, \"is it possible?\").

אֶפְשָׁר מַיִם, בְּבַקָּשָׁה?Could I have some water, please? [efshar mayim, bevakasha?]

Followed by an infinitive, אֶפְשָׁר is used to ask permission, with no pronoun and no agreement:

אֶפְשָׁר לָשֶׁבֶת פֹּה?Can I sit here? [efshar lashevet po?]
סְלִיחָה, אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲבֹר?Excuse me, can I get by? [slikha, efshar la'avor?]
אֶפְשָׁר לָרֶדֶת בַּתַּחֲנָה הַבָּאָה?Can I get off at the next stop? [efshar laredet ba-takhana ha-ba'a?]

בְּבַקָּשָׁה means \"please,\" but also \"you're welcome\" when someone thanks you, and \"here you go\" when you hand something over.

", "

Could you…? Tell me…

As in English (\"could you help me?\"), you soften a request with תּוּכַל (to a man) / תּוּכְלִי (to a woman) + infinitive:

תּוּכַל לַעֲזֹר לִי?Could you help me? (to a man) [tukhal la'azor li?]
תּוּכְלִי לְדַבֵּר לְאַט?Could you speak slowly? (to a woman) [tukhli ledaber le'at?]

To say \"come\" or \"wait,\" Israelis very often use a future form instead of the imperative, which sounds softer. For now, learn them as set phrases; for a woman, you add ִי.

To a manTo a womanMeaning
תַּגִּיד tagidתַּגִּידִי tagiditell (me)
תָּבוֹא tavoתָּבוֹאִי tavo'icome
תְּחַכֶּה רֶגַע tekhake regaתְּחַכִּי רֶגַע tekhaki regawait a moment

תַּגִּיד… at the start of a sentence is the \"tell me…\" that opens a question: תַּגִּיד, אֵיפֹה הַתַּחֲנָה?

", "

Thanks, sorry, no problem

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
תּוֹדָה רַבָּהtoda rabathank you very much
בְּבַקָּשָׁהbevakashaplease; you're welcome
אֵין בְּעָיָהein be'ayano problem
סְלִיחָהslikhasorry, excuse me
אֲנִי לֹא מֵבִין / מְבִינָהani lo mevin / mevinaI don't understand (m. / f.)
עוֹד פַּעַם?od pa'am?one more time?
סְלִיחָה, אֲנִי לֹא מְבִינָה. עוֹד פַּעַם, לְאַט?Sorry, I don't understand. One more time, slowly? [slikha, ani lo mevina. od pa'am, le'at?]

Israelis speak fast and directly: it isn't rudeness. Don't hesitate to ask for לְאַט (slowly): you'll often hear אֵין בְּעָיָה in reply.

Finding your way in town

To…HebrewPronunciation

On a Jerusalem bus

Two names you need to get around Jerusalem. They are nouns followed by an adjective, with the article on both words, like הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל:

הַתַּחֲנָה הַמֶּרְכָּזִיתthe central bus station [ha-takhana ha-merkazit]
הָרַכֶּבֶת הַקַּלָּהthe light rail (\"the light train\") [ha-rakevet ha-kala]

Usually you get on at the front, tap your רַב־קַו near the driver, and don't hesitate to ask the driver to let you know: תּוּכַל לְהַגִּיד לִי?

he-u08-l1.title: The past tense of regular verbs
he-u08-l1.why: First lesson of level A2: after the four-form present, you discover the past tense, which is conjugated with person endings. It's the foundation of any story: your day, your weekend, a trip.

{"lessons": ["

One past tense, with endings

Good news: Hebrew has only one past tense. Where English chooses between \"I wrote,\" \"I have written,\" \"I was writing,\" and \"I used to write,\" Hebrew always says כָּתַבְתִּי [katavti].

In the present, the verb only changed for gender and number (כּוֹתֵב, כּוֹתֶבֶת, כּוֹתְבִים, כּוֹתְבוֹת). In the past, it changes for person (I, you, he, we…): you add an ending to the base כָּתַב [katav], \"he wrote.\" English verbs don't do this, but the system is very regular.

כָּתַבhe wrote: the base, with no ending [katav]
כָּתַבְתִּיI wrote: the base + ti [katavti]

The past base, כָּתַב, is the \"he\" form: it's also the form you find in dictionaries. Its three consonants כ ת ב make up the root, which you also find in כּוֹתֵב and לִכְתֹּב.

", "

The full table

PronounPastPronunciationEnding
אֲנִיכָּתַבְתִּיkatavti־תִּי (ti)
אַתָּהכָּתַבְתָּkatavta־תָּ (ta)
אַתְּכָּתַבְתְּkatavt־תְּ (t)
הוּאכָּתַבkatavnone
הִיאכָּתְבָהkatvaa (final ה)
אֲנַחְנוּכָּתַבְנוּkatavnu־נוּ (nu)
אַתֶּםכְּתַבְתֶּםktavtem־תֶּם (tem)
אַתֶּןכְּתַבְתֶּןktavten־תֶּן (ten)
הֵם / הֵןכָּתְבוּkatvuוּ (u)

Three things to notice:

  • I and we don't change for gender: a woman and a man both say כָּתַבְתִּי. In the present, it was כּוֹתֵב / כּוֹתֶבֶת.
  • You, however, does change: כָּתַבְתָּ [katavta] to a man, כָּתַבְתְּ [katavt] to a woman.
  • They (m.) and they (f.) share the same form: הֵם כָּתְבוּ, הֵן כָּתְבוּ. With הִיא and הֵם, the second vowel drops out: כָּתְבָה [katva], כָּתְבוּ [katvu].

For אַתֶּם, you'll often hear [katavtem] on the street; [ktavtem] is the correct form, the one used in books and on the radio.

", "

The pronoun: optional or required?

The ending already tells you who did the action: unlike English, but as in Spanish or Italian, the pronoun is optional in the 1st and 2nd person.

לָמַדְתִּי עִבְרִית בָּאוּלְפָּן.I studied Hebrew at the ulpan. [lamadti ivrit ba-ulpan]
כְּבָר אָכַלְתָּ?Have you eaten yet? (to a man) [kvar akhalta?]

In the 3rd person, no ending says \"he\" or \"they\": keep the pronoun or the subject.

הוּא עָבַד כָּל הַיּוֹם.He worked all day. [hu avad kol ha-yom]

Negation doesn't change: לֹא before the verb. עוֹד לֹא גָּמַרְתִּי. I haven't finished yet. [od lo gamarti]

With אָכַל and עָבַד, which begin with א or ע, the shva of \"you\" (plural) becomes a short a: אֲכַלְתֶּם [akhaltem], עֲבַדְתֶּם [avadtem]. Everything else follows the table of כָּתַב.

he-u08-l2.title: The past tense of verbs with the vowel a
he-u08-l2.topic: the past tense of גָּר, קָם, בָּא
he-u08-l2.why: Short verbs like גָּר, קָם or בָּא have a very simple past tense: the vowel a stays and you add the endings from the previous lesson. With them, you can tell about your morning, from waking up to arriving at the office.
he-u08-l2.json:
{"lessons": ["

Short verbs in the past

You know the short verbs with the vowel a in the present: גָּר (to live), קָם (to get up), רָץ (to run), בָּא (to come), שָׂם (to put). In the past, they're even simpler than כָּתַב: you keep the base and add the same endings (־תִּי, ־נוּ, ־תֶּם…).

קַמְתִּי בְּשֵׁשׁ.I got up at six. [kamti be-shesh]
גַּרְנוּ בְּחֵיפָה.We used to live in Haifa. [garnu be-Kheifa]

The trap: with הוּא and הִיא, the past is written just like the present! הוּא גָּר בְּחֵיפָה can mean \"he lives\" or \"he lived\" in Haifa. Context and time words (הַבֹּקֶר, קֹדֶם…) decide. With הֵם, there's no confusion: גָּרוּ (past), גָּרִים (present). In speech, stress helps too: in the past, הִיא קָמָה is stressed on \"ka,\" in the present on \"ma.\"

", "

The tables

Pronounto liveto get upto runto put

אַתָּהגַּרְתָּ gartaקַמְתָּ kamtaרַצְתָּ ratstaשַׂמְתָּ samta
אַתְּגַּרְתְּ gartקַמְתְּ kamtרַצְתְּ ratstשַׂמְתְּ samt
הוּאגָּר garקָם kamרָץ ratsשָׂם sam
הִיאגָּרָה garaקָמָה kamaרָצָה ratsaשָׂמָה sama
אֲנַחְנוּגַּרְנוּ garnuקַמְנוּ kamnuרַצְנוּ ratsnuשַׂמְנוּ samnu
אַתֶּםגַּרְתֶּם gartemקַמְתֶּם kamtemרַצְתֶּם ratstemשַׂמְתֶּם samtem
אַתֶּןגַּרְתֶּן gartenקַמְתֶּן kamtenרַצְתֶּן ratstenשַׂמְתֶּן samten

Before an ending that starts with a consonant, the kamats of the base becomes a patah: גָּר → גַּרְתִּי. Both are read a: you won't hear any difference.

As with כָּתַב, I and we are the same for a man and a woman: קַמְתִּי; you changes: קַמְתָּ [kamta] to a man, קַמְתְּ [kamt] to a woman.

he-u08-l3.title: Yesterday, last week
he-u08-l3.topic: time expressions for the past; telling events in order
he-u08-l3.why: The words that place a story in time: yesterday, the day before yesterday, last week, a year ago, then, in the end. With them and the past tense of הָלַךְ, נָסַע and חָזַר, you can tell about a weekend from start to finish.

{"lessons": ["

Placing a story in the past

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
אֶתְמוֹלetmolyesterday
אֶתְמוֹל בָּעֶרֶבetmol ba-erevlast night, yesterday evening
שִׁלְשׁוֹםshilshomthe day before yesterday
בְּסוֹף הַשָּׁבוּעַbe-sof ha-shavu'athis weekend, on the weekend
בַּשָּׁבוּעַ שֶׁעָבַרba-shavu'a she-avarlast week
בַּחֹדֶשׁ שֶׁעָבַרba-khodesh she-avarlast month
בַּשָּׁנָה שֶׁעָבְרָהba-shana she-avralast year

שֶׁעָבַר means \"that has passed\": it's the verb עָבַר (to pass) in the past tense! So it agrees with the noun: שָׁבוּעַ and חֹדֶשׁ are masculine → שֶׁעָבַר; שָׁנָה is feminine → שֶׁעָבְרָה. English \"last\" never changes, so this takes a little attention.

אֶתְמוֹל בָּעֶרֶב לָמַדְתִּי.Last night, I studied. [etmol ba-erev lamadti]

In Israel, the work week starts on Sunday: on Sunday morning at the office, everyone talks about their סוֹף שָׁבוּעַ (weekend, literally \"end of the week\").

", "

\"Ago\": לִפְנֵי comes first (and it isn't יֵשׁ!)

English puts \"ago\" after the amount of time; Hebrew puts לִפְנֵי (before) in front of it: \"a year ago\" is literally \"before a year.\" Don't reach for יֵשׁ (\"there is\") here: it has nothing to do with time.

לִפְנֵי שָׁנָה גַּרְתִּי בְּפָרִיז.A year ago, I lived in Paris. [lifnei shana garti be-Pariz]
הוּא חָזַר לִפְנֵי שָׁבוּעַ.He came back a week ago. [hu khazar lifnei shavu'a]
בָּאנוּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל לִפְנֵי שָׁלוֹשׁ שָׁנִים.We came to Israel three years ago. [banu le-Yisra'el lifnei shalosh shanim]

To tell things in order: קֹדֶם or בְּהַתְחָלָה (first, at the beginning), אַחַר כָּךְ (then, afterward), וְאָז (and then, so), בַּסּוֹף (in the end).

קֹדֶם אָכַלְנוּ, אַחַר כָּךְ הָלַכְנוּ לַיָּם, וּבַסּוֹף חָזַרְנוּ הַבַּיְתָה.First we ate, then we went to the sea, and in the end we went back home. [kodem akhalnu, akhar kakh halakhnu la-yam, u-va-sof khazarnu ha-bayta]

הַבַּיְתָה [ha-bayta] means \"toward home\": you use it with verbs of movement, without לְ, just like \"go home\" in English with no \"to.\" To be at home, it's always בַּבַּיִת.

", "

Good news: הוֹלֵךְ, נוֹסֵעַ, and חוֹזֵר (unit 7) are regular in the past, following the model of כָּתַב.

הִיאהָלְכָה halkhaנָסְעָה nas'aחָזְרָה khazra
אֲנַחְנוּהָלַכְנוּ halakhnuנָסַעְנוּ nasanuחָזַרְנוּ khazarnu

Remember: הָלַךְ on foot; נָסַע by bus, train, or car. For \"you\" (plural), the first vowel weakens, as in כְּתַבְתֶּם: הֲלַכְתֶּם, נְסַעְתֶּם, חֲזַרְתֶּם.

נָסַעַתְּ (you left, to a woman) takes an extra short a because of the final ע: [nasa'at]. In speech, many people just say [nasat].

he-u08-l4.title: "To be" and "to have" in the past
he-u08-l4.why: The verb "to be," missing in the present, really does exist in the past: הָיִיתִי, הָיָה, הָיְתָה… With it, you can say where you were, what it was like, and what you had (הָיָה לִי), making it agree with the thing you had.

{"lessons": ["

\"To be\" in the past: הָיָה

In the present, there's no verb \"to be\": אֲנִי בַּבַּיִת. In the past, it shows up: הָיִיתִי בַּבַּיִת (I was at home). It takes the endings you know, with an i before the ending. The verb עָשָׂה (to do, to make) follows exactly the same pattern.

Pronounto beto do
אֲנִיהָיִיתִי hayitiעָשִׂיתִי asiti
אַתָּההָיִיתָ hayitaעָשִׂיתָ asita
אַתְּהָיִית hayitעָשִׂית asit
הוּאהָיָה hayaעָשָׂה asa
הִיאהָיְתָה haytaעָשְׂתָה asta
אֲנַחְנוּהָיִינוּ hayinuעָשִׂינוּ asinu
אַתֶּםהֱיִיתֶם heyitemעֲשִׂיתֶם asitem
אַתֶּןהֱיִיתֶן heyitenעֲשִׂיתֶן asiten
הֵם / הֵןהָיוּ hayuעָשׂוּ asu

As always in the past, I doesn't change for gender: a man and a woman both say הָיִיתִי. Never say אֲנִי הָיָה or אֲנִי הָיְתָה! The question you'll hear everywhere: מָה עָשִׂיתָ? (to a man), מָה עָשִׂית? (to a woman), what did you do?

For \"you\" (plural), you'll often hear [hayitem] in conversation; [heyitem] is the careful form. And שָׁתִיתִי קָפֶה (I drank a coffee) [shatiti kafe] also follows the pattern of הָיִיתִי.

", "

What was it like?

To describe something, הָיָה agrees with the subject, like an adjective:

הַטִּיּוּל הָיָה מְעֻלֶּה.The trip was excellent. [ha-tiyul haya me'ule]
הַדִּירָה הָיְתָה קְטַנָּה.The apartment was small. [ha-dira hayta ktana]
הַחֲבֵרִים הָיוּ נֶחְמָדִים.The friends were nice. [ha-khaverim hayu nekhmadim]

With no subject, for \"it was,\" you use הָיָה (masculine singular). Where English says \"it was hot,\" Hebrew simply says \"was hot,\" with no \"it.\"

אֵיךְ הָיָה? — הָיָה כֵּיף, אֲבָל הָיָה חַם!How was it? — It was great, but it was hot! [eikh haya? — haya kef, aval haya kham!]

And the past of יֵשׁ / אֵין? הָיָה again, agreeing with whatever existed: הָיוּ שָׁם הַרְבֵּה אֲנָשִׁים (there were a lot of people), לֹא הָיָה מָקוֹם (there was no room).

", "

\"To have\" in the past: הָיָה לִי

You know that \"to have\" is יֵשׁ לִי, literally \"there is to me.\" In the past, יֵשׁ becomes הָיָה… and it agrees with the thing you have, not with the owner. English has nothing like this, so watch out!

The thing ownedHebrewPronunciationMeaning
masculineהָיָה לִי כֶּלֶבhaya li kelevI had a dog
feminineהָיְתָה לִי מְכוֹנִיתhayta li mekhonitI had a car
pluralהָיוּ לִי חֲבֵרִיםhayu li khaverimI had friends

The owner changes with לְ + suffix, as in the present: הָיָה לָנוּ, הָיְתָה לָהּ, הָיוּ לָהֶם… Negation: לֹא הָיָה לִי זְמַן (I didn't have time).

הָיְתָה לָנוּ חֻפְשָׁה מְעֻלָּה.We had an excellent vacation. [hayta lanu khufsha me'ula]

In conversation, you'll sometimes hear הָיָה לִי even before a feminine noun. Still, learn the agreement: it's the correct form, the one expected in writing.

he-u09-l1.why: After the past, here is the future tense of regular verbs: four prefixes to remember and three endings, so you can talk about your plans. It's the gateway to the "Plans and the Future" unit, which will then add the near future, compound nouns, and pi'el.
